text:
The 0500 bell sends a low vibration through the stone walls of the Measured Scholars' dormitory. You open your eyes to the familiar grey ceiling, its cracks mapped in your memory like the trade routes on your study charts.

Your name is Vael. Junior Field Evaluator, Measured Scholars. Twenty-three years old and already trusted with district-level field assessments. You are good at what you do: observation, calculation, the patient art of finding where the cost actually went. The less patient art of finding truth in people has, so far, never featured in the formal curriculum.

The morning air carries the sharp mineral smell of alchemical fuel blocks burning in the city's infrastructure converters—the deep machinery that keeps Orvish's water, heat, and structural maintenance running. Through the narrow window, the spires of the upper city catch the first pale light while the lower districts still sleep beneath a blanket of industrial haze. It is, from this safe altitude, almost picturesque.

Your field kit sits open on the desk: three pre-inscribed diagnostic plates, a pouch of chalk, calipers and stress gauges, and a sealed case holding your Tier 2 fuel blocks. Enough for several days of serious assessment if you ration honestly. Your ledger lies open beside it, unfinished calculations waiting patiently for the version of you that will inevitably be too tired to finish them.
choice2_label: Look out the window at the waking city first.
choice3_label: Go back to sleep. The anomaly can wait.

text:
You stand at the narrow window. Below the Scholar's Quarter, the city of Orvish unfolds in layers.

The upper terraces gleam with white stone and polished brass—the Coordinated Exchange Authority's administrative towers, the academies, the stone assembly halls where the Revolutionary Council holds its public sessions. Their buildings hold their shape because they are properly maintained with high-quality fuel and skilled circle work. You can see, even from here, the difference: clean joints, true lines, no visible patching.

Even from up here, things are not equal. There are those in the upper terrace who trained in the Valdmere Realm before its political troubles, who return now with credentials the republic struggles to officially recognize and unofficial connections it cannot ignore. You have never had occasion to think about them. Today is probably not the day either.

Orvish is the republic's largest port city — not the capital (that's Caldren, far to the northeast, where the Revolutionary Council holds court over problems it can barely see from this distance), but the city where trade actually happens. Where materials flow in and decisions about those materials flow out. Where the distance between an infrastructure commission memo and a collapsing seawall is exactly as long as it takes for a requisition to get lost in transit.

Below that, the working districts descend in concentric rings toward the waterfront. Then the industrial zone, then the lower docks. The buildings get rougher as you go down—timber reinforced with cheaper bonding paste, walls shored up with improvised circle work, the subtle sag of structures running on inadequate fuel.

At the very bottom, pressed against the grey water of the bay, lies Karet Bay. Its skyline is irregular in the way of places that have been repaired many times without the materials to do it properly.

Karet Bay has a particular history. Three generations ago, a trade consortium redirected the bay's freshwater inlet using large-scale alchemical flow manipulation. The port access improved. Then, over the following decade, the freshwater supply failed, the fisheries died, the drinking water collapsed, and tens of thousands of people were displaced.

The consortium's position was that the economic gains outweighed the cost.

The courts disagreed.

The legal principle that followed—environmental harm classified as harm to people—is cited in every environmental assessment you've been trained to file. You have cited it three times. You have never stood in the district it describes.

You will stand in it on this deployment—not as a single afternoon's errand, but as field work that may take more than one day to earn its answers.
choice1_label: Get dressed and check your assignment.
choice2_label: Lean out for a closer look at the lower docks.

text:
In the common hall, Senior Scholar Mireth is already seated behind a desk stacked with incident reports. She is a thin woman with ink-stained fingers and the expression of someone who has been awake since before the bell and intends to make that everyone else's problem.

'Vael,' she says without looking up. 'Field assignment. Karet Bay lower docks, loading district. A harbor crane is operating at twenty-three percent above its rated structural load capacity. The maintenance circle logs show no authorized reinforcement work in the past four months. The fuel allocation records show normal consumption. Nothing explains the numbers.'

She slides a folder across the desk.

'Either the instruments are wrong, or someone has bonded an unauthorized circle to critical load-bearing infrastructure without proper materials or training.' She finally looks at you. 'You know what the Hollow Tower looked like before it fell? Performing fine. Nothing visible wrong. Passed two inspections. Right up until it didn't.'

She pauses. 'This is routine. Observe, calculate, file what the evidence supports.'

Another pause, shorter, harder to read.

'Preliminary findings within a few days. A full report when the numbers justify one—not when the calendar does.'

'And Vael—don't get creative down there.'

She glances at a second folder on the stack. 'Scholar Nev is doing a material audit for the harbor authority three streets from your assessment site. You may run into each other. Nev has been in the field longer than you have. Try not to learn the wrong lessons.'
choice1_label: Understood. Preliminary findings in a few days; full report when justified.
choice2_label: Is there anything else I should know about the district?

text:
Mireth is quiet for a moment. She sets down her pen.

'I've been doing this work for nineteen years,' she says. 'Karet Bay is the third time I've seen this pattern. A district's material allocation gets quietly adjusted—officially, with paperwork—and six months later we're getting anomaly reports from the field. There's always a justification. The justification always sounds reasonable. The field reports never do.'

She's not reading from anything. This isn't briefing language.

She passed her senior field evaluator assessment on her second attempt—she mentioned it once, years ago, without self-pity. Nineteen years of accurate field reports, careful citations, and formally correct recommendations. She has spent her career doing the right work through the right channels. She has watched the channels deliver outcomes like this three times.

'I don't know what you'll find down there,' she says. 'The numbers in that folder are clean. What generates numbers like that is not usually clean.' She picks up her pen again. 'Your job is to assess the crane. That's all I'm asking you to do.'

She looks at you for a beat too long. 'You're good at this work, Vael. That's why I'm sending you. Just—don't forget that good work isn't the same as right work. Those are different things.'

You're not entirely sure what she means by that. You're also not sure she is. The examination system teaches you to see clearly. What to do with what you see—that part, apparently, is self-study.
choice1_label: Take the folder and head out.

text:
You collect your field kit and run through the checklist before heading out.

Three pre-inscribed plates: a diagnostic circle for reading ambient energy distribution, a structural stress assessment circle for mapping load patterns, and a basic reinforcement circle for stabilization work. The plates are Tier 2 copper-alloy, properly maintained. They'll hold for a dozen activations each before the inscribed patterns begin to degrade. Your chalk is for single-use circles when the plates aren't suited to a specific task.

The sealed fuel block case holds three standard Tier 2 blocks—enough for six to eight serious alchemical operations. Clean-burning, reliable, the industrial standard. Down in Karet Bay, you're guessing they'll be working with Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials. The kind that burns wasteful and fails delayed, the way cheap things always fail: not dramatically, not immediately, but later, and worse.

The CEA inspector's authorization—the small brass seal that marks you as a Measured Scholar on official business—goes into your inner pocket. It opens certain doors. It closes others.

The Scholar's Quarter sits on the second terrace, halfway between the gleaming upper city and the industrial sprawl below. The walk to Karet Bay takes you through progressively grimmer streets, each ring down another step away from the world you understand and into the world you've only ever assessed from a distance.
choice1_label: Descend toward the lower docks directly.
choice2_label: Stop at the market terrace for supplies.
choice3_label: Review your field plates before setting out.

text:
You pause in the courtyard and open your plate case, running through the function of each component. Old habit, drilled by your first assessment mentor: you don't enter a field site without knowing exactly what tools you're carrying and what they cost to use.

A circle doesn't provide energy—that's the first thing they teach you, and the first thing most people forget. A circle is a blueprint, a set of instructions. It defines what transformation is allowed and how energy flows through the material. Without fuel, a circle is a drawing. Without you—your own energy to initiate and guide the reaction—the fuel just sits inert. Every alchemical act requires all three: the circle, the fuel, and the person holding it together.

Your diagnostic plate activates with a half-block of fuel and moderate personal output. It reads ambient energy distribution in structures and materials, tells you where work has been done and whether it's degrading. The stress assessment plate costs more—a full block and significant personal energy—but it maps internal load patterns precisely. Worth the cost for structural assessments. This is the tool that catches Hollow Tower failures before they happen.

Your reinforcement plate is the practical one: strengthen an existing joint, stabilize a failing circle, buy time for proper repair. Two blocks and real personal effort. Your structural specialization makes you efficient here—a medical alchemist doing this same work would waste more and get dirtier results.

You close the case. Three blocks. Six to eight operations before you're running on your own reserves.

You have never needed more than that. You think about Mireth's expression when she handed you the folder, and hope that remains true today.

The market terrace sits at the boundary between the comfortable middle districts and the industrial zone below. Vendors sell everything from alchemical components to breakfast pastries, and the air smells of frying oil and copper dust. It's lively in the specific way that places are lively when they exist specifically for people passing through.

A weathered woman selling tonics catches your eye. Her stall displays rows of small glass bottles filled with amber liquid—energy tonics, the kind that dock workers use to push through double shifts. They have the general aesthetic of something you'd find in a drain, which does not appear to be deterring anyone.

'Scholar, eh?' she says, noting your ledger. 'Heading down to the docks? You'll want one of these. The air down there eats at you.' She pauses. 'Not figuratively. Well. Also figuratively.'

She quotes a price. It's cheap. The tonics are crude but functional—a chemical preparation that stabilizes and slightly boosts the body's own reserves, delaying the fatigue that comes from extended self-fueled alchemical work. The label says: DO NOT INGEST IF EXPERIENCING DISTORTION, PREGNANCY, OR OPINIONS.

Further along the terrace, a heavyset woman with Freehands circle-marks on both wrists is selling salvaged construction material from a folding table: reclaimed Tier 1 bolts, repurposed bonding paste, copper tubing straightened and cleaned. The sign on the table reads: BRIN'S BITS. FAIR EXCHANGE OR LEAVE. She is in the middle of explaining to a teenage boy why his offer is—her exact word—'mathematically offensive.' She makes the explanation sound less like a refusal and more like an education. The boy leaves with the copper tubing at a better price and the expression of someone who has just been outmaneuvered and possibly improved.
choice1_label: Buy an energy tonic and continue.
choice2_label: Decline politely and continue.

text:
The descent into Karet Bay is a lesson in erosion—both geological and moral. The white stone of the upper terraces gives way to grey brick, then patched concrete, then raw timber and corrugated metal sheeting. The streets narrow. The infrastructure hum deepens, grating the way rope does when it runs through a block filmed with grit.

You pass workers bound for the morning shift—calloused hands, eyes flat with quota arithmetic. Some glance at your ledger and look away. Others never register you at all. Given what their mornings cost, that is fair enough.

Halfway down, a stone plaque: IN RECOGNITION OF THE DROWNING OF KARET BAY. Beneath it, three sentences in the tongue of historical reckoning—the consortium, the redirected river, the freshwater lost. You know the case from study and have cited it in reports. The street knows it from breath and metered cups.

On the same wall, smaller cut: EIGHTY YEARS SINCE THE SUNDERING. EIGHTY YEARS OF BUILDING WHAT MAGIC DESTROYED. Civic pride on stone, until you look at what you are walking toward.

The district boundary wears a faded sign: KARET BAY LOWER DOCKS — CEA OPERATIONAL ZONE 7.

Beside it, a narrow doorway marked HARBOR LOGISTICS — COORDINATOR SENNA. Through the glass, a woman shuttles between stacks of manifests with the brittle speed of someone holding a schedule that stopped fitting the work months ago. She catches your eye once and snaps her gaze off—a reflex learned where Scholar attention becomes delay, then paperwork.

Chalk below: SOMEONE ALWAYS PAYS.

Below that, another hand, dock-rough: THE UPPER BERTHS STAY DRY.

Pinned between a labor quota sheet and a water ration, a pamphlet on rough stock, careful ink. Header: YEAR EIGHTY. *Year Zero, we buried the nobility for making others pay for their ease. Eighty years later, the council class keeps warm offices and revolutionary portraits. Someone tell me what changed.* No signature.

The smell reaches you—brine, machine oil, sour venting where improvised circles burn cheap fuel wrong. The pavement shivers under overtaxed lines. The hum here is not melody; it is a structure that has been mended so often it no longer recalls its first true note.

Two men shout by the entrance—who eats the cost of a botched reinforcement. Upstairs that becomes a registry complaint. Down here it becomes lung capacity and witnesses. Three workers watch. In Caldris, arguing in the street passes for civic virtue. Here it is ordinary weather.
choice1_label: Head directly to the loading crane.
choice2_label: Stop and take ambient readings before going further.

text:
You press your diagnostic plate to a load-bearing wall at the district entrance and feed it a half-block of fuel from your own reserves. The metal warms; the scan runs; the plate pulses, reads, dims. Old habit: you read the baseline before you chase a single spike, so you know whether what you're looking at is an isolated incident or part of a larger pattern.

The numbers are wrong. Not instrument-wrong—the plate is functioning correctly. The district's embedded maintenance circles are running at roughly forty percent of their designed operating capacity.

Not because they've failed. Because they've been starved. The fuel reserves that should be feeding them have been depleted. Without fuel, the circles are dormant. Without the circles doing their maintenance work, the structural integrity of every building in this district relies on the raw materials alone. And the raw materials in Karet Bay are Tier 1 at best.

You make careful notes. The buildings around you show the signs: hairline fractures in load-bearing walls, slight warping in metal fixtures, a persistent low groan from foundations under invisible stress. Someone has been using improvised patch work—Tier 0 and Tier 1 bonding paste, single-use circles drawn in chalk on untreated surfaces by people who know enough to help and not enough to know when to stop. It holds for now. It always holds for now.

The problem is always later.

Everyone in Caldris knows what later looks like. They have a name for it. You learned the name in your second year of training. It was called the Hollow Tower, and it killed three hundred people who had been assured that everything was fine.

The lower docks stretch before you: a chaotic sprawl of warehouses, loading platforms, and heavy machinery pressed against the grey water of the bay. Massive cranes line the waterfront like iron sentinels, their arms swinging loads of raw material from cargo ships to waiting transport carts. The noise is extraordinary—chains, pulleys, the deep thrum of alchemically reinforced machinery doing what it was designed for—and everyone moves within it like they can't hear it at all.

Your target is Crane Seven, a forty-year-old loading crane that handles ore shipments from the mining barges. Even from a distance, you can see something is different about it. While the other cranes groan and shudder under their loads—operating near stress limits, using their structural capacity the way you'd use muscles you haven't stretched properly—Crane Seven moves with an almost fluid grace, swinging three-ton ore crates as though its rated capacity had been quietly renegotiated upward.

A crew of dock workers operates the crane's base controls. Their foreman—a broad-shouldered man with burn scars on both forearms—watches the operation with the focused tension of someone who has been waiting for something to go wrong long enough that waiting has become a kind of job in itself.
choice1_label: Approach the foreman directly and show your authorization.
choice2_label: Observe the crane from a distance first and take readings.
choice3_label: Talk to some of the other workers before approaching.
choice4_label: A younger worker at the crew's edge is writing in a pocket notebook. Step over before you speak to the foreman.

text:
The dock workers pause for their mid-morning water break, settled on crates and coils of rope in the brief window before the quota clock starts running again. You approach and sit nearby—Scholar's ledger visible, but not open. No one wants to talk to a ledger.

The woman closest to you has a Freehand circle-mark tattooed on her forearm—a small reinforcement pattern, rough but genuine work. She glances at you, then back at the bay.

'You're here about Crane Seven,' she says. Not a question.

'The readings were anomalous.'

'Everything here is anomalous.' She takes a long drink of water. 'We've been running Crane Seven past its rated load for six months. Everyone knows. Nobody acts. The quota gets met, so the quota gets met.' She sets down the cup. 'You know why we can't get it properly maintained? The maintenance budget—the Tier 2 fuel blocks that used to keep this whole waterfront in good order—got redirected seven months ago. Someone in the upper city needed something built. We were the somewhere it came from.'

'That's a serious allegation.'

She looks at you with the patience of someone who has said a true thing to a doubtful person many times before. 'Go ask the crane what it thinks about allegations.' She stands as the break ends. 'You're a Scholar. If you find where the cost actually went, tell someone who has the power to care about it.'

She doesn't say it with bitterness. Just with the steady exhaustion of someone still doing the work anyway.

You find a spot behind a stack of cargo crates where you can observe without being noticed. Opening your field kit, you activate your stress assessment plate, feeding a full Tier 2 block into it and drawing from your personal reserves to guide the reading.

The crane's structural profile is immediately wrong in a way that takes you a moment to parse.

Standard cranes are designed for specific load limits—the engineering accounts for material fatigue, joint stress accumulation, the physics of repeated heavy lifting over decades. Crane Seven's readings show reinforced joint structures where there shouldn't be any. Someone has bonded additional structural support to the crane's primary load-bearing assembly. The reinforcement is real and technically competent—Level 2 reinforcement work—and it explains how the crane is handling 123% of its rated load without visible distress.

But your plate reads something else too. The bonding material used is Tier 1—basic, improvised, the kind that dock workers can mix from common hardware materials. Tier 1 paste works. It degrades. Under repeated heavy stress, the reinforcement circle drawn into that paste will develop micro-fractures that don't show on the surface but compound with every load cycle.

You sketch the analysis in your ledger. The reinforcement is degrading. Your calculations show the pivot joint's structural integrity is already at sixty-three percent of rated capacity. At the current load rate, it will reach critical failure threshold sometime this afternoon.

When it fails, three tons of ore will drop on whoever is standing below.

You look at the workers moving underneath the crane arm like they have four hundred times this week, like they will four hundred more times before the month is out. They have no idea.
choice1_label: Approach the foreman with your findings.
choice2_label: Burn another spare fuel block on a redundant confirmatory scan—extravagant, but the numbers will survive Toris.

text:
You shouldn't. You do anyway. A second Tier 2 block feeds the plate; your ledger fills with curves that agree with the first pass down to the third decimal wherever physics allows.

Overkill is sometimes kindness to future you—the version who will swear to these readings in rooms that smell like incense and budgets.

The joint degradation looks uglier at higher resolution. You almost wish it didn't.

You pack the kit away lighter in fuel and heavier in certainty.
choice1_label: Approach Kaelen with the reinforced file.

text:
The foreman sees you coming. His eyes drop to your ledger, then to the brass authorization seal at your collar, and his jaw tightens in the specific way that means he's already calculating what this is going to cost him.

'Scholar,' he says flatly. Not a greeting. A warning to the crew behind him.

'I'm Vael, Measured Scholars. I'm here about anomalous readings from Crane Seven.' You keep your voice neutral, professional.

'Name's Kaelen.' He doesn't offer his hand. 'The crane works fine. Better than fine. We're ahead of quota for the first time in three months, which is the first time in three months anyone in this district has had anything to be ahead of.'

Behind him, his crew has stopped working. Six men and women, watching you with the particular attention of people whose livelihoods are standing in the gap between your ledger and your pen. You notice the youngest—barely fifteen, lanky in the way of someone who hasn't finished growing into their shoulders—gripping a wrench so hard his knuckles are white. He has the eyes of someone watching something he can't stop.
choice1_label: I can see there's been work done on it. Show me what you did.
choice2_label: This crane is going to fail. I need to understand why, before someone gets hurt.
choice3_label: Step back, drink your energy tonic, then re-approach while you can still feel your face.
choice4_label: Flash your seal and order the crew to stand down immediately.

text:
You turn away for sixty seconds—long enough to crack the tonic vial and swallow something that tastes like copper, stabilizers, and spite. The label warned you about opinions. It did not warn you about foremen.

When you walk back to Kaelen, your hands steadier, he notices anyway. Dock workers always notice who came back different.
choice1_label: I can see there's been work done on it. Show me what you did.
choice2_label: This crane is going to fail. I need the full picture before someone gets hurt.
choice3_label: Flash your seal and order the crew to stand down immediately.

text:
Kaelen's face hardens. 'Nothing is going to fail. I reinforced every joint myself. Spent six nights on it after shift.'

'You're not a trained structural alchemist.'

'And you've never held quota with half your equipment decommissioned.' He steps closer, dropping his voice. 'You want to know what happened to our maintenance allocation? Ask the CEA. The Tier 2 fuel blocks that used to keep this crane's maintenance circles running got officially redirected seven months ago. Not our decision. Not something we were even told until a month after the fact. That material came from Grenvor—the Highland refineries. Took two years to secure the supply contract. Gone in a memo.' His tone is flat. Controlled. The tone of someone who made peace with a bad exchange a long time ago and is just living in what it left behind.

He glances back at his people. 'When the maintenance fails, dock workers don't get to redirect the cost to someone else. We patch it ourselves or we fall behind quota.' A pause. 'That's Dima. Fifteen years old. Supporting his mother and two sisters since his father died in a refinery collapse last year. If this crew loses quota, he goes back to scavenging wharves. You want to tell him that the crane doesn't meet your calculations?' You notice the boy has a small notebook in his front pocket. He's been writing in it since you arrived.

The accusation hangs in the salt air. Your ledger is open to the stress numbers. The numbers are unambiguous.

The system that redirected this district's maintenance fuel is the same system your report will activate. That's worth knowing.
choice1_label: Show me the modification. Let me assess it properly.

text:
Kaelen leads you around to the crane's base and pulls back a heavy canvas panel to reveal his work.

It's crude. It's also real alchemy. He's used Tier 1 bonding paste—the improvised kind, mixed from accessible materials—to draw a reinforcement circle directly onto the crane's primary load-bearing joint. The circle is rough by academy standards, the lines not perfectly even, the radius slightly elliptical where his arm was at an awkward angle. But the structure is sound: a continuous reinforcement pattern that distributes load stress across a wider surface area, allowing the crane to handle tonnage above its original design parameters.

You kneel and activate your stress assessment plate against the bonded circle.

The reinforcement is working. That's the tragedy of it. Kaelen did exactly the right kind of work with exactly the wrong materials. The reinforcement pattern is degrading under repeated stress loads—Tier 1 paste isn't designed to sustain a circle under this kind of repeated activation. Your readings show micro-fractures propagating through the paste layer, disrupting the circle's integrity. The joint is losing structural capacity with every lift.

'It's brilliant,' you say honestly. 'Level 2 reinforcement work with improvised materials and no formal training.' You look up at him. 'That cost you something. Six nights of your own energy.'

'I know what it cost me.'

'The paste is failing. At the current load rate, the joint will reach critical threshold sometime this afternoon.'

Kaelen's face goes grey. Not with surprise. With the expression of someone who suspected this and was hoping to be wrong.
choice1_label: I have to report this to the CEA. The crane needs to be shut down.
choice2_label: Try to stabilize the joint.
choice3_label: Close your ledger and walk away.
choice4_label: Reach toward the active line with a bare hand—the plate says the field is live; your nerves want to disagree.

text:
You read the joint the way you were trained: stress vectors, paste decay, the ugly honesty of a circle doing work it was never rated for. The quota clock does not pause while you think. Neither does arithmetic.

A sanctioned Tier 2 block would arrest the slide—clean, documented, the kind of exchange the Exchange likes on paper. Your own reserves would do it too, slower and meaner, with no receipt but the tremor in your hands afterward.

Kaelen waits without performing patience. His crew pretends not to watch. The crane's iron hums like an argument you have not finished yet.
choice1_label: Use a Tier 2 block from your kit—mercy accounting still allows a sanctioned kit draw.
choice2_label: Both mercy tallies are already logged; this sanctioned block is the crane's second kit draw.
choice3_label: Pay from your own reserves instead.
choice4_label: Pay from your reserves—Kaelen's crew will help you stand.
choice5_label: Pay from your reserves—the Freehands won't let you do this alone.
choice6_label: Step back. You cannot pay this twice in one week—not like this.

text:
You know the shape of the stabilization circle before your chalk touches iron. That is the problem. Your body knows the price of drawing it twice in the same ledger week without a sanctioned buffer.

This is not cowardice. It is bookkeeping. The margin is gone. To force the exchange now would be to borrow against a line of credit your muscles do not actually hold.

You close your kit and let the honest refusal sit where shame usually tries to crowd in.

You reach for your authorization seal. 'Kaelen, I'm filing an immediate hazard report. The CEA will send an inspection team. The crane will be shut down until it can be properly repaired with appropriate materials.'

Kaelen grabs your arm. Not hard. Desperately.

'Please.' He doesn't lower his voice. His crew can hear. 'You file that report and the crane goes dark. We miss quota. The CEA issues reduction notices. My entire crew loses their positions.' He looks at you with the kind of directness that has nothing left to protect. 'You'll write it up clean in your ledger, and six families pay the cost of your clean report. Dima goes back to scavenging.'

His grip tightens. 'I'm not asking you to lie. I'm asking you to give me a day to source better materials and redo this properly. One day. That's all.'

You look at his hand on your arm. At the burn scars. At the crew watching from across the dock. Your ledger is open to the stress calculations.

The crane will fail by evening if nothing changes. Someone will be hurt. But the same system that redirected this district's maintenance fuel is the system your report will activate. The cost doesn't disappear when you file a report. It just moves—and you control where to.
choice1_label: File the report. The math is clear.

text:
You pull your arm free, not unkindly. 'I'm sorry, Kaelen. I don't have another way.'

You write the report in clean, precise notation. Anomaly confirmed. Unauthorized alchemical reinforcement. Inadequate material quality for sustained structural application. Immediate structural hazard. Recommend shutdown and investigation of responsible party.

Within the hour, CEA enforcers arrive. They're efficient. The crane is locked down. Kaelen is placed in restraints without resistance—he just looks at you with an expression that isn't anger. It's something more complicated than anger. It's the expression of someone who already knew the cost and paid it anyway.

His crew scatters. Some curse at you. The boy, Dima, just stands there watching Kaelen being led away, still gripping his wrench. He stops gripping it so tightly. He turns and walks toward the edge of the dock without looking back.

You stand alone at the base of the silent crane. Your report is flawless. The enforcement team thanks you and mentions the district's poor maintenance record as a contributing factor. They say this without apparent irony. You don't share your thoughts on why the maintenance record is poor.

Something sits in your chest like a weight you haven't finished calculating yet.
choice1_label: Continue your assessment of the district.

text:
You are not supposed to do this. Scholars observe and report. They do not kneel at load-bearing joints and spend sanctioned fuel like it belongs to them.

But you can see exactly what is wrong: Tier 1 paste going grainy at the stress nodes, the reinforcement pattern fraying where the crane keeps asking for more than the circle was written to give. A stabilization overlay—drawn clean, fed with a Tier 2 block from your field kit—can arrest the degradation long enough for Kaelen to source better materials and redo the work the way the manuals prefer.

'I can hold it,' you tell him quietly. 'If it comes out that I intervened—'

'You won't hear it from me,' Kaelen says. 'Or my crew.'

You break the seal on a sanctioned block. The mineral smell rises, familiar and expensive. You chalk the stabilization geometry to ride the existing pattern instead of fighting it, then set your palms against the iron and let the block run through you the way the academy taught: measured channel, minimum waste, maximum coherence.

The cost arrives as it always does—in your shoulders first, then behind your eyes. Exhaustion does not negotiate. The circle flares, settles, holds. The joint's readings flatten back into something survivable.

Kaelen watches you stand with an expression you have rarely seen aimed at a Scholar.
choice1_label: Wipe the chalk dust from your hands and stand.

text:
There is no spare Tier 2 block left to hide behind—only you, the joint, and the blunt fact that improvised paste cannot keep pretending it is something stronger.

You chalk the stabilization circle anyway. You align it to Kaelen's rough work the way structural training demands: respect the existing geometry, reinforce what is failing, do not pretend you are rewriting the world from scratch.

When you close the circuit, you pay from the reserves the Exchange never logs. The channel runs hot. Your hands shake before the circle finishes settling—not drama, just physics. The iron cools into a steadier line. The reinforcement pattern stops shedding coherence at the corners.

Same operational outcome as a fueled fix. A harder receipt.

'I know what that cost,' Kaelen says, too quietly for his crew to treat it as theater.

The modification holds. Your plate confirms it: the joint is running clean, the reinforcement pattern stable. It will hold for weeks, maybe months, depending on load—long enough for Kaelen to find proper Tier 2 paste and do the work the way the manuals prefer.

You are lightheaded either way you paid: fuel spent from the kit, or self spent until your margins go thin. You feel it in the slight tremble in your hands, the drag behind your eyes. Level 2 structural work under field conditions is harder than the academy simulations pretended.

Kaelen watches you for a moment after the circle settles. Then, quietly, he says: 'Thank you. I know what that cost you.'

'Get proper Tier 2 paste before you bond another circle to load-bearing infrastructure. The work was sound. The materials were wrong.'

'Where would I get Tier 2 on a dock worker's allocation?' He says it without accusation. It is just a question. You both know the answer—from the maintenance budget—and you both know where that went.

His crew returns to work. The crane swings. Dima looks at you with wide, uncertain eyes—a kid trying to decide whether what just happened was the right thing or the wrong thing. His expression suggests no one has told him the rules yet.

You are not entirely sure yourself.
choice1_label: Resume your assessment—the first mercy tally records.
choice2_label: Continue on—the second mercy tally will record.
choice3_label: Return to your rounds—both tallies are already logged.
choice4_label: Stay and talk to Kaelen a moment longer.

text:
The crew gets back to work. Kaelen stays. You sit on a crate near the crane's base and he sits across from you, and neither of you says anything for a moment. The crane swings. The quota clock runs.

'My father worked on the seawall,' Kaelen says finally. 'When it was first reinforced, years ago. He was one of the crew that embedded the maintenance circles. He used to say the wall would outlast everyone he knew.' A pause. 'He was proud of that. A thing made well, meant to last.'

You look at the water. The seawall is visible from here—a dark mass at the district's edge.

'He died about ten years back. On the wall. A crane failure during maintenance. The official report said operator error.' Kaelen's voice is matter-of-fact. 'But before he went, he took me down to that wall and showed me the circle marks. His work. Still running, still clean. That was fifteen years after he'd done it.' He looks at his hands. 'That's what good materials get you. Work that lasts. Work you can be proud of.'

He doesn't say what happens without good materials. He doesn't need to.

'These people—' he nods toward the crew, '—they're not the district to me. They're Lira, who supports her mother and does the most precise shaping work you've ever seen. They're Maren, who could have gotten a guild position uptown but stayed because she grew up here. They're Dima, who hasn't figured out yet that the world doesn't have a plan for him.' He looks at you. 'I'm not asking you to lie for them. I'm asking you to understand what the numbers actually represent.'

The crane swings. The quota clock runs. You write nothing in your ledger.
choice1_label: Resume your investigation—the first mercy tally records.
choice2_label: Continue on—the second mercy tally will record.
choice3_label: Return to your circuit—both tallies are already logged.
choice4_label: Ask about the circle carved into the crane's base joint. It looks like his father's work.

text:
You close your ledger. The calculations are clear. The crane will fail. But the calculation of what happens to these people if you report it is also clear, and it's not a number you want to write down.

'I didn't see anything,' you say.

Kaelen stares at you. 'You're serious?'

'I was sent to investigate an anomaly. My readings show the crane is operating within acceptable field parameters. That's what my report will say.'

The lie tastes like low-quality fuel—cheap, acrid, something that burns wrong and will vent badly later.

You walk away from Crane Seven without looking back. You do the math in your head as you go: the joint has maybe eight hours of load capacity left at current rates. The afternoon shift runs until 1800. The math isn't good.

Three hours later, as you're taking readings near the seawall, you hear it. A deep grinding shriek of metal, then a terrible silence, then screaming.

A dock worker named Maren was standing beneath the crane arm when the pivot joint failed. Three tons of ore.
choice2_label: Stay where you are and record the event.

text:
You push through the crowd. Kaelen is on his knees beside the wreckage, hauling at the fallen ore crates with bleeding hands. His crew works frantically around him.

Maren is alive, barely. Her legs are crushed beneath a crate. She's conscious, which somehow makes it worse—her eyes are open, fixed on the sky, and she's breathing in the short, controlled gasps of someone managing pain by refusing to acknowledge it.

Kaelen sees you. His eyes are red. He doesn't say anything. He doesn't need to.

You open your ledger. Your hands are shaking. There is something you could try—an attempt at alchemical medical stabilization. Not your specialization. Your field plates are for structural assessment, not biological systems. The principles overlap theoretically. The implementation is different territory. The academy rule is explicit: cross-discipline work without training causes more harm than doing nothing. This is a real rule based on real deaths.

You know it is also sometimes used as an excuse.

Dima is standing at the edge of the crowd. He's not looking at Maren. He's looking at you. His face has the particular stillness of someone in the process of deciding what they think about something they can't take back.
choice1_label: Try to help with what you know.
choice2_label: Stay back. Document the incident and wait for the physician.

text:
You hear the screams from across the dock. You don't go to the site.

Instead, you stand at the seawall with your ledger open, writing down the time, the sound, the approximate tonnage based on the crane's last recorded load. The notation is clean. The handwriting is steady. You are a Measured Scholar and your job is to observe and record, and that is what you are doing.

Your hand trembles slightly when you close the ledger.

Later, you learn her name was Maren. She survived, but her legs are gone. The district physician couldn't save them. Kaelen's crew is dissolved. The CEA shuts down the crane anyway, a month too late to do anyone any good.

Everything you tried to avoid by walking away happened anyway, plus one woman's legs.

The exchange wasn't avoided. It was just moved. You moved it. You told yourself you didn't choose—that walking away wasn't a choice—but the cost landed somewhere, and it landed because you were the last person in a position to catch it and you let it fall.

You push through the crowd and kneel beside her.

Medical alchemy is not your specialization. Your training is structural and systems-level—the same physical principles apply at a theoretical level, but the implementation is different territory. You know this. You do it anyway.

You draw a stabilization circle on the ground around her using your chalk—not a structural pattern, but a basic biological support circle from academy fundamentals, the material from your first year before you specialized. It's rough. A medical alchemist would do this better, faster, with cleaner results.

You press your hands to the chalk line and draw from your reserves. The circle flares, dims, and holds. Not healing—alchemy can't restore what's already gone, and you don't have the skill to attempt anything more complex. Stabilizing: slowing the progression of internal damage, buying her body time until proper help arrives.

The district physician arrives twenty minutes later and gives you a long, measuring look as she takes over.

'Scholar work,' she says. 'Rough work. But it held.' She pauses. 'You may have saved her life. You also overextended into territory you're not trained for.' She meets your eyes. 'I'll note both things equally.'

You wipe the chalk from your hands. Your vision swims. Kaelen watches from the edge of the crowd with an expression that is equal parts gratitude and something you can't quite name—the look of someone who's been surprised by a person doing the harder thing.

The crane incident is behind you—however it resolved—and the district is still standing around it, unchanged. The quota clock still runs. Workers still move. The bay still smells of brine and old fuel. Life in Karet Bay doesn't wait for a Scholar to finish processing its problems.

You walk for a while without taking notes. Down to the water and back. Through the narrow streets between the warehouses, where the buildings lean slightly toward each other as though for warmth.

A family eats lunch on a doorstep—children, a grandmother, someone's dog asleep across everyone's feet. Two old men play a game on a crate, moving pieces made from stamped copper. A woman hangs laundry between two alchemically reinforced posts; the reinforcement is crude, clearly improvised, and the posts wobble slightly when the wind takes the sheets. She adjusts the line without looking up, in the practiced way of someone who has made something work that wasn't designed to work.

This is a place where people live. You write that down. You're not sure why.

Then you walk back toward the dock infrastructure and open your diagnostic plate again—and the district becomes, once more, a problem.

The pattern is everywhere once you know to look: improvised reinforcement circles in Tier 0 paste on load-bearing structures, water pipes bonded with materials already developing micro-fractures, the steady background noise of a system running on patch work because the materials for proper maintenance aren't available. The root problem isn't skill. It's the material allocation. Someone has been steering the requisitions so the flow on paper and the flow through the district are not the same exchange.
choice1_label: Pursue the inland drainage signature—the same network tied to the seawall stress.
choice2_label: Complete structural readings at the seawall while you are still on the waterfront.
choice3_label: Someone is standing near the Drowning plaque. You recognize the posture.
choice4_label: Dima's notebook still circles a building with music and odd emissions—you shelve the hunt tonight.

text:
The climb back to the Scholar's Quarter costs more than steps. Your legs know the docks now; your ledger knows them better—ink smudged where sweat met chalk dust, margins crowded with numbers you will not trust until you have slept on them.

The dormitory corridor is quiet in the particular way of places where everyone is pretending not to listen for the next bell. You wash the bay off your hands. The water runs clean here, a small insult you do not comment on.

Supper is thin soup and bread, the measured ration of people who are not expected to spend themselves in the lower districts every day of a deployment. You eat anyway. Hunger is also a kind of bad accounting.

Your bunk accepts you like a debt settled for a few hours. Before you blow out the candle, you open the ledger one more time—not to add, only to underline three sentences you refuse to misremember by morning. The seawall and the drainage network and the crane are not three separate stories. They are one ledger written in different handwritings.

Sleep comes with the dull certainty that tomorrow you will pick up whichever thread you choose—and that the waterfront will still be there, still asking, whether you closed the book or not.
choice1_label: Next day: resume inland drainage where the signature leads.
choice2_label: Next day: take the seawall pass and finish waterfront readings.
choice3_label: Next day: follow Mireth's plaque thread with daylight on your side.
choice4_label: Next day: follow Dima's notebook to the circled building.

text:
You find him sitting on a concrete barrier at the edge of the dock, watching the water. He still has the wrench in his hands, though he's not gripping it anymore—just holding it, the way you might hold onto something when you're not sure what to do with your hands. The notebook is in his lap. He was writing something in it when you approached; he didn't close it when he saw you coming.

He notices you but doesn't leave. That's either courage or exhaustion. Possibly both.

You sit nearby. The bay moves.

'Was he wrong?' Dima asks eventually. He doesn't look at you. 'Like. Actually wrong. Not against-the-rules wrong. Actually wrong.'

It's a harder question than it sounds. You think about the stress calculations in your ledger. You think about the reinforcement circle, rough but technically sound. You think about six nights of his own energy spent on borrowed time—the foreman you haven't spoken to yet, only watched from the edge of the crew.

'He did real work,' you say, 'with the wrong materials. The work was an honest attempt. The materials were what was available to him.' You pause. 'The people who decided those were the only materials available—that's a different question.'

Dima thinks about this. He has the stillness of someone who's learned to think before responding, probably because responding wrong has cost him something before.

'So the wrong thing wasn't what he did,' Dima says. 'It was what he had to work with.'

'Yes.'

Another silence. Then: 'That doesn't feel like it's enough to know.'

'No,' you agree. 'It doesn't.'

He nods slowly, in the way of someone receiving an answer they already suspected and were hoping was wrong. He sets the wrench down on the barrier. Then he picks it up again.

He writes something in the notebook. You don't ask what.

You leave him there, watching the water.
choice1_label: Your wider brief starts with the name on the permit: Crane Seven's foreman. Cross the apron while you still have daylight.
choice2_label: You mean to reach the seawall cross-section before dark—but dock protocol says the crane foreman signs off on waterfront access. Start there.
choice3_label: That inland drainage spike is screaming for context. Get the foreman's account of recent loads before you chase it inland.
choice4_label: Look at what he's writing in the notebook.

text:
The CEA substation is a blocky concrete structure about two meters on each side, sitting on a raised pad at the intersection of the district's underground maintenance conduit network. Standard construction, unremarkable. Your diagnostic plate disagrees.

You run a full scan, spending a Tier 2 block to get precise readings. The substation is actively running—processing and distributing something through the conduit network. But the fuel consumption your instruments measure is effectively zero. The substation is operating at full capacity with no material input you can identify.

In three years of field assessment, you have never read a clean zero on a fuel cost measurement for operational equipment. Everything has a cost. That is not a philosophical position. It is physics.

You check your instruments twice. Three times. The reading doesn't change.

There are explanations: instrument error, a shielded fuel source your equipment can't read, or an extremely high-HI material working at near-zero loss. The first seems unlikely—your diagnostic plate is functioning correctly everywhere else. The second is possible but would be unusual for district infrastructure. The third—Tier 3 materials are expensive and tightly controlled. Tier 4 is essentially mythological.

You make a detailed note in your ledger. You add a question mark. Then another.

This isn't your primary assignment and you have no explanation. But something here is being paid for in a way your instruments can't detect. In this world, when something appears free, the cost is hidden somewhere. And hidden costs are always the most dangerous kind.
choice1_label: The fuel diversion pattern confirms your earlier readings. Head to the CEA.
choice2_label: Ask around the docks about this substation.
choice3_label: The cross-reference confirms it—the drainage signature leads inland.

text:
A dock worker approaches you before you can approach anyone—a woman of maybe fifty, with the careful eyes of someone who has spent a long time reading situations quickly. She has a Freehand circle-mark at her wrist, a small reinforcement pattern, worn smooth at the edges from years of rubbing against work gloves.

'You're the Scholar who came about Crane Seven,' she says.

'Word travels fast.'

'In this district, bad news is the fastest thing there is.' She walks beside you without asking. 'Seren. Freehands network. We've been doing the maintenance work the CEA stopped doing seven months ago—patching, reinforcing, keeping things from collapsing on people. On our own time. With our own materials.'

She says it without expectation of praise. Just as a fact.

'There's a woman in the slum quarter who built a water purifier,' she continues. 'Elara. The district's water supply started failing when the maintenance budget was cut—contamination from the foundation drainage. She built something that actually works. You'll want to look at it.' A pause. 'Two things before you do. First: it works. Second: there's a cost to it that Elara couldn't see from where she was standing. I think you'll be able to see it.'

She stops walking. Looks at you directly. 'I've been doing this work for twenty years. I've seen three districts go the same way as this one—slow material bleed, infrastructure patch, infrastructure fail, people hurt. Every time, the institution says it was unforeseeable.' She holds your gaze. 'It was foreseeable. Someone just decided the cost of foreseeing it was higher than the cost of pretending not to.'

She presses a rough map of the district's drainage network into your hand and walks away.

Then she stops and turns. 'If you need supplies—real supplies, not the black-market junk—find Brin. She runs the Freehands safehouse in the old chandlery off Dock Street. She's the reason half this district still has working water. Tell her Seren sent you. She'll decide whether you're worth the materials.'
choice1_label: Take the map and follow the drainage signature.

text:
The Karet Bay seawall is a massive structure of reinforced stone and iron, built two generations ago to protect the district from storm surges after the Drowning altered the bay's currents. It runs the entire eastern waterfront—thirty feet high at its lowest, embedded deep into the substrate, a structure designed to last.

Up close, it looks like it has been trying to.

You activate your stress assessment plate, pressing it against the base of the wall, feeding in a full Tier 2 block for a thorough scan.

The embedded maintenance circles are there—cut into the stone during original construction, Tier 2 reusable circles designed to run indefinitely as long as their fuel chambers are replenished on schedule. But the fuel chambers in the wall's foundations are nearly empty. The maintenance circles are running at minimal capacity—barely slowing structural degradation, not maintaining it. The alchemical bonds that hold the stone matrix together have been weakening for over a year.

Your plate shows something else too: an additional stressor you weren't expecting. A chemical disruption in the foundation soil—concentrated toxic runoff seeping into the fuel chambers from the drainage network, rendering the remaining fuel inert. Whatever is producing that runoff is accelerating the wall's degradation beyond what simple underfueling would cause alone.

You do the math. The seawall isn't failing in years. Months at most. Possibly much less.

Kaelen's father's circle work is in here somewhere. You can see the signature of the original reinforcement—careful, precise, Tier 2 quality that has been maintaining integrity for decades. It is being slowly undone by a fuel shortage and something in the drain water that no one was supposed to know about.

You write in your ledger: who made this happen?
choice2_label: Conduct a deep technical survey of the foundations.
choice3_label: Recheck the CEA substation two blocks north—the fuel readings were anomalous.

text:
You follow the drainage pattern upstream through the residential slums—narrow streets where buildings lean against each other like people on a crowded shift, sharing load whether they chose to or not.

The chemical runoff traces through the underground drainage to a cluster of tenements near the old cistern district. Here, the ambient fuel readings in the surrounding soil are so depleted your diagnostic plate barely registers. It's like walking into a system that has already paid everything it had and is running on the memory of what full felt like.

But in the middle of the depletion, there's a secondary signature: small, steady, operating independently. Someone is running active alchemy down here—not draining, but producing. A working circle, regularly activated with real fuel. Someone who cares enough about something to pay for it themselves, in a district where caring enough to pay costs real money.

The signature leads to a basement entrance beneath a crumbling tenement. The door has been reinforced with crude alchemical binding—basic bonding paste with a simple lock circle. Freehand work, rough but functional. Someone with genuine skill who doesn't want visitors.
choice2_label: Use your authorization seal to force the binding.
choice3_label: A very old man is sitting outside in the afternoon sun. Speak to him first.
choice4_label: Verify drainage appendix K-B-11 (cistern ring—secondary).
choice5_label: Follow stenciled routing marks that do not match the dock manifests.

text:
The slum streets channel you the same way they did before—leaning brick, shared load, thin light—but this time you are not finding the trail for the first time. You are walking it with the disturbance already named in your head, your plate confirming what memory already sketched.

Chemical runoff still threads toward the tenements by the old cistern ring. The soil reads spent—almost nothing left—yet that secondary signature holds: small, steady, someone's fuel paying for a private circle in a place where private fuel is its own kind of vow.

The path returns you to the crumbling tenement and the basement door: crude bonding paste, a simple lock circle, Freehand work—rough but functional. Someone with genuine skill who doesn't want visitors. The purifier's echo lives behind that threshold; the district's larger arithmetic waits beyond it.
choice2_label: Use your authorization seal to force the binding.
choice3_label: A very old man is sitting outside in the afternoon sun. Speak to him first.
choice4_label: Verify drainage appendix K-B-11 (cistern ring—secondary).
choice5_label: Follow stenciled routing marks that do not match the dock manifests.

text:
He's maybe seventy, settled on a low stool in a patch of weak afternoon sun, wearing the careful stillness of someone who has been very sick recently and is still learning to be well again.

You slow as you pass. Something in how he's sitting—hands loose in his lap, face turned toward the warmth with the specific attention of someone who hasn't been able to do that in a while—makes you stop.

'Good afternoon,' you say.

'Good afternoon.' He has a quiet voice, slightly surprised at being spoken to. 'You're not from here.'

'No. I'm a Scholar. Investigating some anomalies in the district.'

'Ah.' He turns back toward the sun. 'There's a woman inside who fixed the water. About six, seven months ago. The water here made you sick—stomach sickness, the fever kind, the kind that takes weeks off your life each time. My wife had it. I had it. Everyone had it.' He pauses. 'Then the woman fixed the water, and we didn't have it anymore.'

He says this as simply as he might say that the weather changed.

'Is the water going to stay fixed?' he asks.

You think about the readings from the seawall. About the drainage patterns. About a question you can't answer yet.

'I'm working on that,' you say.

He nods, not pressing. 'My wife made tea this morning. With the good water. She laughed when she drank it.' He looks at his hands. 'It's a small thing. But it's the first time she laughed at something in months.'

He closes his eyes and turns his face back to the sun. You stand there for a moment, holding that.

Then you go to the door and knock.
choice2_label: Return to the disturbance trail.
choice3_label: Return to the disturbance trail.

text:
You knock three times. 'Measured Scholars. I'm here about energy anomalies in the district. I'm not CEA enforcement.'

Silence. Then footsteps. The door opens a crack, and a woman's face appears—sharp-featured, dark-eyed, maybe forty. Her hands are stained with alchemical residue in the specific pattern of someone who spends significant time working with copper and catalyst compounds.

She looks at you the way a cat looks at something that has wandered into its territory and has not yet made clear whether it's a threat or an annoyance.

'A Scholar,' she says. 'In the slums. You're either genuinely here about anomalies, or you're the worst spy the CEA has ever employed.'

'Genuinely here. Your active circle work showed up on my readings. I'm trying to understand what's happening to this district's infrastructure, and whatever you're running is part of the pattern.'

She studies you for a long moment—really studies you, not just the ledger and the seal. Then she opens the door wider.

'Come in.' A pause. 'There's something you should know before you do, though. What's in here is helping people. And it's also making things worse. I know that. I've known it for months. I just couldn't see where the worse part was going.' She looks at you steadily. 'Tell me you can.'
choice2_label: Enter the basement.
choice3_label: You've already settled what lives down here. Step back into the district's larger pattern.

text:
You press your authorization seal against the alchemical binding. The seal's pattern disrupts the crude lock circle—a higher-quality application overriding a lower-quality one—and the door swings open.

Inside, a woman stands in the center of a cluttered basement workshop, holding an iron pry bar with the practiced grip of someone who's used one in anger before and is deciding whether this is one of those times.

'CEA?' she demands.

'Measured Scholars,' you say, holding up your ledger. 'I'm investigating energy anomalies in the district. Your active circle work appeared on my readings.'

She doesn't lower the bar immediately. 'You just forced my door. Scholars observe. They don't break in.'

'I'll note the property damage in my report alongside everything else I'm noting today.' You look past her at the apparatus in the center of the room—copper tubes, a custom circle plate, a sealed fuel chamber with refined catalyst blocks. 'What is that?'

She follows your gaze. Holds the bar for one more beat of decision. Then slowly lowers it.

'Sit down,' she says. 'And don't touch anything without asking. Last person who touched my equipment without permission lost two fingernails and an argument.'
choice2_label: Continue into the workshop.

text:
Her name is Elara. She makes tea—from the purifier's clean output, automatically, without asking—and sets a cup in front of you before saying anything else. It's the gesture of someone who grew up with hospitality as a reflex, regardless of circumstance.

'It's a water purifier,' she says, sitting across from you. 'The district's water started showing contamination signs about a year ago — chemical compounds from the foundation drainage seeping into the water table. The CEA said repairs were scheduled. Said that for two years. Seven months ago the materials were cut and it went from bad to undrinkable. I built something instead.'

She says it simply, not defiantly. The way you'd say: it was raining, so I made a roof.

The device in the center of the room is remarkable work. A multi-stage purifier constructed from salvaged copper tube and refined catalyst blocks—Tier 1 material, chosen carefully for specific chemical separation properties. At its center, a custom circle plate she inscribed herself: a reconfiguration circle designed to separate dissolved chemical compounds from water at the molecular level. The craftsmanship isn't perfect—the circle has minor asymmetries, the tube joints show signs of repeated adjustment—but it works. Your diagnostic plate can see it working.

'Twenty families have clean water because of this,' she says. 'Sixteen children who had the water-fever recovered. Old Tomas next door, who was close to the end—he recovered.' A small pause. 'I know there's a cost I couldn't see. There's always a cost I couldn't see. I built it anyway, because the cost of not building it was people dying of thirst in a city with a bay full of water.'

She looks at you. 'What did I miss?'
choice1_label: Run a full analysis on the purifier first.
choice2_label: Take a sip of the purified water to test it.

text:
The basement smells of copper and tea. Elara looks up from her workbench—not surprised to see you, exactly, but weighing how much time she can spare.

'Back already,' she says. Her gaze skims the cellar walls and the bench, tallying a space that is still hers whether the machinery cooperates or not. 'Same workshop. Ask what you need.'
choice1_label: Run a full analysis on the purifier first.
choice2_label: Take a sip of the purified water to test it.

text:
You spend an hour with your diagnostic plate and measurement tools mapping the purifier's exchange ratios. Elara watches you work in silence—she understands enough to know that what you're doing matters, and has the discipline to let you finish without filling the time with her own uncertainty.

The purifier is ingenious. Elara's reconfiguration circle restructures dissolved contaminants at the molecular level, separating them from the water matrix. The exchange is real and functional: clean water flows out, isolated toxins stay behind. It is good work done with imperfect materials, and it is doing what she built it to do.

But the toxins have to go somewhere. Equivalent exchange—the compounds don't disappear. They are displaced. And your analysis shows exactly where. Elara's drainage system channels the isolated toxins downward through the building's outflow pipes, into the district's underground drainage network, and from there into the soil around the seawall's foundations.

Over seven months, the compounds have been accumulating in the fuel chambers embedded in the seawall's base—reacting with the maintenance fuel and rendering it inert, preventing the wall's support circles from receiving the energy they need to maintain structural integrity.

Each liter of clean water costs a fraction of the wall's structural capacity.

You show Elara the analysis. She reads it with the focused attention of someone who has been waiting for the answer and is experiencing the particular pain of finding out they were right to worry.

'I didn't know,' she says quietly.

'I know,' you say. 'That's the hardest kind of bad exchange. When everyone thought they were doing the right thing.'

She doesn't say anything else for a moment. Neither do you.
choice1_label: Give her a moment. Then talk about what she built and why.

text:
She makes more tea. It seems to be what her hands do when her mind needs space.

'I had a cousin,' she says, not looking at anything in particular. 'Years ago. Different district, same problem—contaminated water supply, infrastructure failure, CEA moving slowly. She was twelve.' A pause. 'She died. Water-fever, when it gets bad enough. It's not a spectacular death. It's just a long, degrading one.'

She turns the tea cup in her hands.

'I started learning alchemy because of that. Not from an academy—I couldn't afford it, and I didn't have the kind of background they look for anyway. I learned from watching, and from people who were willing to teach, and from failing a hundred times in small ways before I started failing in medium ways.' A very faint smile. 'It took me fifteen years before I could do anything I would call good work. I've been doing Freehand repairs in this district for six of them.'

The Freehands don't have offices. They have people. In districts like Karet Bay, where the Secretariat's authority runs thin and official repair orders wait months in queue, it's Freehand networks that adjudicate disputes, coordinate labor, and fill the gaps. You knew this abstractly. Watching Elara, you understand it practically.

'When the water started failing, I thought—I know how to do this. Not perfectly. With what I have. But I know how to do this.' She looks at the purifier. 'I knew there would be a cost I couldn't see. There always is, with work you do in a hurry with imperfect materials. But the alternative was to wait for a perfect solution while Old Tomas and sixteen children got sicker. That's also a cost. Waiting is a cost. I just—chose which cost to pay.'

She meets your eyes. 'I'm not asking you to tell me I was right. I know I wasn't completely right. I just want you to understand why I built it.'

You do. That's the problem.

'Seven months,' she says. 'And now it's part of the problem.'

'It's part of what made the problem visible. That's different.'

She looks at you. 'Is it?'

You think about that. 'The seawall was already compromised by the material redirection. Your purifier accelerated the timeline. Without your purifier, the wall would still fail—just later, and without warning. With your purifier, the timeline is urgent enough that someone has to act.'

'That's a generous interpretation.'

'It's an accurate one.' You close your ledger. 'The question now is what to do about it. You have three options, and none of them are good.'

'I'm listening.'

'If we shut the purifier down, the water goes back to being contaminated. The people who recovered may relapse. New cases will develop. If we leave it running, the seawall continues to degrade. If the wall fails, the entire district floods.' You pause. 'There's a third option—I may be able to modify the drainage to redirect the chemical runoff into a sealed vessel instead of the drainage network. It would stop the wall damage while keeping the water clean. But it would cost fuel and personal energy I can't easily replace, and someone would need to empty the vessel every three days.'

Elara looks at the purifier for a long time.

'Red Harrow held because people made it hold,' she says quietly, almost to herself. 'People paid costs they didn't choose. That's not a lesson. That's a warning.'

The silence between you has weight.
choice1_label: Shut it down. The seawall risk is too great.
choice2_label: Try to modify it to redirect the runoff.
choice3_label: For now, leave it. I need the full picture before acting.

text:
Elara watches as you draw the neutralization circle around the purifier's core. Her hands stay at her sides, knuckles pale; she does not step in to correct your radius the way she would for anyone helping her keep a seal honest.

'Twenty families,' she says. 'Their marks are on the draw sheet I keep beside this tap—names on today's ration roster at the spout, jug by jug.'

'Six thousand people in the district if the seawall fails.'

'The seawall won't collapse tonight.'

'No. But it will collapse. And the longer your purifier runs, the sooner that is.'

The circle is complete. You activate it, drawing from your reserves—a clean, deliberate operation. The purifier's reconfiguration circle loses coherence, its carefully designed exchange pattern dissolving. The copper tubes stop humming. The catalyst blocks cool. Clean water stops flowing from the output tap.

The fuel chambers in the wall's foundations will slowly clear as the toxic runoff stops flowing. The maintenance circles will begin to recover. Slowly, but they'll recover.

Elara does not look at you. 'Get out of my house, Scholar.'

You leave. Behind you, you can hear her—probably checking the tap, finding it dry. In the stairwell, you think about Old Tomas and his wife's morning tea. In your ledger, the calculations are flawless. The math says you made the right call.

The math does not explain why climbing the stairs feels like something is getting heavier with every step.

You commit to the modification: a secondary exchange loop that catches the isolated compounds before they reach the drainage network, sealed in a vessel Elara can empty on a schedule.

The method is the variable. A sanctioned Tier 2 block can carry part of the load and keep your body from doing all the accounting. Without it, the same geometry still works—it simply charges a different account.

Elara sets the lamp where you need it. 'Then we do it properly,' she says. 'Or we do not do it at all.'

choice2_label: Route runoff through yourself—no spare block.

text:
You sketch the secondary loop while Elara keeps the lamp honest and your chalk dry. She passes tools before you ask—pliers, a straightedge, a rag for a bead of condensation that would have lied to the seal.

The purifier was never built for two-stage exchange. That is the insult and the puzzle: making the first circle accept a neighbor without treating the neighbor like an intruder. You route the runoff into a copper vessel, bond a containment pattern to the specific compound profile, and let the block eat the part of the cost the textbooks prefer to hide behind inventory lines.

When the hum changes, it is not theater. It is alignment. Clean water still answers at the tap. Dark runoff gathers where it is supposed to gather—inside a circle that knows its name.

Elara exhales once, controlled. 'Three days on that vessel,' you say. 'CEA collection will hate the paperwork.'

'They can hate it on their own time.' She watches your hands. 'You paid.'

You did. The block is gone from your kit. What remains is tiredness with clean edges—the kind that does not pretend it was free.

text:
There is no sanctioned block left to feed the second loop—only your body, your chalk, and Elara's steady hands when the lamp needs tilting.

You build the containment geometry anyway. You force the purifier's first-stage circle to accept a neighbor it never asked for, sealing the isolated compounds into copper with a bond tight enough to shame the drainage network. The work takes longer. The cost does not spread across fuel inventory; it stacks in your joints, behind your eyes, in the quiet place where you keep track of what you can still spend.

When the hum settles into its new note, clean water still answers at the tap. The vessel fills with the dark runoff you refused to send downstream.

Elara does not thank you in flourishes. She nods once, as if confirming a measurement. 'Three days,' you say. 'Empty it. CEA will complain.'

'Let them.'

You lean against the doorframe until the room stops sliding sideways. The exchange is balanced. The receipt is yours.

text:
'I won't call this finished while the upstream numbers still lie,' you tell Elara. 'The tap, the wall drains, and the northern substation pull from the same throat—I need the trail straight before I pretend one mouth ate it all.'

She looks at you for a long moment. Then, quietly: 'That's the Scholar's answer. The Freehand answer is that people are drinking clean water today, and today matters.'

'Both things are true.'

'Yes.' She crosses to a cabinet and pulls out a hand-drawn map—the district's underground infrastructure, marked with months of her own observations. 'I've been tracking the depletion pattern. It's directional. The fuel reserves in the northern sector feed through a CEA substation and then out somewhere. I don't know where. But seven months ago, the flow changed, and that's when the contamination went critical.'

She gives you the map. 'Find out where the district's material allocation is going. Then come back and tell me whether my machine is really the problem, or whether it's one small piece of a much larger one.'

You take the map. You both know the answer already.

The pattern is pointing upward—not deeper into the slums, but toward the CEA's own infrastructure.

You may not have tied off every thread you started. What you can still show—the crane's unauthorized reinforcement where you saw it, the drainage signatures you've mapped, and everything else you've pulled since you arrived, Elara's purifier included if you traced the runoff that far—points the same way: this district's infrastructure has been systematically starved. The question is who decided to starve it.

The CEA district office is at the top of the administrative quarter. You walk toward it through streets that never quite empty—foot traffic, handcarts, the low rhythm of work that does not wait on any single bell—past children who have not yet learned to carry the particular exhaustion of the district on their faces. You pass the Drowning plaque again. Someone has left a single flower at its base. The flower is wilting.

You stop for a moment at the plaque. You have cited the Drowning incident three times in your work. From inside the district, the memorial reads less like a citation and more like a receipt—three sentences of formal accountability, polished thin by weather and by the habit of being read.
