choice2_label: Investigate the CEA substation first.
choice3_label: Put the escalation on formal record before you confront the Overseer.
choice4_label: Meet Elara by the bronze—she holds the district's unspent answer.
choice5_label: Check the purifier thread in your ledger.

text: You flip to the basement entry and reread what you already decided—not for doubt but for precision. Memory lies. Ink does not unless someone smudges it on purpose. Three outcomes are still legible. You touch the line that matches the flag your week actually set.
choice2_label: Read the modification entry.
choice3_label: Read the withdrawal entry.

text:
You chose the wall over the tap. The ledger calls that coherent. Your body still remembers Elara's kitchen going quiet when clean water stopped answering.

The entry ends where it should: resolved, documented, paid.

You chose a second loop and a vessel Elara can empty. The toxins do not get to use the drainage as a hiding place anymore.

The cost sits in fuel or marrow, depending on the line you wrote—but the outcome reads the same: modified, contained, still running.

You stepped back before the basement forced a third shape onto your week. The entry is shorter than the others because omission is also a kind of receipt.

You did not rewrite Elara's machine. You left the problem labeled instead of solved.

Before you knock on the Overseer's door, you walk the northern substation and burn your last full Tier 2 block on a scan that leaves your hands steadier than your stomach.

Behind the maintenance panel: redistribution orders, Overseer Toris's signature, neat as surgery. The district's Tier 2 fuel—the stuff meant to feed maintenance circles in the seawall, the grid, the water system—has been formally redirected, not hidden. Authority-approved. Highpoint Transit Rail. Seven months running.

At forty percent of normal supply, the circles were built to fail slowly. They did.

The substation still lies to you in a smaller voice. The rail shows full capacity; the structural work on the line outruns what those redirected loads can explain—twelve, maybe fifteen percent with no receipt on the page.

Your ledger spells it out: that slice of maintenance has no identifiable material cost.

Either your instruments are wrong, or someone is feeding the exchange from somewhere your scan cannot name.

Seven years of training, and the rail's output still matches nothing in the codex you were taught to treat as exhaustive—not even worn down. The Survey of Material Properties has a phrase for it, tucked in a footnote like a splinter: *output above calculable input, source unknown.* Last confirmed case, eight hundred years ago, at a site that no longer exists. The footnote does not say what happened to the site.

You mark it with three question marks and close the panel. You still don't have an answer. Your shoulders stay tight anyway—the kind of tight that means your body understood before your mouth caught up.

The CEA district office sits at the intersection of the administrative quarter and the main loading street—a blocky, well-maintained concrete building with the Authority's seal engraved above the entrance. It is, without question, the best-maintained building in the district.

You stand outside it for a moment.

A woman is waiting on the steps with a permit application. She has clearly been there for some time—her food, wrapped in paper, has been eaten, and she's working on what looks like a second cup of tea from a vendor cart. The entrance guard glances at her occasionally with the expression of someone who knows exactly what the answer to her application will be and hasn't been asked to deliver it yet.

Across the street, two boys are patching a wall with Tier 0 paste and a chalk circle—basic shaping work, the kind anyone can do. The circle is drawn with the careful focus of someone who has done it a few times and hasn't yet made it reflexive. They're fixing something that wouldn't need fixing if the district's maintenance circles were running properly.

The transit rail is visible in the far distance, running elevated through the upper city. From here it catches the late afternoon light. It looks clean. Finished. Properly maintained.

Across the road from the CEA office, leaning against a wall with the deliberate patience of someone waiting for permission to enter, a set of Measured Scholars field equipment is stacked neatly beside a folding desk. Diagnostic plates, fuel inventory, a calibration ledger—the same kit you carry, but older and more worn. The owner isn't here. The equipment says: another Scholar was in this district before you. The fact that it's parked outside the CEA building says they were working the same problem.

The Authority's entrance is a few steps away. The folding desk across the street is a different door into the same question—which you open first is up to you.

choice3_label: Check the Scholar field camp across the road. That equipment belongs to someone.

text:
The clerk spends thirty seconds pretending not to care. Your authorization seal hits the wax tray with a sound that says *procedure* louder than you meant it to.

Friction drops a notch. Your personal reserves pay a small, immediate tax for the performance. Fair exchange, if the exchange is honest.

Overseer Toris is a heavyset man with immaculate clothes and the hands of someone who has not touched raw material in many years. His office smells of expensive incense—a sharp and particular contrast to the chemical reek outside. On the wall behind his desk hangs his Revolutionary Council appointment seal, polished to a mirror shine, and below it a framed portrait of the First Citizen above a plaque reading YEAR ZERO TO PRESENT: THE REPUBLIC HOLDS. The whole arrangement says: I belong here, and I have the documentation to prove it. He listens to your report with practiced patience, fingers steepled, nodding at appropriate intervals in the way of a person who has learned to receive information without reacting to it.

When you've laid out what the day actually yielded—the depletion figures where you have them, the infrastructure thread wherever it led, the downstream effects you can document without pretending the picture is finished—he's quiet for a moment. Then he opens a drawer and pulls out a large schematic—the material distribution grid for the entire city.

'Citizen Vael. Your data is thorough. I appreciate thoroughness.' He taps the Highpoint Transit Rail on the schematic. 'When complete, this project will generate a forty percent increase in trade throughput for all of Caldris—including the lower districts, including Karet Bay. Thornfeld Compact contracts worth a decade of infrastructure funding are conditional on this rail network being operational. Three Free Ports League cities have already renegotiated their material rates based on projected capacity.' He taps Karet Bay. 'To achieve that, we temporarily reallocated resources from lower-priority maintenance networks. The exchange is calculated. The net benefit outweighs the transitional cost.'

He says it with the smoothness of something he's said before, and believed before, and possibly stopped believing at some point but has continued saying anyway. The portrait of the First Citizen watches from behind him.
choice1_label: You're redirecting material from a district that already paid once in the Drowning?
choice2_label: Flip his desk over.

text:
Toris doesn't flinch. 'Redirecting. Not removing. The formal authorization specifies that Karet Bay's allocation will be restored at project completion. This is a temporary measure.'

The office air is too clean; it makes every word sound filed.

'Seven months isn't temporary for the people living in it.'

'Infrastructure projects operate on infrastructure timelines. The transit rail is nine months from completion.' He leans forward slightly. 'The assessments on my desk assume current depletion rates. The restoration of materials at project completion will—'

Your pulse ticks against your collar. You cut in anyway.

'The seawall is failing now. Not at project completion.'

He stops. Something passes across his face—not guilt, exactly. More like a calculation being rerun with an unexpected variable. He pulls an internal packet from the stack beside him and reads a page the way a person reads when the numbers stop behaving.

'Our projections had a fifteen percent structural failure rate as the acceptable range for this district during the reallocation period,' he says, more quietly than before.

Fifteen percent. Six thousand residents. You do the math without meaning to. Nine hundred people.

'I understand why you used the word acceptable,' you say. 'I need you to understand that I cannot.'
choice1_label: Your models are wrong. The seawall situation is far more critical than fifteen percent.
choice2_label: Who authorized this above you? Give me the full chain.
choice3_label: Fifteen percent is not acceptable. Those are people's lives.
choice4_label: Lay down the crane file: grade, loads.
choice5_label: Read Kaelen's testimony aloud. Let the workers' account stand as part of the record.

text:
Toris's expression closes. 'The authorization chain is above your clearance level, Scholar. You were sent to investigate a crane anomaly. I would suggest filing your report on the crane.'

'I'm a Measured Scholar. Assessment is my function.'

'You're a junior field evaluator on a field investigation. Don't mistake one day in the docks for an understanding of how city-scale systems work.' He stands, which is a clear signal that the meeting has reached its end. 'I've been managing this district's resource allocation for twelve years. I've served on three successive Revolutionary Council infrastructure commissions. The mathematics of governance require perspective that extends well beyond one failing circle and one contaminated drain.'

He opens the door for you. 'File your crane report. Anything else you've placed on the record will be weighed when the docket allows.'

You go. But as you pass his desk, you see something: a stamped requisition for emergency structural reinforcement of the transit rail supports. Dated yesterday. If the transit rail itself needs emergency reinforcement, the material pressure is more aggressive than Toris's numbers acknowledged.

You note the requisition number. You're going to need it.

Toris regards you with the patience of a teacher addressing a student who has confused sentiment with precision.

Outside the window, the upper city stays bright and distant.

'Scholar, I respect your concern. But the fundamental law of this world is that nothing happens without cost. The question has never been whether cost will be paid—it always will be. The question is how to distribute it for the maximum collective benefit.' He gestures at the glass. 'If the transit rail is delayed, two hundred thousand people experience economic harm. Trade contracts default. Employment falls across every district. The ripple effects damage Karet Bay as much as any other district.'

You keep your hands flat on the chair arms. Stillness as anchor.

'And if the seawall collapses?'

'Then six thousand people in one district experience a catastrophe. Terrible. But contained. The math is clear.'

He meets your eyes. Not cruelty. Not indifference. Genuine conviction, which is worse.

'I do not enjoy this,' he says, and you believe him. 'I have not slept well in seven months. But if I assign cost based on my emotional responses rather than systemic calculation, I cause more harm, not less. Red Harrow held because someone coordinated it—because someone made difficult decisions about who stood where and in what order.' A pause. 'I make those decisions. Every day.'

'At Red Harrow,' you say quietly, 'the people who stood in the dangerous positions knew what they were standing in. They chose.'

He wields equivalent exchange the way old power invoked divine right, laying cost on people who never agreed to carry it. The founding texts called that bargain the Right of Exchange: governance stays legitimate only while cost stays fair—and the rebellion already proved what happens when it does not.

Something shifts in his face. Something small and quickly closed.

He doesn't answer.

You spread your seawall analysis on his desk. 'Your models account for gradual material depletion. They don't account for compound effects. There's chemical contamination in the drainage network—toxic compounds building up in the seawall's fuel chambers and rendering the remaining fuel inert. Combined with your material redirection, the wall's maintenance circles aren't degrading gradually—they're accelerating toward cascade failure.'

Toris picks up the seawall analysis and studies it. He reads with the focused attention of someone whose professional competence is real even if his judgment is not. When he sets it down, he's quiet.

'This is outside our projected parameters,' he admits.

'Yes. Because your projected parameters assumed the system would fail in the ways you modeled, not in the ways that actually emerged from the conditions you created.' You hold his gaze. 'I'm not projecting gradual failure. I'm projecting cascade failure within the next day, possibly less.'

He is quiet for a long time. Something moves in his face that might be the beginning of a reckoning or might be the closing of one. You genuinely can't tell.

'I'll submit your analysis for emergency review,' he says at last. 'The reallocation schedule will be reassessed at the department level.'

'That takes days.'

'The process takes as long as it takes.' He stands. 'File your crane report. I'll ensure the seawall assessment receives priority.'

You leave. You don't believe him. Men like Toris don't reassess—they recalculate acceptable losses and issue new projections.

You lay the crane file in the lamp's circle—timestamps, load figures, the blunt story of a hoist asked to carry more stress than its maintenance circle was fed to absorb. Toris reads the summary line first, then the next, then stops pretending the numbers are news. His mouth settles into something courteous.

'Crane work,' he says. 'File it on the crane docket. That's the channel this office expects.'

'The crane isn't an island.'

'Neither is my schedule.' He sets the page down with care, as if neatness could end the conversation. 'If you want credit for thoroughness, earn it in the right box. Don't waste my afternoon turning an equipment complaint into district philosophy.'

The incense makes impatience smell like virtue. You don't gather the file back up.

You lay your seawall analysis beside the opened crane file so he can't pretend they're different conversations. 'Your models account for gradual material depletion. They don't account for compound effects. There's chemical contamination in the drainage network—toxic compounds building up in the seawall's fuel chambers and rendering the remaining fuel inert. Combined with your material redirection, the wall's maintenance circles aren't degrading gradually—they're accelerating toward cascade failure.'

He is quiet for a long time. Something moves in his face that might be the beginning of a reckoning or might be the closing of one. You genuinely can't tell.

'I'll submit your analysis for emergency review,' he says at last. 'The reallocation schedule will be reassessed at the department level.'

'That takes days.'

'The process takes as long as it takes.' He stands. 'File your crane report. I'll ensure the seawall assessment receives priority.'

You leave. You don't believe him. Men like Toris don't reassess—they recalculate acceptable losses and issue new projections.

Outside the CEA building, you stand in the late afternoon air, organizing your notes. The woman with the permit application is still on the steps, still waiting. The guard is looking at her less and less.

A figure approaches you from the direction of the warehouses—a man about your age, well-dressed in the way of someone who wants to appear not to be anything in particular, carrying himself with the particular ease of someone who has made difficult decisions before and found them easier than expected.

'You came out looking like you found something you couldn't file, Citizen,' he says.

'That's a generous reading.'

'I've seen that expression on a lot of faces coming out of that building.' He falls into step beside you without asking. 'The Red Balance has been watching this district. Toris is doing exactly what the system is designed to do: assign cost downward, defer consequences, call it management. It's not malice. It's architecture.' He pauses. 'The council class controls the Revolutionary Council. The Revolutionary Council controls infrastructure allocation. Infrastructure allocation assigns cost. The only thing that changed from the old system is the credential you need to wield the authority—rebellion heritage and Council appointment instead of noble bloodline. Different name. Same function. The nobility said they were born to govern. The council class says the rebellion gave them the right. I'm not sure the people living in that district can tell the difference.'

'That sounds like a justification for something destructive.'

'It's a description of what's already happened.' He glances at you. 'Red Harrow was paid in blood. Those who paid it chose to. What Toris is doing is Red Harrow without the consent—the cost falls on Karet Bay whether they chose it or not. Someone could take that choice back.' He pauses. 'The cost will fall somewhere, Scholar. It always does. The question is whether we decide where, or we wait.'

He leaves before you can ask his name. You notice he left no pamphlet, no name, no seal. Nothing that could be filed, traced, or officially received. That, too, is a kind of architecture.

Night has fallen over Karet Bay. You are in a dockside tavern because it's the first place you found with light and a table, and your ledger is open but you haven't written anything in it for forty minutes.

You've been running the numbers since you sat down. Every time you finish, you start again. The numbers keep being right. That's the problem.

The material redirection. The maintenance circle failures. Chemical contamination in the drainage network displacing toxic compounds into the seawall's fuel chambers. Each one is a separate problem with a separate cause. None of them would be catastrophic alone. Together, they are converging on a single point.

You think about the Hollow Tower. You studied the incident report in your second year. What you remember is a phrase from the final section: *Multiple small acceptable deviations converging into catastrophic systemic failure.* At the time, you thought about it as an engineering lesson. You thought about it the way you thought about all the incidents—as patterns to recognize and avoid.

You're inside one. You're calculating it from the inside, and the pattern recognizes you back.

The difference between the Hollow Tower and this—the real difference—isn't the physics. It's that the Hollow Tower was a building, and the people inside it were variables. The people inside this district are not variables to you anymore. The faces from the day. The people who held things together with what they had. The ones who didn't ask for your calculations—they just did the work.

Mireth said: the numbers are clean.

The numbers are clean. And they're not enough.
choice2_label: Order another drink and sit with what you know.
choice3_label: Step into the alley, drink your energy tonic, let your hands stop shaking before you talk to anyone else.
choice4_label: Walk the district at night. See what changes after dark.

text:
The workers around you are talking about the same things you've been calculating—but in the language of people who live inside problems rather than analyze them.

An older woman describes how the water pressure in her building dropped three months ago. 'Filed with the CEA. Filed again. Showed them the damage. They sent someone to look. He looked, wrote something down, and left. Two months ago now.' She shrugs. 'It's not personal. They just don't care.'

'That's not true,' says the man across from her. 'Caring isn't the right word for it. They do care—about the transit rail, about the throughput numbers, about the city-level projections. They care about everything except this.' He gestures at the table, at the tavern, at the district outside. 'This doesn't fit in a city-level projection.'

The Freehand woman—the one who spoke to you this morning—leans toward you. You didn't realize she was there until she spoke. 'You know what gets me? The Drowning happened three generations ago. The courts ruled. The principle was established: environmental harm is harm to people. It's the law. And somehow, redirecting the maintenance fuel that keeps this district standing—that's fine. That's an economic decision.' She tilts her head. 'Tell me how those two things coexist.'

You can't. 'One hand pays. Many hands carry,' you say, reciting the saying without thinking.

She gives you a look that is not unkind. 'We've been the many hands for two years, Scholar. We're tired.'

The man across the table adds: 'You want to know where Toris was this afternoon before you came to see him? Someone saw him at the Breakwater — that tavern in the upper quarter where the Council people take their real meetings. Three hours of wine while the maintenance requisition sat on his desk.'

He says it without particular bitterness. Just the flat statement of someone describing the architecture of the world.

The Freehand woman from the morning—Seren—catches your eye. 'There's a pamphleteer,' she says quietly. 'Shows up at the night markets. Never gives a real name. The workers call them Ash because the pamphlets always look like they were printed in a forge.' She pauses. 'Some of what Ash writes is reckless. Some of it is the clearest thinking in this district. If you end up walking the streets tonight—the night market runs until the third bell. Just follow the ink.'

You close your ledger. You don't open it again for a while.

The tavern empties slowly. You stay.

At some point you stop looking at the ledger and start looking at your hands. There is chalk dust in the creases of your palms from the work you did today. The residue of your own expenditure, dried and pale.

You think about something Mireth said on your first day of field training. She said: 'The numbers are the most honest thing in this work. People will lie to you and factions will mislead you and your own feelings will distort things, but the numbers are just the numbers. Learn to trust them.'

You trusted them. You trust them now. The seawall calculations are correct.

What Mireth didn't say—or what you didn't hear—is that the numbers can be correct about what's happening and still be wrong about what matters. The Hollow Tower incident report was numerically accurate. It precisely described what failed and when. It did not say: and here is what was lost in the minutes before the collapse. It did not say: and here is what the three hundred people who died were to each other. It was not equipped to say those things. It wasn't built for them.

You think about the pamphlet you read on the way down—the header in block capitals, YEAR EIGHTY, and what stayed legible after a long day: *Year Zero, we buried the nobility for making others pay for their ease.* Later lines about council offices and portraits blur; the last phrase does not. *Someone tell me what changed.* You joined the Measured Scholars three years ago, rising through the guild's internal assessment process. You had guidance, mentors, connections—the accumulated capital of people who thought you showed promise. Not everyone who wanted to do this work had the same starting point. You know this. You have never thought hard about it.

You are a Measured Scholar. You were trained to find where the cost actually went.

You've found it. It went here. To this district. To Kaelen's hands and Dima's wrench and Elara's fuel chambers and Old Tomas's wife's morning tea. The cost went to people.

The numbers are clean. And they describe something that cannot be described cleanly.

You open your ledger to the last page and write the final timeline. Then you look at it for a long time without moving.
choice1_label: The calculation is complete. You have to act.

text:
The final numbers resolve sometime after midnight.

Timeline to critical structural failure: twelve to twenty-four hours. More likely the shorter end—there's a high-tide surge expected before dawn. When the wall fails, bay water will flood the entire lower docks district. Not a crack. Not a partial failure. The wall's foundation has been compromised along its entire length. Six thousand people.

You sit with the numbers for a long time.

Here is what you have learned today: the Hollow Tower didn't fall because one person made one mistake. It fell because a system of individually acceptable decisions accumulated into an unacceptable result, and no one was in a position to see the whole of it until it was too late. The CEA's material redirection was formally approved. Someone built a water purifier that genuinely helped people. Kaelen's reinforcement circle was the best available option. Every actor made their best calculation with the information they had.

And every calculation failed to account for the connections—the way cost, when pushed down by one hand, flows sideways into someone else's foundations.

No one broke the law of exchange. The cost was paid in full. It's being collected now, from the ground up.

You think about Mireth's folder. The clean numbers. The routine assessment.

You think about what you were sent here to do, and what you found.

You close the ledger, stand up, and run.

You run through the dark streets of Karet Bay. The district is mostly asleep—a few late-shift workers, some tavern stragglers, a dog that watches you with professional interest as you sprint past.

None of them know. They are sleeping in what the seawall assessment describes as an acceptable loss distribution. They are sleeping with the calm of people who trust that if something were critically wrong, someone in authority would have told them.

The seawall is at the district's eastern edge, a dark mass against the faintly lighter darkness of the bay. As you approach, you can hear it—a deep, rhythmic groan that vibrates through your boots. The sound of a structure that has been holding past its limits for a long time and is beginning to feel the arithmetic of that catching up.

You press your diagnostic plate against the cold stone. The reading confirms everything: fuel chambers critical, maintenance circles dormant, structural integrity in the lower sections approaching cascade failure threshold. The high-tide surge is already building pressure against the outer face.

You look back at the sleeping district behind you. Six thousand people who have been paying the cost of this for seven months without being told why they were paying it or what it was going toward. People who patched things with what they had and held the line with what remained and did not know—could not know—that the line would not hold.

Three options. None of them clean. The cost falls somewhere regardless.
choice2_label: Use your remaining preparation time well.
choice3_label: Find Elara before you decide.
choice4_label: Punch the seawall in frustration.
choice5_label: File the formal escalation. You have his orders—make them public record before you face the wall.
choice6_label: Coordinate the evacuation first—the district needs time before any solution.

text:
You find her basement workshop lit, as always—Elara doesn't sleep when her fuel chambers need checking, and she's been awake since your visit. She looks up when you come down the stairs, reads your face, and doesn't ask why you're there.

'The seawall,' she says.

'Tonight. The tide surge.'

She closes her eyes for a moment. Opens them. 'How bad?'

'The whole district, if nothing changes.'

She's quiet for a long time. Then she stands and starts moving—going to a cabinet, pulling out what turns out to be a detailed map of the district's underground conduit network, her own hand in the margins until the page reads like an argument with the official charts.

'What are you going to do?' she asks.

'I don't know yet. I have three options. None of them are good.'

She sets the map on the table and looks at it. 'Tell me.'

You tell her. All three. She listens the way she listens to everything—fully, without interrupting, giving the ideas the weight they deserve. When you're done, she's quiet again for a moment.

Then she says: 'The math will tell you the optimal answer. It's what you're trained for.' She looks up. 'But I've been doing this work for fifteen years, and I've learned that there's a difference between the optimal answer and the right answer. Sometimes they're the same. Sometimes they're not.' She meets your eyes. 'Whatever you decide—make sure it's because you decided it. Not because the calculation decided it for you.'

You stand there for a moment, the map between you.

'One hand pays,' she says quietly. 'Many hands carry. Whatever you need from me—I'm here.'

You send the escalation through the Scholar network relay—Toris's own signed orders, timestamped, annotated against every structural failure you've documented since this morning. Your hands shake slightly as you seal the message. You do not stop to watch them.

It is the most complete formal record you have ever compiled. Material redirection authorization, projected failure rates, current readings, the seven-month timeline from memo to crisis. Everything the process needs to move.

Whether the process moves in time is not a question you can calculate. The seawall is. You run.

You force yourself to stop and think. Preparation is part of the exchange too—acting badly is a higher cost than taking a moment to act well.

You have minutes before you need to commit. What do you have?

Your fuel: one Tier 2 block remaining. Your plates: the reinforcement plate at full activation capacity. Your chalk. Your personal energy: depleted from the day's work, but enough for one serious operation if you're careful. Enough, maybe, for something more if you're not.

What you don't have: enough to hold the seawall alone. No single person can pay the full cost of what's about to happen. But you know people in this district now. People who have been holding it together with less, for longer.

One hand pays. Many hands carry.

You force yourself to breathe. To think like a Scholar. Your ledger is open to the last page and you write the three primary options with a steady hand—the only thing about you right now that is steady. Another line may present itself should the commitments you have gathered align. Which paths you are actually offered next will follow your tallies, what you carry, and who in this district would still answer you—not from the ink alone.

OPTION ONE: Controlled Failure. The seawall has a weak section near the old tenement row where the original maintenance circles were cut into lower-quality stone—a known compromise in the original construction. If you manipulate the structural exchange to direct the failure toward that section, you can create a controlled collapse that plugs the breach with debris before the flood reaches the main residential areas. The district survives. The tenement block doesn't. It houses over a hundred people. You would be choosing them.

OPTION TWO: Redirect the Source. The CEA's material extraction conduit—the pipe that has been feeding the transit rail for seven months—runs directly under this district. If you reverse the flow, you can force the transit rail's accumulated structural reserves back into the seawall's fuel chambers, giving the maintenance circles enough to run through the surge. The transit rail loses power. It is elevated. During early morning operation, with hundreds of commuters already aboard.

OPTION THREE: The Red Harrow Option. A trained alchemist can serve as a living fuel source—using their own body as a catalyst to sustain dormant circles when no external fuel remains. At this scale, with this much accumulated chemical toxicity in the seawall's fuel system, it means running the wall's maintenance circles through your own body and filtering the toxins as they pass. The theory is sound. The accounts from the few recorded cases used clinical language. They used it very carefully.

Every option has a cost. Every cost falls on someone.

Who pays?

text:
Your hands move with the precision that took three years of training to develop. You draw the redirection circle on the seawall—a multi-stage pattern that routes the structural failure toward the single weakest section: the old tenement row.

You tell yourself the calculation justifies it. One hundred people at concentrated risk versus six thousand at distributed risk. The math produces the same answer every time you run it. This is what the CEA would do. This is, in fact, exactly what Toris calculated as an acceptable outcome. You are doing the work his projection said someone would eventually have to do—just without the formal authorization and the managed distance of an office.

The circle activates, drawing from your last fuel block, guided by your personal energy. The seawall groans, shifts—and a section thirty meters wide gives way in a controlled cascade. Stone and iron tumble inward. The tenement's foundation receives the impact. Fractures race up its facade. The lower floors collapse.

The debris pile does exactly what your calculations predicted. It plugs the breach. The rest of the seawall holds. The flood is contained to a single block.

Emergency teams arrive within minutes. They work through the rubble. Some of the people they pull out are alive.

You stand at the edge of the destruction zone, your ledger closed, your chalk snapped in half somewhere in the last few minutes. You don't remember snapping it.

Your calculations were perfect. The district is saved.

And you have become, with your own hands, exactly what Toris would have done with paperwork.

Dawn breaks over Karet Bay. Emergency crews have been working all night. Seventeen people are confirmed dead from the tenement collapse. Forty-three injured. The seawall breach is being temporarily reinforced with emergency materials that were apparently available all along when the situation became visible enough to require them. Interesting.

A CEA official finds you sitting on a chunk of broken masonry at first light and reads your preliminary report. He nods approvingly. 'Controlled failure mitigation. Excellent methodology, Scholar. You saved the district.'

You look at the sheet-covered forms being carried from the rubble. Seventeen of them.

In the days that follow, the CEA formally commends your assessment and decision-making. Controlled failure mitigation becomes a referenced protocol. Your name appears in technical documents. Senior scholars speak of you with something approaching awe. You are given a better office.

Nobody in Karet Bay speaks of you at all.

But Dima—Kaelen's youngest crew member—has started learning structural alchemy from a Freehand teacher, a woman whose name never made it into your paperwork. She was heard telling him: 'You need to know this because no one should ever have to make the choice that Scholar made. We give you knowledge so the exchange has more options.'

He asked her once what she thought of the Scholar who saved the district. She was quiet for a while. Then she said: 'I think they made the calculation correctly. I think the calculation was missing something important. I think they'll spend the rest of their life trying to figure out what it was.'

She didn't say that was a bad thing.

Your calculation was correct. You will spend the rest of your career wondering what correct means.

**[ENDING: THE PERFECT CALCULATION]**

*The Scholar's interpretation of Red Harrow: 'It wasn't a miracle. It was minimized loss.'*

You sprint to the material conduit junction—the access point where the district's redirected fuel flows upward toward the transit rail. Seven months of documentation and three hours of investigation have told you exactly where it runs and exactly how to reach it.

You draw a reversal circle around the junction using your chalk—custom work, fast and precise. This is Level 5 systems alchemy, the outer edge of your training, and you know it. The chalk blazes as you run your last fuel block through it, force-reversing the flow: the accumulated structural reserves in the transit rail's fuel systems begin moving backward, down through the conduit, into the seawall's empty fuel chambers.

The wall shudders as fuel floods the dormant chambers. The maintenance circles snap awake, one by one, as their reserves recover. The structural groaning quiets. The fracture propagation slows, stops, begins to reverse.

The seawall holds.

In the upper city, the transit rail loses power. The emergency braking systems engage across the elevated network. On two of the steeper sections, they engage a moment too late.

You can't hear it from here. The bay is already calmer.

You sit at the base of the seawall and watch the water. It is no longer trying to come in.

By noon, the full picture has emerged. The transit rail incident killed two hundred and twelve people. Two elevated cars failed on the Highpoint loop. The economic damage to the upper city is enormous. The political damage to the CEA is larger.

The lower docks of Karet Bay are intact. Not one resident lost.

The CEA declares you a fugitive. The Measured Scholars suspend your credentials pending investigation. Warrants are issued across three districts. But Kaelen's crew—dock workers who know every hidden passage in the waterfront—move you to a Freehands safehouse before the enforcers reach the district. They do this without being asked.

Elara finds you there. She doesn't offer comfort. She offers clarity.

'You redistributed the cost,' she says. 'The CEA assigned Karet Bay's cost to Karet Bay without asking. You took that cost and moved it to the people who made the assignment.' She pauses. 'Two hundred and twelve people died, and none of them were Toris, or the officers who signed the reallocation order, or the developers who profited from the transit rail.'

'I know.'

'I'm not saying what you did was right. I'm saying the math was never going to be clean.' She looks at you steadily. 'The question was always: who decides where the cost falls? You decided. For once, it didn't fall here.'

You sit with that for a long time.

The district holds together. Word spreads through the lower districts—the Scholar who turned the river uphill. The Freehands grow bolder. Workers organize. The CEA, facing public evidence of the material redirection and its consequences, agrees to a formal review. Toris is reassigned.

You are still a fugitive. You find that you are able to live with this.

**[ENDING: THE RIVER RUNS UPHILL]**

*For the first time in Karet Bay's history, someone asked: why do the same people always pay? And paid the cost of asking.*

You press your hands against the seawall and open yourself to it.

The theory is sound. Under extreme conditions, an alchemist can serve as a living fuel source—using their own biological energy as a catalyst to sustain dormant circles when no external fuel remains. The body becomes the fuel chamber. The maintenance circles draw from you directly.

The few records of this describe it clinically. You have read those records. The clinical language does not fully prepare you.

The wall's maintenance circles connect through your palms and begin to draw. The toxic chemical compounds in the fuel chambers flow through the connection—your body is processing them as catalyst, filtering the useful energy from the contaminated material, feeding it back into the circles. It works. The physics are correct.

The physical cost is not clinical.

Your hands begin to change—the skin darkening, hardening, taking on a crystalline texture where the compounds are being processed and deposited. Something adjusts in your spine. Your nervous system registers the overload as pain, then more pain, then something past pain that doesn't have a name.

You hold. Because the math says: thirty minutes to tide peak. If you hold for thirty minutes, the surge passes, and the wall holds with it.

Behind you, in the dark streets, someone has found you. Then someone else. Kaelen's crew—dock workers who know this waterfront in the dark—begin organizing. Elara's Freehands network moves through the district. Evacuation routes, just in case. They saw you running. They followed. They don't know what you're doing but they can see that you're holding something.

They've been holding this district together for two years. One more night.

You wake in Elara's basement workshop. Your hands are the first thing you see. They are wrong.

The skin is mottled—patches of dark, crystalline growth interspersed with raw tissue. Your fingers bend correctly but feel different, as though the bones have been rebuilt from a slightly different material. They have, in a sense.

You sit up. Moving hurts. Elara is sitting across from you, watching with an expression that has given up trying to hide what it is.

'You're alive,' she says. 'The wall held through the surge. The whole district got out in time—Kaelen's crew started the evacuation when they found you at the wall. Everyone who needed to be somewhere else, was somewhere else.' A pause. 'The CEA is sending emergency repair teams. Apparently a seawall crisis is difficult to reclassify as within acceptable parameters when six thousand people watched it happen and have been telling that story since dawn.'

She pauses again. 'You're distorted, Vael. What you filtered through yourself—the chemical compounds, the seven months of accumulated toxic cost—it changed you. Permanently. The district physician has looked at your hands. She says the crystallization is stable. She says a lot of other things too, in clinical language.'

You look at your hands. The crystalline patches catch the light.

They're not beautiful. They're the visible record of a choice to pay a debt yourself instead of assigning it elsewhere. This is what it looks like, when the exchange is honest and the cost is yours.

In the weeks that follow, the CEA cannot ignore Karet Bay anymore. Evidence of the material redirection becomes public record. Overseer Toris is reassigned. The transit rail review begins. The district's material allocation is restored.

You don't return to the Scholar's Quarter. The Measured Scholars don't know what to do with a colleague whose hands are a demonstration that calculations have physical weight.

You stay in Karet Bay. Elara teaches you practical alchemy—built on direct relationship with materials, not just analysis of them. Kaelen's crew treats you as one of their own. Dima asks you, once, if it hurt. You say yes. He thinks about this for a while. Then he asks: 'Was it worth it?' You say: 'I don't know yet. Ask me in ten years.'

He writes that down.

Your hands are changed. But when you press those crystalline palms against a failing wall or a fractured pipe or a joint that needs honest work, the energy flows clean.

The cost was real. The cost was yours. In a world where someone always pays—choosing to pay yourself is not the only form of courage. But it is the most honest one.

**[ENDING: THE COSTLY GOOD DEED]**

*'This position will not hold. If I leave, it fails now. If I stay, it fails later. Later is enough.'*

You roll over and pull the thin blanket over your head. The anomaly has waited this long. It can wait another hour.

You wake to the sound of Mireth's voice directly above you, which is somewhat like waking to the sound of a glacier expressing disappointment.

'Vael. The crane you were assigned to investigate collapsed at noon. Three workers injured. The CEA is demanding answers. I sent you seven hours ago.'

She pauses. She has a talent for pauses that contain entire essays.

'You were asleep.'

'I was—'

'Asleep. While infrastructure failed and people were hurt. Because you decided your bed had higher priority than your assignment.'

She sets a document on your chest. It is a formal notice of dismissal from the Measured Scholars. Effective immediately. You are to vacate the dormitory by evening.

You stare at the ceiling. The cracks are still there, mapped in your memory. You'll have plenty of time to memorize new ones wherever you end up. The anomaly, it turns out, could not wait.

**[GAME OVER — THE SNOOZE BUTTON OF DESTINY]**

You lean further out the narrow window for a better view of the lower docks. The morning air is bracing. The view is spectacular. The windowsill, it turns out, has been quietly degrading for years due to the same ambient maintenance failures affecting all structures in the Scholar's Quarter's cheaper annexes.

The stone crumbles under your weight with the gentle finality of a metaphor.

You have approximately two and a half seconds of freefall to appreciate the irony: a Measured Scholar undone by a structural failure they didn't measure. Your ledger flutters open beside you in the wind, pages catching the light like the world's most tragically earnest butterfly.

The groundskeeper later files a report describing the incident as 'unscheduled rapid vertical transit.' The Measured Scholars add 'window maintenance inspection' to their quarterly checklist. Mireth stares at the checklist for a long time before signing it.

**[GAME OVER — GRAVITY: THE ORIGINAL EXCHANGE]**

You hold up your CEA authorization seal and adopt your most commanding voice.

'By the authority vested in me by the Coordinated Exchange Authority, I order this crew to cease all operations immediately! Anyone who resists will be noted for obstruction of an official investigation!'

There is a brief silence. Kaelen blinks. His crew blinks. The boy with the wrench blinks.

Then six dock workers who have spent their entire adult lives hauling three-ton ore crates—six people with forearms thicker than your thighs and the collective patience of people who have been having a bad year—take one slow, unified step forward.

'Scholar,' Kaelen says, with something approaching genuine regret, 'you just threatened the livelihoods of six people who bench-press your body weight for warm-up. In a district where the nearest CEA enforcer is forty minutes away.'

What follows is less a beating and more a brief, unanimous editorial on the limits of institutional authority. The boy with the wrench just watches. He's learning something, but not what you intended him to learn.

You wake up two hours later in a drainage ditch. Your ledger is gone. Your chalk is gone. Your authorization seal has been taken, presumably as a trophy. You are alive, which is more than the mathematics of the situation necessarily required.

**[GAME OVER — AUTHORITY IS A SOCIAL CONSTRUCT]**

Kaelen's hand closes on your wrist before your fingers cross the chalk. 'Don't,' he says quietly—too quietly for theater, loud enough for the crew. 'That's live reinforcement. Discharge follows the path of least resistance. Right now that's shaped like a Scholar with wet palms and a guilty conscience. My people use gloves. Grounded tools. You have a plate—use it without inventing new data points.'

You can step back into what you already measured. You can ask him to prove the reading another way. Or you can finish the thought your body started before your ethics caught up.

text:
You already had the warning. Your scholarly curiosity still gets the better of your scholarly self-preservation. You reach out and touch the active reinforcement circle with your bare finger.

In your defense, you have handled alchemical circle work before. In the laboratory. Under controlled conditions. With proper equipment. None of those qualifiers apply here.

The circle discharges directly into your hand. Every muscle in your body contracts simultaneously. You experience a moment of crystalline clarity in which you understand, with perfect mathematical precision, exactly how much activation energy is currently moving through your nervous system and exactly how much your nervous system was designed to handle. The ratio is deeply unfavorable.

Kaelen drags your twitching body away from the crane. Your hair is standing on end. Your ledger has somehow caught fire. One of your boots is on the wrong foot, a mystery that will never be solved.

'I told you not to touch it,' Kaelen says, though you cannot hear him because your ears are producing a frequency that your own calculations would describe as structurally inadvisable.

The district physician gives you the same look she apparently has ready for visiting Scholars.

**[GAME OVER — PEER REVIEW (IMMEDIATE)]**

The basement entrance is right there, but the alley to the left offers a shorter approach. You know this because it's on the district map. What the map does not indicate—because maps are generally disinterested in such details—is that the alley serves as the established territory of a feral cat colony.

Not ordinary cats. Karet Bay cats. Cats that have been subsisting in a fuel-depleted district for over a year and have responded by becoming larger, more strategic, and possessed of an unsettling collective sense of grievance.

You are halfway through the alley when twenty-seven pairs of luminous eyes open in the darkness. The alpha cat—a scarred, one-eared animal the size of a small dog—drops from a fire escape onto your shoulder with the precision of a trained operative.

What follows is, by objective measure, the most one-sided conflict in Karet Bay's recorded history. The cats don't want your food. They don't want your ledger. They want to make a specific point about territorial sovereignty and what happens when Scholars fail to read maps properly.

You emerge forty minutes later, shredded, comprehensively humbled, and missing your authorization seal. The alpha cat appears to have taken it. You suspect you have been issued a citation.

**[GAME OVER — THE FERAL EXCHANGE]**

'May I?' you ask, gesturing to the purifier's output tap. Elara shrugs.

The water comes out clear. It smells clean. You take a sip.

Here is what Elara's purifier does: it removes chemical contaminants from the district's water supply and displaces them elsewhere. What it does not do is remove the trace alchemical flux that leaches into the water from the active circle work itself. For the residents of Karet Bay—who have spent their lives building tolerance to ambient alchemical conditions—this trace flux is a nonissue.

For a Scholar who has spent their entire career in a hermetically maintained dormitory, it is a very significant issue.

Your digestive system stages an immediate and emphatic protest. It is not subtle about this. Elara watches you turn three colors she was not aware humans could access.

'You're not from around here,' she observes.

The district physician later describes it as 'a notable response to localized alchemical flux.' This is clinical language for: you spent the next four hours regretting a sip of water. The investigation does not progress in this time.

**[GAME OVER — LOCAL WATER FOR LOCAL PEOPLE]**

Something inside you snaps. Possibly it's the incense. Possibly it's the smooth hands. Possibly it's the word 'acceptable' applied to nine hundred human lives by a man sitting in a chair that costs more than a dock worker earns in a year.

You grab the edge of Toris's mahogany desk and flip it.

It is, you discover mid-flip, an extraordinarily heavy desk. The physics require full commitment. Your back makes a sound that spines are not designed to make. The desk goes over anyway, because you have committed.

Toris's inkwell, schematics, documents, incense burner, and a small crystal paperweight all achieve independent flight. The inkwell lands on his immaculate shirt. The incense sets fire to the nearest schematic. The paperweight exits through the window at speed.

Toris looks at you. You look at Toris.

'Guards,' Toris says, with the precise calm of a man who has apparently prepared for this possibility.

The guards are very large. They do not ask questions. You are removed from the building and placed in the district holding facility, where you will have several hours to calculate exactly how many years of professional credibility you have exchanged for three seconds of catharsis.

In retrospect: extremely poor exchange rate.

**[GAME OVER — FLIPPING THE TABLE ON DIPLOMACY]**

Rational thought has abandoned you. Six thousand people are facing catastrophe because of a convergence of failures that nobody saw coming, you are standing at the epicenter of it with depleted fuel reserves and no plan, and something in you has given up on calculation entirely.

So you punch the seawall.

You put your full body weight behind it—all one hundred and forty pounds of sleep-deprived, fuel-depleted Scholar, fist against three meters of reinforced stone and iron.

Two things happen simultaneously. First, you break four bones in your hand. The pain is extraordinary and immediate. Second, and more consequentially, the impact sends a percussive shockwave through the wall's already critically stressed foundation, which has been waiting for exactly this kind of activation. The micro-fractures that your earlier assessment described as 'propagating at an alarming rate' receive precisely the energy they needed to complete their work.

The section of wall directly in front of you gives way with the resigned certainty of something that has been trying to hold on and has finally been given permission to stop.

Your last clearly formed thought is a calculation: the mass of incoming water versus the structural resistance of one human body. The math is not in your favor.

In your field notes, the entry for Crane Seven remains unfinished. Mireth reads it three times before filing it.

**[GAME OVER — THE SCHOLAR'S FIST]**

You hesitate. Dima has been writing the whole time—not pretending to write, actually writing, with the focused efficiency of someone who has been doing this for a long time.

You lean over slightly. The handwriting is careful and small, the kind developed when paper costs something. Sketches fill the margins—crane joint diagrams, drainage maps, structural stress patterns that any first-year Scholar would recognize. Labeled in a neat hand: 'crane seven joint stress 3wks ago,' 'substation 2 — reading wrong,' 'where does the fuel go?'

You are looking at seven months of district-level field notes kept by a fifteen-year-old dock worker with a borrowed pencil.

'You've been documenting the infrastructure failures,' you say. It comes out sounding more like an accusation than you intended.

Dima glances at the notebook. Then at you. 'I didn't know what else to do with the information. Nobody official was doing anything with it.' A pause. 'My dad said the first step to fixing something is knowing exactly what's wrong.'

He flips to a page near the back. A hand-drawn map of the lower district, annotated with arrows and question marks. At the bottom of the map, circled three times: a building location. The circle has a note beside it: '????? music???? alchemy???? both????'

'What's this?' you ask.

'That's the thing I haven't figured out,' Dima says. 'Some nights I can hear something from that building. Sounds like singing. But there's also alchemical runoff in the drain gutter beside it—Tier 1 emissions, weird patterns, nothing that matches any standard operation.' He pauses. 'I was going to investigate but the foreman said to mind my own business. He says that about most things. He's not always right.'

He looks at you. 'You're a Scholar. You have instruments. You're supposed to figure out what things are.'

The building is three streets south, in a part of the lower district that doesn't appear in any recent administrative record—which means it either doesn't exist officially or exists under a classification that nobody has updated in at least twenty years. Both options are entirely plausible for Karet Bay.

You find it without difficulty. A three-story structure of old stone, windows bricked over on the upper floors, a cellar entrance that would look completely unremarkable except for two things:

First: you can hear music. Not faint music. Actual music, punctuated by what sounds like enthusiastic applause from an audience that has not calibrated its enthusiasm to the acoustic properties of a stone basement.

Second: your diagnostic plate is registering alchemical emissions from inside. Level 2 reinforcement energy, with trace indicators of flow manipulation and what appears to be—you check this three times—drainage reconfiguration. Someone is performing fairly sophisticated structural alchemy in what appears to be a cultural venue.

These are not activities that typically co-occur.

You look at the cellar door. It has a sign on it. The sign has been painted with some care and reads: TONIGHT — 'THE ACCEPTABLE LOSS REVUE' — KARET BAY AMATEUR THEATRICAL SOCIETY — ADMISSION: ONE FUEL BLOCK OR ONE HONEST CONVERSATION.

Your diagnostic plate is still going. The readings are getting more interesting the longer you stand here.

The door is slightly ajar. Someone has left a playbill in the gap.

You look at the last line for a long time. Then you look at your diagnostic plate, which is currently registering the kind of alchemical output that you would normally file a priority report about.

You go inside.

The stairs descend into a basement that has been transformed into a proper theater with approximately forty seats, actual curtains (alchemically hemmed, your instruments confirm), stage lighting achieved through what appears to be a series of modified fuel chamber arrays, and an audience of roughly thirty dock workers, market vendors, and neighborhood residents who all look at you with the particular expression of people who are deeply unsurprised that a Scholar has just walked in.

A woman with chalk dust on her hands and the general bearing of someone who has been running this institution for years appears at your elbow.

You emerge from the basement with your field ledger open and your instruments giving readings you are going to have to explain very carefully when you get back to the Scholar's Quarter.

Petra—the director, whose last name turns out to be Voss, who has been running the Karet Bay Amateur Theatrical Society for six years—is standing at the top of the stairs with her arms crossed and the expression of someone who has just watched a Scholar process an extremely unusual experience.

'Well,' she says.

'You have been performing alchemical reinforcement on the district's seawall infrastructure for four months,' you say. 'As a theatrical byproduct.'

'I have been performing structural art,' she says. 'The structural integrity of the wall is a side effect.'

'The drainage reconfiguration in your stage floor. The reinforcement circle embedded in your practice set. The fuel chamber arrays you've been feeding into the—'

'Art,' she says.

'The readings from the wall's north foundation show a measurably higher integrity coefficient than your parameters should have allowed for at this point in the—'

'Art,' she says again, but this time a small smile has appeared. 'Functional art. Art that holds things together while the people who are supposed to hold things together are busy filing requisitions.'

You look at your instruments. The seawall's north section is in better condition than your earlier assessment indicated. Not good condition—still failing, still urgent, still a crisis tightening across days rather than giving you seasons to argue. But the section nearest the theater's drainage output has about twelve percent more structural reserves than your model predicted. Twelve percent. Not enough. But something.

'I should file a formal assessment of this,' you say.

'I know,' says Petra. 'You should probably also mention that thirty people have been watching a satirical play about the situation every week for four months and nobody in an official capacity showed up until now. That seems like relevant data.'

She hands you a second playbill. Dima's map is on the back. She's already written her drainage circle design in the margin.

'You know Dima,' you say.

'He drew the map,' she says. 'He's been our audience data analyst. Very thorough kid.'

'Have you been aware,' you ask, 'that your drainage modifications have been partially offsetting the toxic compound buildup in the seawall's fuel chambers?'

Petra considers this with the focus of someone absorbing a calculation.

'No,' she says. 'We just noticed the wall smelled better. We thought that was the incense.'

'It was the chemistry.'

'Some things are both.'

You stand at the top of the stairs in the late afternoon light. Behind you, the theater is already filling for the evening house—you can hear Dima explaining the playbill annotations to someone, hear the stage crew testing the modified fuel array lights, hear what sounds suspiciously like an argument about whether the Toris character's hat reads as too literal for satire or too thin to land.

'You should file a counter-report,' you say. 'Against Toris. Formally. With evidence. You've been documenting this longer than I have.'

'I know.' She looks at the street. 'I'm waiting until the run ends. Bad luck to open a bureaucratic dispute mid-production.' A pause. 'Also I wanted to see how it ends.'

You look at the seawall in the distance. You think about endings. About the difference between writing them and living them.

'The wall doesn't care about curtain times,' you say. 'Whatever happens next, it happens on a short clock—district time, not stage time.'

She nods once, with the gravity of someone accepting a stage direction. 'Then we'll have our best material by morning.'

You leave at a run.

You stay. Behind you, Petra is already shifting chairs for the next rehearsal block, the sound like dry punctuation against stone. Dima sits at a low table with his notebook and a candle-stub, watching you with the careful attention of someone who has been waiting to see what you would do.

The seawall is failing. The district will pay for that failure on a timeline you cannot unwrite—but you were never the only person who mattered here.

You sit down across from Dima. 'Show me what you've written. We finish the record while the margin still exists.'

He opens the notebook. The first page is titled: *Karet Bay, Volume Four — Redirection Ledger.*

Beneath it: everything.

text:
The instinct overwhelms you mid-applause. You stand up.

'STOP,' you announce, in the voice you have been practicing for situations exactly like this one. 'This performance constitutes unauthorized alchemical activity within a residential zone. Under CEA assessment protocols, I am placing the organizer of this activity under—'

The theater is very quiet.

Thirty dock workers, market vendors, and neighborhood residents look at you. Then at each other.

Then the entire cast, still in costume, walks off the stage in a body and sits down in the audience seats. Petra walks to your chair, sits down in it, and opens your field ledger to a blank page.

'Counterpoint,' she says. 'You walked into a free community performance and declared yourself an authority figure. In Karet Bay. While half the district is still trading gossip about Toris and the crane.' She looks at the audience. 'Show of hands: who thinks the Scholar should apologize and sit back down?'

Every hand goes up.

'Show of hands: who thinks the Scholar should be escorted out, gently, before they embarrass themselves further?'

Every hand goes up again.

'The audience has voted,' Petra says, in the tone of someone whose production values are, apparently, impeccable even when off-script.

What follows is less an arrest and more a collective theatrical experience in which you are very politely escorted to the cellar stairs by cast members who manage to make even this feel like choreography. Dima is at the top of the stairs when you emerge. He's writing something in his notebook. He shows it to you before you go.

It says: 'the Scholar tried to arrest the play. This is also information about what happens when you try to enforce authority without understanding cost.'

You don't have a response to that. You walk back to the Scholar's Quarter. The seawall doesn't wait.

**[GAME OVER — THE SCHOLAR MISSED THE POINT, AND ALSO THE ENDING]**

'Wait,' you say.

Petra turns. The cast looks at you with the identical expression of people who have learned to take unexpected developments in stride.

'Do you need someone for Act III?' you ask. 'I don't know if you have an Act III. But if you do—I've only been in this district a few days and I've accumulated substantially more material than most of your scripts seem to contain, and I'm a very precise annotator.'

'We don't have an Act III,' Petra says.

'I could write one,' you say.

The seawall is failing. Six thousand people are at risk. You have instruments. You have training. You have one Tier 2 fuel block and a reinforcement plate and the calculations that Mireth sent you here to complete.

You understand, in this moment, that none of that is currently as compelling to you as the idea of sitting in this theater and writing the ending of a play about the stretch you've just lived through.

'It would take maybe three performances to get it right,' you say.

Petra watches you for a long moment. Then she pulls a chair to the front of the stage and sits down across from you.

'The lead character,' she says, 'is a Scholar who walks into a district, sees everything that's wrong, has all the information needed to act, and then stays at the theater to write a play about it instead.'

'That's not quite—' you start.

'That's exactly it,' she says. 'That's always been the fourth act. We just never had a Scholar show up to play it.'

You sit down.

The seawall fails before dawn. The district floods. You survive. So does the theater—Dima had the presence of mind, in the chaos, to drag your diagnostic plates and fuel blocks to the upper story. When the waters recede, you are still there. You write the play. It is very accurate. You perform it 47 times. Eventually, someone in the audience knows someone on the Revolutionary Council. A formal investigation of Toris begins.

It takes three years. The play is more efficient.

You are no longer a Scholar. You're something else. You're not sure the title has been invented yet.

**[GAME OVER — THE ACCEPTABLE LOSS: A LIFE IN THEATRE]**

*(This is technically also an ending. Mireth would like a word with you.)*

Kaelen's hands go still on the crane's base section. He's looking at a particular junction—the join between the original construction and the later extension. His finger traces a circle carved into the stone.

'My father did this section,' he says. It's the most quiet you've heard him.

You look at the circle. It's a standard Tier 2 reinforcement design—efficient, clean, the kind of work that suggests someone who had absorbed their specialization deeply enough that they stopped thinking about the technique and started thinking only about the material. The circle is decades old. It still reads as structurally active on your instruments.

'He worked the seawall construction crew. The original build—not the extensions. He said it was the most important work he ever did because it would outlast him by a hundred years if they did it right.' Kaelen pauses. 'They did it right.'

'When did he—'

'Going on ten years. Routine wall work—a maintenance lift on his crane crew; the rigging gave. The official file still stamps operator fault.' He says it the way people say things they have said many times—without bitterness, just with the particular flatness of a fact that has been carried for long enough to become part of the landscape. 'He would have taken one look at what's happening to this district and he would have known exactly where to start.' A pause. 'He would also have known exactly who to blame.'

You look at the circle again. Then at your instruments. The circle is still active because it was done with Tier 2 materials and genuine expertise. It has been maintaining itself—slowly, quietly, doing exactly what it was designed to do—for thirty years. Around it, the hastily-added Tier 0 patches are already beginning to fail.

You think: the people who built things well are not here to defend what they built. The people who degraded the materials aren't here either. What's here is the building.

'He did good work,' you say.

Kaelen looks at you. 'Yes,' he says. 'He did.'

Wind off the water snatches at your sleeve. Your plates remember the crane. Your notes remember the district—circles starved, walls whispering strain, redirection signatures pointing the same direction every time you look. You thumb your Scholar seal and your field ledger open and start drafting a formal escalation to the CEA Regional Authority: urgent priority, preliminary evidence, recommendation to freeze transit-rail allocation and open Overseer Toris.

Halfway through the authorization codes you stop typing.

The crane is documented. The pattern in the streets is real. The redirection, though—you have Kaelen's word, worker testimony, instrument readings that *suggest* without yet *proving*. A full CEA escalation wants a chain of causation on paper. Without substation orders or a finished seawall assessment, you have a strong case and not yet a closed one.

File now and the machinery wakes: routing, review, someone upstream notified while your file is still half-empty. Paperwork can outrun a person carrying plates.

Your ledger stays open. The escalation sits half-written.

The choice is: file now and trust the process, or gather more evidence first.

text:
You submit the escalation through your Scholar authorization portal. Priority: urgent. Status: preliminary assessment with pending full documentation.

The CEA's administrative system confirms receipt. A case number is generated. The case is routed to the Infrastructure Dispute Review division.

Two hours later, you receive a formal response from Overseer Toris's administrative office.

The response notes that you have submitted a 'preliminary and incomplete' assessment with 'insufficient documentation to support the requested authorization review.' It further notes that Measured Scholar assessments require either a full assessment report or a direct supervisor cosignature to trigger authority-level review. It further notes—with the particular precision of a document written by someone who has handled Scholars before—that 'submission of incomplete reports may be noted in the Scholar's field record as indicative of insufficient field judgment.'

At the bottom of the document: your field authorization has been 'temporarily suspended pending consultation with your Senior Scholar,' and you are advised to 'return to the Scholar Quarter and await assignment review.'

You look at the document. You look at the district around you. You look at your instruments, which are still showing the readings that the CEA has just formally declined to act on.

Your field writ is in procedural abeyance. The pavement under your boots and the readings on your plates are not.

Mireth is going to have a remarkable amount to say about this.

Exit opportunity: you could contact Mireth directly and explain the situation before the consultation review begins. Or you could go back and gather the documentation that would have made this unnecessary.
choice1_label: Contact Mireth immediately. Explain everything. Request emergency cosign.
choice2_label: There is nothing to be done now but return and face the review.

text:
You return to the Scholar Quarter.

Mireth is waiting. She has the suspension notice in her hand. She is looking at it the way she looks at calculations that fail to account for human behavior—not with surprise, but with the particular disappointment of someone watching a prediction come true.

'Walk me through the decision,' she says.

You do. She listens without interrupting. When you finish, she sets the notice down.

'You had an urgent situation. You had preliminary evidence. You escalated before the evidence was complete.' She is quiet for a moment. 'By the time the authorization review committee meets—assuming they expedite it, which they will not—the situation you were trying to report will have resolved itself. In one direction or another.'

'The seawall—'

'I know.' She picks up her pen. 'I am going to cosign a new authorization right now and personally walk it to the Infrastructure Director. We may still catch it.' She writes quickly. 'But your field authorization is suspended until I complete a supervisory review. You're not returning to Karet Bay today.'

She hands you the new authorization form for delivery. Then she looks at you with the expression of someone who chose her words very carefully this morning and is wondering if they were the right ones.

'Good work,' she says, 'is not the same as right work.'

A pause. 'In this case, you did neither.'

The authorization reaches the Infrastructure Director at 1900 hours. The seawall assessment is formally prioritized at 0200. The surge hits at 0330. The response teams are assembled by 0500. By then, the lower docks have been underwater for two hours.

You file a full report. It is accurate, complete, and too late. It references the suspended authorization. The review committee finds your field judgment 'developmentally concerning but improvable.' You are assigned a mentor. The mentor is Mireth.

She never mentions it again.

**[GAME OVER — THE CORRECT PROCESS, INCORRECTLY TIMED]**

She's standing at the base of the Drowning of Karet Bay plaque when you see her. Not examining it—she has clearly read it before, many times—just standing near it with the stillness of someone who came here with a purpose and is taking a moment before completing it.

'Mireth,' you say.

'Vael.' She turns. She looks the same as she does in the Scholar Quarter, except that here she looks slightly wrong—the way someone's familiar face looks unexpected when you see them in a context that doesn't belong to them. 'Don't make that face. I do come to the field sometimes.'

'I've never seen you come to the field.'

'I come when I think it's necessary.' She looks at the plaque for a moment. 'I sent you here because you're good at the technical work. I came because I wanted to see what you were finding before you decided what to do with it.'

She has your briefing in her hand. She has clearly read it twice.

'Your assessment is accurate,' she says. 'The crane, the material redirection, the seawall projections—all sound.' A pause. 'You've also been talking to people.'

'That's part of field assessment.'

'Not the way you've been doing it.' She looks at you with the precision of someone who is being very careful about what she says next. 'There are three previous assessments of this district in our files. Two of them have identical recommendations: continue monitoring, flag for review, defer to Authority decision. The third one—mine, from nine years ago—says the same thing but with different wording.'

She is quiet for a moment.

'I sent three previous Scholars here. They all filed correct reports. They all recommended proper channels. They are all still waiting for the proper channels to respond.' She tucks the briefing under her arm. 'I wanted to see if you would do the same. I wanted to see if you would—' She stops. 'I am going to give you a piece of information that is not in any official document. You will not find it in your briefing materials or in your training or in nineteen years of my field reports, because I have never known how to file it.'

She looks at the plaque again.

'The Drowning of Karet Bay happened because good work was done correctly, thoroughly, and in compliance with every protocol—and nobody stopped to ask whether correct and good were the same thing that day.' A pause. 'I've been asking myself that question for nineteen years. I still don't have the answer.'

She hands you the briefing. 'Whatever you decide—decide it. Don't defer it. This district does not have time for deferred.'

She leaves the way she came, without looking back at the plaque.

There is no internal memo K-B-11. You invented it on the spot because sounding like paperwork is the only camouflage your brain could find.

The cistern annex is what happens when civil engineering loses an argument with gravity and wins anyway out of spite. The floor is a lasagna of incompatible patches, each generation convinced *this* layer will be the adult in the room.

The walls wear chalk stripes—human load marks, until you notice the second alphabet: claw-grooves at knee height, grouped in threes and fives like a tally of sins only cats can count.

Your diagnostic plate makes a noise you have never heard it make before. It is the acoustic equivalent of "I refuse."

Ambient readings: near-zero district fuel, maximum attitude. Copper dust in the mortar as if someone has been buffing the building with pennies and resentment. Fish oil older than your ethics seminar. Fur. So much fur. The fur appears to be doing *governance*.

Eyes open in the dark. More eyes. The number is somewhere between "enough" and "prime minister."

You are not in the alley shortcut. You are in their lobby. There is no reception desk. There is a rock that is absolutely a reception desk if you value your ankles.

text:
You kneel with the solemnity of someone about to misfile reality.

Up close, the scratches resolve into notation that should not work but does: a spiral with a deliberate break at the seventh turn—drainage bleed-off grammar—married to vertical ticks that look like a ledger of meals, shipments, or vendettas. Possibly all three. Possibly the cats use the same column for all of them.

An orange tomcat with one ear and the moral authority of a dock foreman drops onto your knee without asking permission. Permission is a human concept. He is reviewing your soul.

You understand, with the clarity of a nightmare, that this colony has spent months performing *unauthorized structural grooming*: fur and oil and copper dust packed into stone grooves until the stone behaves slightly differently—just enough to nudge the nastiest seepage away from the worst crack, like a crowd parting for someone carrying hot soup.

It is a circle. It is also a hobby. It is also, technically, tax evasion if taxes are made of physics.

The tomcat stares at your chalk. You get the distinct impression he is waiting for you to embarrass yourself scientifically.
