You unwrap dock rations. The fish is so salty it could serve as a Tier 0 desiccant in a pinch.

The orange tomcat performs a sniff so judgmental it should count as adversarial examination. Then—protocol collapses—he accepts tribute.

Other cats teleport in. You did not see them move. You are no longer sure they obey Euclidean rules. They arrange themselves around a flat stone that is obviously the Prime Minister of stones. Stains on it are older than the Republic.

For several minutes, the annex sounds like a wet percussion section. Nobody removes your face. You mark this as a diplomatic win in your ledger next to a question mark shaped like a cat.

The tomcat returns, tail high, and stamps your notes with his nose. Wet ink. Binding precedent.

You write: *Non-human maintenance behavior observed. Possible passive circle analog via organic deposition. Political status: unclear. Theological status: worse.*

The tomcat watches you write the word "theological" and seems offended on behalf of science.

You whisper to the assembly like a lunatic: 'There is a woman downstairs running clean water through actual alchemy. Your weird fur-math is nudging sludge so her intake doesn't drown in spite. I need to reach that door without becoming a folk tale.'

The cats do not clap. Cats do not clap. They *align*, which is clapping for people who think in conspiracy.

The orange tom walks toward the back of the annex like he is leading you to committee. You follow. You have followed worse directions today. Those directions had letterhead.

Ahead: a lintel, a hollow, and the distinct sensation that democracy is about to occur in a laundry pile.

The chamber is socks and string and bottle caps and one brass CEA button that absolutely fell off someone's coat and absolutely became a religious object.

The orange tom knocks a cap off a crate. It rings like a gavel. Twelve cats and you achieve quorum, assuming "quorum" means "enough glaring to bend light."

A kitten tries to steal your fuel block. You negotiate it back with eye contact and shame.

This is not in your field manual. Your field manual is weeping in another room.

The Clerk of the Hairball—this is not a title you assigned; it is a title that *happened*—stares at you until you accept that you are about to sit through formal procedure.

When the parliament adjourns, reality rushes back in like a tide of paperwork that forgot to knock.

You are kneeling on wet stone with a strip of ration cloth, three fish scales, and a chalk spiral that is not activated but is definitely *sincere*. The tomcat nose-bumps each scale. Other cats witness by whisker. One abstains on grounds of being a sock.

You have signed something. You are not sure which jurisdiction it belongs to. You're fairly sure it's not Caldris. You're fairly sure it's older.

The colony escorts you through a gap labeled UNSAFE on the map. The map is correct: it is unsafe for dignity. It is very safe for ankles if you walk like you mean it.

Elara's door waits ahead, chalk binding humming like a polite threat.

You have joined a parallel government whose cabinet meetings involve yarn.

You announce, in ringing tones, that each animal will receive a provisional index line in the colony ledger.

The cats do not boo. Booing is inefficient. They open an adversarial examination in triplicate, using claws.

What follows is the dark alley encounter's director's cut: now with thematic coherence. You have *opted in*. The colony treats this as enthusiastic consent to become a training exercise.

Forty minutes later you possess: no spare chalk, one fewer glove, a new understanding that filing gloss can draw blood, and the distinct memory of being used as a training prop for a kitten learning the word "no."

The alpha returns your authorization seal. Not out of mercy. Brass upsets the stomach.

**[GAME OVER — ADVERSARIAL AUDIT (FERAL, DOUBLE-BLIND, CLAWED)]**

You kneel. You lift your Scholar's seal. You attempt to crown the tomcat as First Citizen of the Cistern Autonomous Zone.

The tomcat interprets this as: (1) a dominance challenge, (2) a dinner bell, and (3) an unsolicited performance review. He responds in triplicate.

The Revolutionary Council's founding documents are famously silent on cats. The cats are not silent on you. Their silence was strategic. Their noise is educational.

You discover that the Right of Exchange applies even when the other party trades exclusively in indignity.

**[GAME OVER — THE CROWNING: STRUCK FROM THE MINUTES]**

You follow the crate markings inland. The stenciled codes on the supply crates at the dock—"KBD-T2-M" for Karet Bay District, Tier 2, Maintenance—told a simple story of materials arriving where they were supposed to go. But you've been watching crates all morning, and the ones with that code stopped arriving three loads ago. The ones still moving have different codes. Fresher paint. Newer stencils.

The warehouses rise around you like a second coastline—brick and corrugated iron, CEA shipping labels pasted over older labels pasted over labels so old they've become part of the wall. The air changes here: less brine, more dust and machine oil. The ground is hard-packed clay over old cobblestone, and every surface carries the fine grey residue of materials being moved in bulk.

A cart passes you heading upriver, loaded with crates bearing the same fresh stencils you noticed at the dock. The driver doesn't look at you. He has the focused blankness of a man who moves things from one place to another and has learned not to wonder why.

You check the stencil code against your allocation charts. "TRP-UC-PRI." Transit Rail Project. Upper City. Priority. You check it again, because you want to be wrong.

You are not wrong.

The materials allocated to maintain Karet Bay's infrastructure—the fuel blocks, the reinforcement paste, the bonding agents that keep seawalls standing and water pipes sealed—are being loaded onto carts and shipped upriver to build a railway in the part of the city that already works. Someone signed the authorization for this. Someone approved the transfer. Somewhere in the CEA's filing system, there is a form that says this is fine.

You keep walking toward the logistics office.

The stencils are not a riddle anymore. You read TRP-UC-PRI the way you read weather—Transit Rail, Upper City, Priority—and the scam is old news that still tightens your jaw.

You cross the warehouse quarter on intent, not accident: brick and iron, labels pasted over labels, the grey film of everything moved in bulk. Carts roll upriver under fresher paint; drivers keep their eyes on the loads. You are not here to prove the redirection again—you are here for the office, the paper, the honest count kept inside a dishonest channel.

The logistics building stays squat at the heart of it all—faded pennant, tired glass—and you walk straight toward the door.

text:
The logistics office is a squat building at the center of the warehouse complex, distinguished from the warehouses only by its windows and the fact that someone has hung a CEA pennant from a bracket over the door. The pennant is faded. Nobody has replaced it because replacing it would require someone to notice it, and noticing things is not, apparently, part of the operational culture here.

Outside, a loading dock runs the length of the building's north face. Workers move crates from warehouse doors to waiting carts with a rhythm that speaks of long practice—lift, carry, stack, strap, next. No wasted motion. No conversation. The efficiency is remarkable, and the efficiency is the problem, because these people are very, very good at moving materials away from the district that needs them.

You count the carts. Fourteen, currently being loaded. Each holds roughly two tons of mixed maintenance materials. You do the math in your ledger: twenty-eight tons of Tier 2 stock, departing in a single morning shift. The district's monthly maintenance allocation, according to the last published schedule, is forty tons. You are watching two-thirds of a month's supply leave in three hours.

The contrast sits in your throat. Behind you, the district is held together with improvised circles and Tier 0 paste. In front of you, enough material to repair every critical system in Karet Bay is being loaded onto carts by people paid to not think about where it's going.

A woman appears briefly in the office window, surrounded by what appears to be a small fortress of paper. She looks tired in the way that structural fatigue looks—not the kind that sleep fixes.

text: The door is the same door: the same worn brass plate cool under your palm, the same faint stick in the latch before it gives. text:
You push open the door and step into a room that has been colonized by paperwork. Shipping manifests cover the desk in overlapping layers. Filing cabinets line the walls, several drawers hanging open with documents protruding at angles that suggest a system somewhere between "organized chaos" and "cry for help." A map of the bay's shipping routes is pinned to one wall, annotated so heavily that the original cartography is barely visible.

The woman behind the desk—mid-forties, dark hair pulled back with a pen shoved through it, ink on her fingers and the side of her jaw where she's been resting her face on her hand—looks up when you enter. Her eyes find your Scholar insignia before they find your face.

Something happens to her expression. It's complicated. Relief, first—the kind you see when someone has been drowning quietly and spots a boat. Then fear, immediate and practical, the recognition that the boat might also be a problem. Then something harder to name: the expression of a person who has been carrying numbers that don't add up and has just realized someone might finally ask her to explain them.

"Scholar," she says. The word carries about four different meanings.

"Senna?" you ask, reading the nameplate half-buried under a requisition form.

"Harbor Logistics Coordinator. Eleven years." She says it like a diagnosis. "I—" She stops. Starts again. "The allocations. You're here about the allocations."

It wasn't a question. You let the silence confirm it.

She sits back in her chair and presses both hands flat on the desk, as if bracing against something. "I have the numbers," she says. "I've had them for months. I just—" Another stop. "The people I would normally report this to are the same people who signed the transfer orders."

She looks at you. Waiting.
choice2_label: Demand to see the full records.

text:
You step inside and the room is unchanged in the only way that matters: still overrun—manifests in drifts, drawers half-open, the shipping map on the wall half-lost under its own corrections.

Senna looks up from the crush on her desk and recognizes you in a single tired beat—not relief, not performance, just the flat fact that you are back in a conversation neither of you finished. Ink marks her fingers; she does not bother squaring the stack in front of her.

She waits, hands resting on paper as if bracing a small raft, for your next move.

text:
You don't start with the numbers. You start with her.

Senna has been harbor logistics coordinator for eleven years. Before that, she was a shipping clerk. Before that, a dock worker's daughter who learned to count before she learned to read because her father's pay was docked by the number and the numbers were wrong often enough that someone in the family needed to check them.

She tells you this without self-pity. It's context. She's a woman who became good at counting because counting wrong had consequences she could see.

"The allocations shifted gradually," she says, pulling out a chart she's clearly drawn herself—hand-ruled columns, meticulous entries. "It wasn't one order. It was a series of small redirections. Five percent here. Eight percent there. Like water finding a new channel. Each individual change was within the discretionary adjustment authority of the Regional Allocations Board. None of them, individually, would trigger a review."

She traces the line on her chart. It goes one direction. Down.

"But together—"

"Together, the district lost seventy-three percent of its Tier 2 maintenance supply in seven months."

She nods. You notice her hands are steady. She's had time to be angry about this. The anger has hardened into something more like determination, or maybe just exhaustion wearing determination's face.

"I wrote three internal reports," she says. "They were received and acknowledged. Nothing changed. The acknowledgments came from the same office that approved the transfers." A pause. "I stopped writing reports after the third one. Not because I stopped caring. Because I realized the reports were going to the people who already knew."

She looks at the window. Beyond it, another cart of materials rolls past, heading upriver.

text:
Senna pulls a thick folder from the second drawer on the left—she knows exactly where it is, because she's been waiting to show it to someone—and spreads three months of shipping manifests across the desk. The desk isn't big enough. She moves to the floor.

The story the manifests tell is not subtle. It is, in fact, painfully clear, which makes the fact that nobody has acted on it either an indictment of the system or a feature of it.

"Karet Bay District is allocated forty tons of Tier 2 maintenance materials per month," Senna says, pointing to the allocation column. "Standard for a district of this size and infrastructure age. Here—" she traces her finger across the row "—is what actually arrives. And here—" she pulls out a second set of documents, transfer orders "—is where the difference goes."

The difference goes to the Transit Rail Project. Upper city. Priority allocation.

Seventy-three percent of Karet Bay's Tier 2 maintenance materials, redirected over the last seven months. Not stolen—redirected. With paperwork. With signatures. With the full bureaucratic apparatus of legitimacy wrapped around an act of systematic neglect.

"They're building a railway," Senna says flatly. "And they're building it with the materials that are supposed to keep this district's seawall standing, its water pipes sealed, and its cranes operational." She pauses. "The railway is on schedule. The seawall is not."

She has it all documented. Every transfer order, every allocation shortfall, every discrepancy between what was promised and what arrived. Seven months of institutional failure, catalogued in a logistics coordinator's meticulous handwriting.

"I made copies," she says. "I wasn't sure anyone would come. But I made copies anyway."
choice2_label: Ask where the materials physically go.
choice3_label: Ask about her—how she ended up in this position.

text:
Senna agrees. She says the word "yes" and then sits very still for a moment, as if listening to the echo of it.

"If Toris finds out I talked to a Scholar about this, I lose my position," she says. Not a protest. A calculation. "And then who watches the numbers?"

It's not a rhetorical question. She genuinely wants to know. In a system where the oversight mechanism has been captured by the people it's supposed to oversee, one logistics coordinator with honest books might be the only functional safeguard left. She knows this. It's why she hasn't quit. It's also why she hasn't spoken up until now—because speaking up and losing her position might be worse for the district than staying silent and keeping the records.

You write down her account. Name, position, tenure. The dates of her internal reports. The non-responses she received. The pattern she identified. She speaks carefully, choosing words with the precision of someone who understands that words, in bureaucratic systems, have material consequences.

When she's done, she looks at the folder on her desk. Seven months of documentation. Then she looks at you.

"I need you to understand something," she says. "I'm not doing this because I'm brave. I'm doing this because the numbers are wrong and I can't make them right from inside the system. The system is the problem." She straightens a stack of papers that doesn't need straightening. "You're the first person from outside the system who's asked."

You close your ledger. The weight of her testimony sits in it alongside the engineering data and the material assessments. Numbers and a name. Evidence needs both.

You take the copies. Senna hands them over with both hands, like someone passing a child across a gap—careful, deliberate, unable to take it back once the transfer is complete.

The manifests are dense with logistics notation: allocation codes, transfer authorities, routing numbers, weight tallies, receiving signatures. To most people, they would be unreadable. To you—a Measured Scholar trained in the patient art of making systems confess their sins through their own documentation—they are a confession.

Seven months of material redirection, documented in the CEA's own ledgers. Every transfer authorized, every shortfall acknowledged in the margins by someone who initialed the discrepancy and moved on. The system didn't hide what it was doing. It simply expected no one would read the evidence it left in plain sight.

You fold the copies carefully and place them in your field satchel, between the diagnostic plates and the fuel block case. Physical evidence. The kind that doesn't change when someone edits a filing cabinet.

Senna watches you with the expression of someone who has just handed over something they can't take back. Not regret—she made this decision before you walked in. But awareness. The awareness that a thing has shifted, and the shape of what comes next depends on what you do with what she's given you.

"The staging area is at the district boundary," she says quietly. "Where the materials transfer to upper-city transport. If you want to see the scale of it." She pauses. "You should see the scale of it."

You nod. The manifests are evidence of what was decided. The staging area is evidence of what that decision looks like when it's built.
choice1_label: Follow the material trail to the staging area.

text:
You find a position near the warehouse wall where you can watch without being watched. An old skill for a Scholar—or perhaps the oldest skill: standing still while systems reveal themselves.

The loading process is a machine made of people. Workers move in pairs, one on each end of a crate, with the synchronized efficiency of a crew that has done this exact job hundreds of times. Lift from the knees. Three steps to the cart. Lower on the count. Strap. Next. The rhythm doesn't vary. There's no conversation, no hesitation, no moment where anyone stops to consider what they're moving or where it's going.

They've been doing this for months. You can tell by the way the work has worn grooves into their muscle memory—the same crate sizes, the same cart dimensions, the same route from warehouse to loading position. This isn't new. This is routine.

The crates are labeled clearly: "Transit Infrastructure Project - Priority Allocation." Fresh stencils on clean wood. Someone is investing in good packaging for materials being taken from a district that can't afford to maintain its own seawall.

A foreman stands at the edge of the dock with a clipboard, checking each cart against a manifest before waving it through. He's efficient. Thorough. He counts every crate and marks every entry with the careful attention of a man who does his job well and has never been given a reason to question what his job actually accomplishes.

He doesn't look conflicted. He doesn't look guilty. He looks like a professional doing professional work. The banality of it settles in your stomach like cold water.

You make your notes. You wish the notes were wrong.

The foreman sees you coming and his expression arranges itself into the particular blank politeness reserved for people who might be inspectors. He's a broad man, weathered in the way dock workers are—salt and sun and the particular kind of patience that comes from physical work done in all conditions.

Your Scholar insignia doesn't impress him. He's seen credentials before. Credentials come and go. Crates stay on schedule.

"I move what the manifests say to move," he says, before you've finished introducing yourself. He's had this conversation before, or one close enough to it. "Manifests come from the routing office. Routing office reports to the Regional Allocations Board. If you want to know why the crates go where they go, ask upstairs." He gestures vaguely toward the upper city with his clipboard. The gesture encompasses roughly everything above the poverty line.

You ask when the current shipping pattern started. He checks his logs—not because he doesn't know, but because he's the kind of man who references documentation.

"Seven months ago. Maybe seven and a half. We were doing standard district maintenance runs before that—seawall resupply, water system maintenance, crane upkeep. Good work. Regular." He shrugs. "Then the priority orders came in and everything shifted to transit rail. Same materials. Same crews. Different destination."

Seven months. The same timeline as the crane anomaly. The same timeline as the seawall's accelerated degradation. The same timeline as everything going wrong in Karet Bay, traced back to a set of routing orders that changed where the carts went.

He turns back to his clipboard. "Anything else? These carts don't load themselves." A pause. "Well. They could, if we had the fuel blocks for the autoloaders. But those got shipped upriver too."

He says it without irony. You're not sure that makes it better.

You don't ask. You inform Senna that you require access to the full shipping records under your authority as a Measured Scholar conducting a district infrastructure assessment. The language is formal. The tone is polite. The implication—that refusal will be noted in a document that ends up on someone important's desk—is not stated but doesn't need to be.

Senna hesitates. Not because she doesn't want to show you—she clearly does—but because showing you is a door that only opens in one direction. She looks at the filing cabinets. She looks at you. She reaches into her pocket, produces a key, and unlocks the back room.

The records room is small, windowless, and filled floor to ceiling with bound shipping manifests on wooden shelves. The organization system is chronological and meticulous—Senna's work, clearly. Labels in her handwriting. Color-coded tabs. The kind of filing that happens when someone cares about accuracy in an institution that doesn't.

What catches your eye immediately is the shelf against the far wall. The last seven months of records occupy it entirely, and the volumes are thicker than the previous five years combined. Not because there are more shipments—the district's total allocation hasn't changed on paper—but because there are more transfer orders, more routing amendments, more authorization addenda. The paperwork of redirection is voluminous. Every theft in this system requires a form, a signature, and a filing number.

You stand in a small room surrounded by the documentary evidence of a district being quietly dismantled by its own bureaucracy. The air smells like old paper and ink. It is a very specific kind of archive: the kind that proves something everyone already knows but no one has been willing to say.
choice1_label: Analyze the records carefully. This will take time.
choice2_label: Take what you need and leave. Speed over thoroughness.

text:
The material trail leads you to the district boundary—the invisible line where Karet Bay ends and the transit corridor begins. Here, the infrastructure changes mid-sentence. On the Karet Bay side: cracked pavement, patched walls, improvised reinforcement circles. On the transit corridor side: fresh concrete, new lighting, alchemical conduits humming with properly fueled maintenance circles.

The contrast is architectural violence. Two systems, sharing a border, separated by the simple question of where the materials went.

A CEA staging area occupies the boundary zone—a fenced compound where materials arriving from the dock warehouses are transferred to upper-city transport. The compound is busy. Carts arrive from the direction you came; larger vehicles depart toward the upper terraces. The transfer operation runs smoothly, because someone has invested significant resources in making sure it runs smoothly. Resources that came from somewhere.

Through the fence, you can see the scale. Crates stacked three high in organized rows. Fuel block containers on pallets. Reinforcement material in sealed drums. Structural alloys bundled in transit frames. All of it labeled for the Transit Rail Project. All of it sufficient to maintain several districts' worth of infrastructure, sitting in a staging area on the border of a district that is falling apart.

A guard stands at the gate—not military, but private security with a CEA contract badge. He notices you. He's not hostile, but he's not inviting either. The kind of presence that exists to make you decide whether what you're doing is worth the conversation. His jacket buttons sit one hole off true across his chest, as if someone else's measurements were issued as law and he wore them without comment long enough for the mismatch to become its own kind of uniform.

Behind the staging area, the transit rail construction rises against the skyline. It gleams. Below it, Karet Bay does not.
choice2_label: Observe from a distance.

text:
You settle in. The chair is uncomfortable. The light is bad. The work is the kind you were trained for, and you lose yourself in it.

An hour passes. Maybe more. The manifests yield their patterns reluctantly at first, then all at once, the way structural failures do—nothing, nothing, nothing, then everything.

The redirection isn't limited to Karet Bay. Three other districts—Morrow Reach, the Ashton Flats, Old Saline—show identical material draws over the same seven-month period. Different routing codes, different authorization chains, but the same destination: the Transit Rail Project. The same gradual erosion. The same bureaucratic camouflage of small, individually unremarkable transfers adding up to systematic deprivation.

You cross-reference the total material volume. The transit rail project, according to its published budget, requires roughly 40% of the resources it's actually consuming. The remaining 60% is being drawn from maintenance allocations across the eastern seaboard, hidden in the aggregate by the same trick Senna identified—small individual transfers, each within discretionary authority, that combine into something far larger than any single authorization would permit.

The scale reframes the problem. This isn't a local logistics failure. This isn't one district being neglected. This is a regional policy decision disguised as a series of administrative adjustments. Someone—or some office, some committee, some authority with the power to coordinate across multiple allocation boards—decided that the transit rail was worth more than the infrastructure that keeps four working districts functional.

You write it all down. The numbers. The districts. The pattern. Your hand cramps. You keep writing.

When you're done, the clarity sits with you the way a good measurement does—exact, unwelcome, and impossible to unread. The apparatus did not misfire; it fed what it was aimed at. The people it was meant to keep whole are simply not where the aim settled.
choice2_label: Confront Senna about the scale of this.

text:
You take what you can carry. Three months of transfer orders. The allocation summaries. Senna's hand-drawn comparison charts. Enough to prove that materials were redirected from Karet Bay to the transit rail project. Enough for an assessment. Not enough for a prosecution, if it comes to that, but enough to start asking questions that have answers someone won't want to give.

You work fast, selecting documents with the practiced eye of a Scholar who has learned which paperwork matters and which is camouflage. Transfer authorizations—yes. Routing confirmations—yes. The seven pages of interdepartmental memoranda about updating the filing system's color-coding protocol—no.

Speed over thoroughness. It's a trade-off you've made before. In field assessment, you rarely have the luxury of complete information. You learn to take the signal and leave the noise, and hope you've correctly identified which is which.

Senna watches you from the doorway. She doesn't help—not because she's unwilling, but because she understands that what you're taking now is evidence, and evidence has chain-of-custody implications. A logistics coordinator knows about documentation chains. She stays outside the room while you work.

When you emerge with a folder of documents under your arm, she looks at it the way a shipwright looks at a vessel leaving harbor—with the knowledge that she built it as well as she could and the rest is up to the water.

"There's more in there," she says. "If you need it later."

"I know where to find it."

She nods. The conversation has the quality of a transaction that both parties understand is larger than the words being exchanged.

"Three districts?" Senna's voice is steady but her face isn't. The color leaves it in stages, like a tide going out. "I thought it was just us."

She sits down. Not in her chair—she misses it by a foot and ends up on the edge of her desk, scattering a pile of transfer orders onto the floor. She doesn't pick them up. She's staring at the wall map with the shipping routes, and you can see her re-reading it with new eyes, tracing the lines she knows by heart and seeing, for the first time, where they connect to a pattern larger than one district's logistics failure.

"Morrow Reach," she says, almost to herself. "They had a dock collapse last month. Old Saline's water treatment—" She stops. "I read the incident reports. Everyone reads them. We assumed they were separate failures. Maintenance debt. Aging infrastructure. The usual."

The usual. The comfortable explanation that allows everyone to nod and move on and not ask the question that would make the nodding stop.

"It's not the usual," you say.

"No." She presses her palms against the desk. Her hands are shaking slightly. Not with fear—with the particular tremor of someone whose understanding of a problem has just expanded beyond the walls of their office and into something they're not sure they can hold. "Someone is making a choice. Not for one district. For all of them. They're choosing the rail over everything."

She looks at you with an expression that has moved past fear into something more urgent.

"You have to stop this. Someone has to stop this. Four districts—" She shakes her head. "The seawalls alone—if Morrow Reach is in the same state as us—"

She doesn't finish. She doesn't need to. You can do the math.

The CEA staging area is larger up close than it looked from the district boundary. The fence is new—galvanized iron, properly anchored, with alchemical deterrent sigils worked into the posts. Someone spent real money on this fence. The kind of money that could have repaired a seawall, or sealed a water main, or kept a crane from failing.

A guard at the gate watches you approach. Private security, CEA contract. His uniform is clean and well-fitted—another small insult to a district where the dock workers mend their own gear. He has the posture of someone paid enough to be polite and not enough to be curious.

Through the gate, the operation spreads before you. Crates organized by destination code. Transport vehicles—large, well-maintained, alchemically assisted—waiting in a loading queue. Workers in clean overalls moving with the efficiency of a system that has everything it needs. The contrast with the dock workers on the other side of the boundary is so stark it feels like crossing between two different cities. Which, in every way that matters, it is.

You can see structural alloys in transit frames. Fuel block containers by the dozen. Reinforcement paste in sealed industrial drums—the same Tier 2 material that Karet Bay's maintenance circles are starving for, stacked here in quantities that would supply the district for a year.

The guard is still watching. Your Scholar insignia is visible. The question is whether you want to engage the system on its own terms—walk in with credentials and create a documented interaction—or stay outside it, observing from a distance that preserves your anonymity but limits your information.

Each choice has a cost. As always.
choice2_label: Observe from here. Write down what you can see.

text:
Your CEA authorization gets you through the gate. The guard examines it, nods, and steps aside with the mechanical courtesy of a man who has been trained to respect documentation regardless of what it authorizes. You walk in.

Behind you, the gate seats with a quiet metallic click; he holds his line without turning, letting distance do the rest of the check.

The operation is larger than the manifests suggested. The staging area isn't just a transfer point for Karet Bay's redirected maintenance materials—it's a regional hub. You can see routing labels from at least six districts. Structural components, reinforcement alloys, fuel stocks, bonding agents, specialized maintenance compounds. The transit rail project is consuming everything, and the machinery of consumption is running at full capacity.

You walk between the rows of crates, doing mental inventory. Your field training kicks in: estimate volume, cross-reference with standard district allocation tables, calculate the deficit. The numbers are staggering. What's sitting in this staging area right now—waiting for transport to a railway—could maintain the infrastructure of every district in the eastern quarter for three months.

A supervisor finds you. She's businesslike, clipboard in hand, the kind of middle-management efficiency that keeps systems running without asking whether they should be. "Sign here if you're auditing," she says, offering the clipboard.

The audit form is standard CEA documentation. Signing it creates an official record: a Measured Scholar conducted an inspection of this facility on this date. It alerts the system that someone is looking. It may accelerate whatever response the CEA decides to mount. But it also creates a paper trail—your name, your authority, your presence, documented in the system's own records.

You could decline, walk out, and preserve the advantage of the CEA not knowing exactly what you've seen. Information asymmetry. The Scholar's oldest tool.
choice1_label: Sign the audit form. Put it on record.
choice2_label: Decline. Leave quietly with what you know.

text:
You stay outside the fence. From here, with a Scholar's trained eye and a diagnostic plate pressed against the nearest alchemical conduit for passive resonance reading, you can see enough.

The scale is the thing. Not the individual crates or the specific materials—you've already documented those from Senna's manifests—but the sheer physical volume of resources concentrated in one place for one purpose. The staging area covers roughly two acres. Every square foot of it is occupied by materials in transit, organized with the ruthless efficiency of a system that has been optimized for exactly one thing: moving resources upward.

You count transport vehicles. Eighteen, currently loaded or loading. You estimate tonnage from the vehicle suspension compression—a trick your field instructor taught you, and one of the few things from the Academy that turns out to be consistently useful. The number you arrive at is larger than the annual maintenance allocation for the entire Karet Bay district.

You write it all down. Vehicle counts. Estimated tonnage. The routing codes visible on the nearest crate rows. The guard rotation pattern, because you're a Scholar and pattern recognition is what you do, even when the pattern is just two men walking back and forth.

From here, you can see the transit rail construction on the upper terrace. The skeleton of the railway rises against the sky, gleaming with new alloy and fresh alchemical bonds. It is, you have to admit, an impressive piece of engineering. It is being built well, with good materials, by competent people.

It is being built with the bones of four districts' infrastructure. And from up there, you probably can't even see Karet Bay.
choice1_label: Return to the district with your observations.

text: You pause where the warehouse dust thins and the older paving takes over—neither fully inside the complex nor committed to what comes next. One more breath at the seam, then you let yourself move.
choice2_label: Continue.

text:
You leave the warehouse district with more weight in your satchel and considerably more weight in your understanding.

The picture has resolved. Not completely—there are still questions, still gaps, still the particular kind of uncertainty that comes from seeing a system's outputs without yet seeing who designed it. But the outline is clear now, drawn in shipping manifests and allocation tables and the quiet testimony of a woman who counted the numbers and couldn't make them add up.

Materials flow upward. Maintenance flows downward—into deficit, into improvisation, into the slow structural failure of infrastructure that was built to last but wasn't built to be starved. The transit rail gleams on the upper terrace, a monument to the principle that some districts' futures are worth more than others' presents. Below it, Karet Bay's seawall holds by the memory of maintenance it hasn't received in seven months.

The exchange is not balanced. It hasn't been balanced for seven months, and the imbalance is not an accident. It's a policy. Somewhere in the CEA's administrative structure, someone decided this was an acceptable trade. The rail for the wall. The future of the upper city for the present of the lower. An exchange made without consulting the people on the losing end, because the people on the losing end don't sit on allocation boards.

You stand at the edge of the warehouse district, between the world that's being built and the world that's being consumed to build it. Your ledger is full. Your fuel blocks are lighter. Your assessment is no longer preliminary.

The question is what you do with knowing. The question is always what you do with knowing.
choice1_label: Next day: follow the drainage signature inland—the disturbance in the district interior.
choice2_label: Next day: go directly to the CEA. Confront the institution.
choice3_label: Next day: check on the seawall. Time may be shorter than you thought.
choice4_label: Next day: investigate the CEA staging area.

text:
You are back at the rim of the warehouse district with a satchel that already knows this weight and a ledger that has stopped behaving like blank paper.

The pattern needs no second introduction—materials climbing, maintenance bled downward, the same seven-month sweep you already traced in manifests and quiet testimony. The rail still catches light where Karet Bay does not; naming the imbalance did not soften the air.

Someone decided the trade was acceptable long before you arrived. Your fuel blocks are lighter. Your certainty is not.

You stand again between what is being assembled and what is being stripped to feed the assembly—the question unchanged except that you have less room to pretend you might still misunderstand it.

The next stretch will cost whatever you spend on it—time, nerve, the small coin of being seen to take a side—and drifting spends quietly, without giving you a receipt. You already know the pattern; pretending otherwise would be another withdrawal from an account you have been careful not to overdraw. You shift your weight, choose a bearing, and let your feet commit before your mind can rehearse a cleaner excuse.
choice1_label: Next day: return to the drainage trail—inland signature again.
choice2_label: Next day: go directly to the CEA. Confront the institution.
choice3_label: Next day: check on the seawall. Time may be shorter than you thought.
choice4_label: Next day: investigate the CEA staging area.

text:
The old chandlery smells of tallow and turpentine, overlaid with the sharper mineral tang of bonding paste. Whatever this place used to sell, it now trades in something more essential: continued structural existence.

The ground floor has been gutted and rebuilt into a working space that would make any logistics officer weep with recognition. Along the left wall, salvaged tools hang on pegged boards with the organizational precision of someone who knows exactly how many hammers she has and exactly how many she needs. The difference between those numbers keeps Brin awake at night. Along the right, stacked crates of reclaimed construction materials: bonding paste in mismatched containers, salvaged pipe sections sorted by diameter, fuel blocks of indeterminate tier. On the far wall, hand-drawn diagrams of Karet Bay's water and structural systems cover the plaster in overlapping layers of chalk and charcoal. They are accurate. You can tell because they match the readings in your diagnostic plate, and your diagnostic plate cost more than everything in this room combined.

A dozen people work in the controlled silence of those with too much to do and not enough hours to waste on conversation. Two are repairing water pipe sections at a workbench. Three are sorting materials with the grim focus of field medics triaging supplies. A teenage boy runs numbers on a chalkboard—material allocation calculations that look roughly correct.

At the center of it, Brin. Heavyset, steady, with Freehands circle-marks on both wrists—not the discreet single mark of someone who dabbles, but the doubled declaration of someone who has committed. She looks up when you enter, reads you in about three seconds, and goes back to the supply manifest she is reviewing.

"Seren sent you," she says. It is not a question.

This is mutual aid made physical. The gap between what the CEA provides and what people need, measured in pipe sections and bonding paste and hours of unpaid labor. You have seen the gap in your numbers. Here, it has a smell.
choice2_label: Explore the workshop.
choice3_label: Attend the repair briefing.
choice4_label: Leave for the disturbance trail.
choice5_label: Kaelen is waiting in the back room.
choice6_label: Leave and return to the investigation.

text:
Brin sets down her manifest and gives you her full attention. It is a substantial thing. She has the focus of a guild-certified structural lead—someone accustomed to holding the shape of a large problem in her head and directing people toward its solution.

'Twenty years,' she says, when you ask what she did before this. 'Structural work. Load-bearing walls, foundation reinforcement, the kind of circle work that keeps buildings standing. Guild-certified, Tier 2 rated. I built things right because that is what the work demanded.'

She picks up a length of salvaged pipe and turns it in her hands. It has been repaired with Tier 0 paste—the kind of fix that holds for months instead of years.

'Then the CEA restructured the maintenance contracts. Centralized procurement. Materials that used to come through the guild started routing through the Exchange instead—allocated by priority assessment. You know what priority assessment means?' She sets the pipe down. 'It means someone in an office decides which district gets its walls fixed and which district gets a memo explaining why the walls will be fixed later.'

She is not angry. That is what strikes you. She is past angry and into the territory beyond it, where the landscape is flat and practical and the only question that matters is what to do next.

'Seven months since the last proper material shipment. Seven months of us scraping together what we can from salvage and barter and the occasional sympathetic supplier. My question is—' She looks at you. 'More important than people's homes? What exactly is more important than people's homes?'

It is, you note, a genuinely good question. Your ledger does not contain the answer. You suspect that is the point.
choice2_label: Ask about Kaelen.
choice3_label: Ask what Brin's file adds after the dock.
choice4_label: Tell her you already broke the rules for the docks once.

text:
Brin's expression tightens—not with disapproval, but with the quick recalculation of someone who just moved you from observer to participant.

'Once is how it starts,' she says. 'Then the district asks for twice, and the ledger asks why you should be the one paying.' She taps her manifest once, neatly. 'Say it again when you mean it. Until then, keep the chalk off your cuffs when you walk past CEA clerks.'

She does not smile. She does not need to. You have been catalogued.

Brin spreads a hand-drawn map across the workbench. It is detailed in the way of someone who has walked every street and counted every building—not the clean abstraction of your Scholar-issued district charts, but the lived cartography of someone who knows where the puddles form and which staircase has the loose third step.

'Seven nodes.' She taps circles drawn in red chalk. 'Here, here, here—' She moves across the map like a general reviewing positions. 'Each one has at least one person who can do basic alchemical repair. Shaping work, simple reinforcement, bonding paste application. Nothing above Tier 1. We do not have the materials for Tier 1 half the time and we do not have the training for Tier 2.'

The nodes are connected by dotted lines—runner routes, you realize. Human messengers carrying material requests, repair reports, and warnings about CEA inspection schedules.

'When someone's pipe bursts at midnight, they do not file a requisition with the Exchange. They send a runner to the nearest node, and whoever is on shift goes to fix it. When a wall starts cracking, we pool materials from three workshops to get enough paste for a proper patch.' She taps the map again. 'We share what we have. We cover for each other when the inspectors come through, because half of what we do is not technically permitted under the current licensing framework.'

She rolls the map up with the practiced motion of someone who hides it several times a week.

'It is not complicated. People need things fixed. We fix things. The complication is that fixing things someone else broke is not supposed to be our job.' She meets your eyes. 'But it is. Because the people whose job it actually is have decided the materials are needed elsewhere. And the people who live here cannot eat a requisition form.'

You walk through the workshop's working floor. The air is thick with chalk dust and the faint ozone-burn of activated bonding paste—the smell of alchemy performed at close quarters by people who cannot afford proper ventilation.

Near the entrance, a teenage girl is crouched over a stone slab, drawing a basic reinforcement circle under the supervision of an older man whose hands look like they were carved from the same material he works with. The girl's chalk lines are unsteady but the geometry is correct—the proportional relationships between the binding nodes are sound, even if the execution wobbles. She is learning by doing, which is the only way anyone in this district learns anything, because the formal training institutions are three districts up and a licensing fee away.

'Hold the angle,' the man says. 'You drift at the third node every time.' She corrects. He nods. The circle will not win any prizes at the Scholars' Academy, but it will hold a pipe joint together for six months, and six months is the planning horizon when your district's maintenance budget exists primarily as a theoretical concept.

In the far corner, someone has set up a water treatment station that operates with the quiet confidence of a thing that works and the quiet illegality of a thing that is not supposed to exist. The filtering compound in use is not CEA-approved. You can tell because CEA-approved compounds come in sealed containers with official stamps, and this compound comes in a repurposed cooking pot with a hand-written label that reads 'WATER STUFF—DO NOT EAT.'

Everything here operates in the gap between 'illegal' and 'necessary.' It is a gap that gets wider every month the maintenance budget does not arrive, and the people inside it have stopped waiting for someone to tell them it is allowed.
choice2_label: Return to Brin.

text:
The water treatment setup occupies a corner of the workshop that has been partitioned off with salvaged timber and a hanging oilcloth. Inside, it is cleaner than the rest of the building—scrubbed surfaces, organized containers, the controlled environment of someone who takes contamination seriously because she has seen what contamination does.

The system is a three-stage filtration: settlement basin, activated mineral filter, and a simple exchange circle that strips remaining impurities through low-HI material conversion. It is not elegant. The settlement basin is a repurposed brewing vat. The mineral filter uses crushed aggregate packed into a wooden frame. The exchange circle is drawn in permanent chalk on a stone slab, fed by fuel blocks that are definitely salvaged from somewhere the CEA would prefer they were not salvaged from.

But it works. The woman running it—Lisse, small and precise, with the calloused hands of someone who spends her days handling rough materials—explains the system without being asked, in the steady cadence of someone who is proud of useful work and does not get enough opportunities to show it.

'Three buildings on Dock Row get water through here. Two more on Salt Lane. About ninety people total.' She runs a hand along the edge of the exchange circle, checking the chalk lines by touch. 'It is not as clean as a proper municipal filter. It is not as fast. But people drink clean water today, and today matters.'

You have heard this philosophy before. It is the philosophy of people who have stopped believing in institutional timelines. It is not wrong. It is also not sustainable. Your diagnostic plate confirms the system is running at its limit—one component failure from serving contaminated water to ninety people who have no backup plan.

You note this in your ledger. Lisse watches you write and says nothing. She has seen ledgers before. She is still waiting for one to help.

Brin runs the morning briefing from a cleared workbench that serves as a command table. Around it, eight people stand in the patient readiness of workers who know the list will be long and the materials will be short.

'Three priorities today.' Brin's voice carries without effort. She has the projection of someone who spent two decades shouting over construction noise. 'First: tenement block on Fisher Row, three water pipe joints showing active failure. Residents reported flooding in the lower units overnight. Tassin, your crew takes that—you know the pipe layout. I have allocated two units of bonding paste and a section of salvaged copper.'

She marks the chalkboard behind her. The board is divided into a grid: locations, crew assignments, material allocations, estimated completion times. It is a dispatch grid with the systematic layout Scholars favor for sanctioned logistics—except drawn in chalk, here, where no sanctioned office would acknowledge it.

'Second: fishmarket load-bearing wall. The stress fractures we flagged last week have progressed. Mira and Dorek, I need a full assessment before we commit materials. If it is beyond patching, we need to know today.'

She pauses. Looks at the board. You can see her doing the calculation—materials available versus materials needed, the arithmetic of scarcity that governs everything in this room.

'Third: cistern drainage backing up again. Same problem as last month. The main junction needs clearing and the outflow circle needs reactivation.' She assigns a name. The person nods without enthusiasm. Recurring problems generate a specific kind of weariness.

Then she looks at you. Reads you the way she reads a structural assessment—quickly, professionally, looking for load-bearing capacity.

'You want to understand what we do? Come with us. Observation from a distance is how the CEA does things, and you can see where that has gotten us.'
choice2_label: Join the wall assessment team.
choice3_label: Observe from here.

text:
The tenement basement on Fisher Row smells of standing water, rust, and the particular despair of infrastructure that has been failing slowly enough for people to get used to it.

You join a crew of three: Tassin, a wiry woman with a toolbelt that outweighs her; Ren, who carries the salvaged pipe sections and does not talk; and Gerd, who does the circle work. Gerd is heavyset, careful, and entirely self-taught. He learned alchemical bonding by watching a Freehands volunteer three years ago and has been approximating what he saw ever since.

The damaged section is obvious—a joint where two pipe segments meet has corroded through the bonding paste, and water seeps through in the persistent, patient way of water that has found a weakness and intends to exploit it fully.

Tassin cuts the corroded section with a hand saw. Ren fits the replacement segment. Then Gerd crouches down with his chalk and begins drawing.

His reinforcement circle is functional. That is the most precise word for it. The geometry is approximate—the binding nodes placed by eye rather than by measurement, the proportional relationships close but not exact. He compensates for imprecision with extra fuel, drawing harder, pushing more energy into the activation than a properly drawn circle would require. The chalk lines glow, dim, glow again. Gerd's face is tight with concentration. Self-fueled alchemy without proper training is like running uphill in the dark—you can do it, but it costs more than it should and you feel every step.

The pipe holds. Gerd stands up, visibly drained, and nods once. The repair will last months. A proper repair would last years.

You note the difference in your ledger. The difference has a name: materials. Training. Support. Things that used to arrive and now do not.
choice2_label: Spend a sanctioned block and help anyway.
choice3_label: Let Kaelen's mark steady you—then help.
choice4_label: Let the Freehands' goodwill carry part of the cost.
choice5_label: You cannot pay this basement twice—not without help you do not have.

text:
The joint is there. So is your training. What is not there—what the ledger refuses to fake—is another full payment this soon without a buffer you do not currently hold.

Gerd watches you close your chalk case without opening it. He does not take it personally. That is almost worse. He has seen institutions run out of materials before he has seen them run out of excuses.

You still know the cost of the help you are not giving. Arithmetic does not care whether shame would be convenient.

You kneel beside the next damaged joint and take out your chalk. Gerd steps back, uncertain, and you realize he has never seen a trained Scholar do circle work at ground level before. Scholars assess. Scholars report. Scholars do not generally get their knees wet in tenement basements.

'May I?' you ask, because the pipe is his responsibility and the courtesy matters.

He nods.

You draw the reinforcement circle properly. Measured nodes, precise geometry, proportional relationships calculated rather than estimated. The chalk moves with the muscle memory of three years of academy training—quick, clean strokes that lock into position with the certainty of mathematics rather than the hope of approximation. You activate the circle with a controlled fuel expenditure, channeling your own energy through the binding pattern in the way you were taught: minimum input, maximum structural coherence.

The bonding paste flows into the joint and sets with an audible click. The pipe segment locks into place with the solidity of something that will still be here when the building around it is not.

Your hands are shaking when you finish. Self-fueling at this scale is draining—the academy warned about field expenditure, about the cost of channeling without external fuel blocks, about the way your body makes up the difference when your supplies run short. You feel it in your joints, a deep weariness that sits behind the eyes and waits.

But the pipe will hold for years instead of months. That is the difference between training and approximation, between resourced institutions and abandoned communities. The difference is years of someone's plumbing working.

Gerd looks at his own chalk circles—the rough, functional ones that have kept this district's water running through sheer stubborn repetition—and says nothing for a long time.

When he speaks, it is quiet. 'Could you show me where I am going wrong on the third node?'
choice2_label: Continue.
choice3_label: Continue.

text:
The fishmarket's load-bearing wall tells a story, if you know how to read structural palimpsest. And you do. It is the kind of story that starts with good intentions and ends with the phrase 'catastrophic failure event' in someone's incident report.

You accompany Mira and Dorek—both Freehands veterans, both carrying diagnostic tools that were state-of-the-art fifteen years ago. The wall runs the full length of the market hall, supporting the upper floor where three families live in the resigned comfort of people whose ceiling is also their landlord's structural compromise.

The original construction is solid. Good stone, proper reinforcement circles, Tier 2 bonding work that was built to last a generation. But layered over it, like geological strata of increasingly desperate interventions, are the patches. At least seven distinct reinforcement circles, applied at different times by different hands with different materials. Some are Tier 1. Some are Tier 0. Two of them are actively conflicting—their binding geometries pulling the stone matrix in incompatible directions, like two people trying to hold a door open and closed simultaneously.

'Every month someone adds another patch,' Dorek says, running his palm along a crack that branches like a river delta. 'Nobody has removed the old ones because nobody is sure which ones are still load-bearing. The wall does not know what shape it is supposed to be anymore.'

It is a metaphor for the district, and everyone here knows it. Layer upon layer of improvised solutions, each one reasonable in isolation, each one adding complexity that makes the next crisis harder to solve. The wall is holding. But it is holding the way a person holds who is carrying too many things—with visible strain and the growing certainty that something will be dropped.

Mira writes her assessment in a notebook with no cover. The numbers are not encouraging.
choice2_label: Return to Brin.

text:
You tell Mira and Dorek you need an hour. They trade the look of people who have watched officials promise and vanish—but they step back.

You sweep the wall with your diagnostic plate: seven active patterns, three material types, two outright conflicts, one circle inert so long it generates stress like a bad tooth. On paper you assemble a single correction geometry that threads the living work—canceling the clashes, reinforcing what still carries load, retiring the dead inscription before its ghost load shears stone.

You fuel it from your own stores. The price arrives as weight and heat; your instructors had a long clinical name for self-fueled high-load drain, but the ribcage only knows someone stacked years there while you weren't watching.

The wall eases. Micro-fractures ease in the readings. Critical drops to stable, and for a breath the noise of the place thins.

Mira says: 'Wish we had one of you six months ago.'

You wish they had. Six months ago this was maintenance. Now it is a lesson in how neglect compounds—and neglect never sends an invoice.

You stay at the edge of the room and watch. It is what you were trained to do, after all. Observe. Assess. Calculate the cost.

Brin assigns the pipe crew first—Tassin's team, three people, two units of bonding paste. The allocation takes thirty seconds. Brin knows who works well together, who has experience with which pipe layouts, who needs a lighter load today because they worked a double yesterday. This knowledge lives in her head, unwritten, irreplaceable. It is the most critical piece of infrastructure in the room and it has no backup.

A brief disagreement flares over material allocation—a man named Oster wants additional paste for a retaining wall he has been watching, but Brin has already committed the reserves to the cistern drainage. The argument lasts ninety seconds. Brin listens, acknowledges the risk, explains the priority calculation, and offers a compromise: Oster gets first allocation from tomorrow's salvage run. Oster accepts. It is not consensus in the formal sense—it is the practical agreement of people who trust the person making the decision because she makes good ones.

The Freehands operate by consensus, technically. But Brin is the kind of person around whom consensus naturally forms, the way water finds a channel. She does not command. She presents reality so clearly that the correct course of action becomes obvious, and then people choose it because they can see it for themselves.

It is impressive. It is also unsustainable. One person holding together a system that should not be one person's job. If Brin gets sick, gets arrested, gets tired enough to stop—the network does not have a second Brin. The knowledge, the relationships, the daily arithmetic of scarcity that she performs in her head: none of it is written down. None of it is transferable. The Freehands have built their own single point of failure, and her name is Brin.

You write this in your ledger. You do not show it to anyone.

You return to the safehouse in the late afternoon. The light through the chandlery's high windows has gone amber, catching the chalk dust that hangs in the air like a visible measure of the day's work. Your hands ache. Your energy reserves are lower than they should be. Your ledger is fuller than it was this morning.

Brin is waiting. She has the particular stillness of someone who has been managing crises all day and has briefly run out of crises to manage. She hands you a cup of something hot. It is probably tea. The taste suggests it was tea at some point in its history and has since undergone a transformation that your alchemical training cannot fully explain.

'You have seen what we do,' she says.

You have. You have seen pipe repairs that cost three times the energy they should because the materials are not available. You have seen a load-bearing wall held together by seven conflicting repair attempts because no one had the training to do it once and properly. You have seen a water treatment system serving ninety people from a repurposed brewing vat, and a teenage girl learning reinforcement circles because the alternative is that no one in her building knows how to stop a wall from collapsing.

'Here is what you need to know.' Brin sets down her own cup and looks at you with the direct gaze of someone who has decided you are worth the truth. 'We cannot keep this up. Six months, maybe eight, before we run out of materials completely. After that, things start failing that we cannot patch. Pipes we cannot fix. Walls we cannot reinforce. The seawall.'

She lets that last word sit in the room by itself.

'Whatever you are writing in that ledger of yours, write that.'
choice2_label: Seek the CEA answers.
choice3_label: Return to Brin for more.

text:
Karet Bay at night is a different district. Not better. Not worse. Different in the way a body is different when it stops holding its breath.

The shift change happened two hours ago. Workers spill from doorways in loose clusters, shoulders dropped, voices louder than they were at noon. Braziers line the main thoroughfare—improvised heating circles bolted to iron drums, burning fuel blocks that smell faintly of copper and something sweet you can't identify. The light they throw is warm and unsteady, painting the cracked walls in shades of amber that almost look like maintenance.

The maintenance hum sounds different in the dark. During the day, the collective noise of the district smooths the failures into a general drone. At night, with fewer machines running and fewer people shouting, you can hear each one individually. A water pump cycling at the wrong frequency. A structural reinforcement circle on a load-bearing wall that clicks off for two seconds every thirty. A drainage valve somewhere below the street that opens and closes with the rhythm of something breathing.

You stand at the junction of the old canal path and the fishmarket lane. To your left, the night market stretches along the canal—a chain of stalls lit by alchemical lanterns that flicker with the inconsistent fuel supply, some burning steady white, others guttering amber, a few dark entirely. To your right, the narrow streets lead deeper into the residential blocks where off-duty workers gather in taverns and doorways. Ahead, fresh ink gleams on the wall: another pamphlet, recently pasted. The ink hasn't dried.
choice2_label: Follow the ink.
choice3_label: Find the dockside tavern.
choice4_label: Return to your calculations.
choice5_label: A familiar figure falls into step beside you.

text:
The night market runs along the old canal path like a sentence that keeps adding clauses. Stalls made of salvaged timber and canvas, lit by whatever light source each vendor could secure. The smell hits you first: fried dough, rendered fat, alchemical solder, fish paste, lamp oil. The smell of a district feeding itself after the official economy has gone home for the evening.

A woman sells dumplings from a cart with an alchemical heating circle embedded directly into the metal surface. The smell is extraordinary—garlic, ginger, something fermented that burns the back of your nose in a way that makes your mouth water. She works with the mechanical efficiency of someone who has done this ten thousand times and will do it ten thousand more.

Three stalls down, a man offers black-market fuel blocks arranged on a cloth. He doesn't call out or advertise. He doesn't need to. Everyone here knows what he sells and what it costs. The blocks are smaller than regulation and the crystalline structure is wrong—Tier 1, not Tier 2—but they'll keep a heating circle running through the night.

Two children sit cross-legged between stalls, trading comic illustrations by lantern light. The drawings are surprisingly good. One shows a figure holding up a crumbling wall. The other shows a figure in a CEA uniform walking away from the same wall. The children are laughing.

Further along, past the food vendors and the repair-supply dealers, there's a quieter stall. A woman sits behind a table covered in hand-bound booklets. No sign. No lantern brighter than necessary. The information stall.
choice1_label: Buy food from the dumpling vendor.
choice2_label: Buy black-market fuel blocks.
choice3_label: Browse the information stall.

text:
You buy four dumplings for three marks. They are unreasonably good. The wrapper is thin and slightly chewy, the filling dense with pork and scallion and something sharp that might be pickled radish. You eat them standing at the edge of the canal path while the market moves around you, and for thirty seconds you are just a person eating good food in a place that smells like good food, and nothing is failing.

The vendor—an old man with deep lines around his eyes and an alchemical heating circle embedded in his cart that he clearly maintains himself, because the inscription work is idiosyncratic but precise—watches you eat with the satisfaction of a professional.

'Twelve years,' he says, when you tell him the dumplings are good. 'Every night, right here. The district works shifts. People need to eat at 2300 as much as they need to eat at 0700. The CEA doesn't fund night services. Never has. The day-cycle economic model doesn't account for people who work after dark.' He shrugs. 'So we account for ourselves.'

He says it the way people here say most things: not as complaint, not as manifesto, just as description. The way you'd describe the weather or the tide schedule. The district's night economy exists because the official economy doesn't serve these people's actual needs, and rather than petition or protest, they simply built a parallel system. It is, from an economic standpoint, remarkably efficient.

You feel better than you have all day. The simple alchemy of hot food and a moment of stillness. Your hands have stopped shaking. You hadn't noticed they were shaking until they stopped.

Black-market fuel blocks. You shouldn't know what you're looking at, but you do, because the Academy taught you to identify fuel grades by crystalline structure and these are unmistakably Tier 1. The lattice pattern is coarser, the edges less defined. Less efficient combustion, higher waste particulate, shorter burn duration. A Tier 2 block runs a standard heating circle for eight hours. These will manage five, maybe six, and leave residue that degrades the inscription over time.

The seller is a thin man with steady hands and a face that has decided not to have an expression. He doesn't make eye contact. He arranges the blocks on their cloth with the care of someone who respects the product even if he can't respect the circumstances that created the market for it.

'Twenty-five marks per block. That's fair for what it is.'

It isn't fair. A regulated Tier 2 block costs nine marks through official channels—channels that have been empty in this district for seven months. The markup isn't greed. It's logistics: acquiring Tier 1 blocks from wherever they're being diverted, transporting them without official documentation, storing them without the proper containment circles. The cost of doing business in the gap between what a district needs and what an institution provides.

You look at the blocks. They'd work in a pinch. They'd keep a diagnostic circle running long enough to take readings in the field. They'd also identify you, to anyone who checked your kit, as someone willing to operate outside sanctioned supply chains. Which is either a liability or an asset, depending on who's checking.
choice2_label: Decline.

text:
The information stall is run by a woman in her forties with ink-stained fingers and the unhurried manner of someone who has been paying attention for a very long time. Her table is covered in hand-bound booklets—small, dense, printed on whatever paper was available. Some pages are uniform; others are clearly salvaged from different sources, the text crammed into margins and gaps.

She calls them almanacs. They are, in fact, a one-person journalism operation.

'Water pressure readings for the last six months,' she says, tapping one booklet. 'Structural assessment summaries—not the official ones, the ones we do ourselves with borrowed equipment. Maintenance schedules the CEA stopped publishing in Month Four.' She looks at you. 'You're the Scholar. Word travels.'

You pick up the latest almanac. It's meticulously organized. Pressure readings by block and building. Structural stress indicators mapped to specific infrastructure points. Fuel allocation records reconstructed from delivery observations—someone has been counting the supply carts. The data is rough but consistent, and the trend lines are unmistakable.

'Nobody tells us anything official anymore,' she says. 'The monthly infrastructure bulletins stopped. The public maintenance logs went dark. The CEA office posts notices about transit rail schedules and leaves the rest blank. So we tell each other.' She pauses. 'Cost me about forty marks a month in paper and ink. People chip in what they can. Some months it's enough. Some months I eat less.'

She is doing, with salvaged paper and counted supply carts, what the CEA's entire district monitoring apparatus is supposed to do. The data quality is lower. The commitment is not.
choice2_label: Ask her about the pamphleteer.

text:
You follow the ink.

Fresh pamphlets are pasted on walls along a specific route—not random, you realize after the third one. Deliberate. A walking argument, designed to be read in sequence by someone moving through the district at night.

The first: *The CEA redirected 340 tonnes of structural maintenance material from Karet Bay in the last fiscal year. The transit rail received 290 tonnes of supplementary allocation in the same period. These are public figures. The CEA published them. They just published them in two different reports, six months apart, in different units of measurement.*

The second: *Who decided this was acceptable? Not the Council—they weren't consulted. Not the district committee—they were informed after the fact. The decision was made by the Material Allocation Subcommittee, which has nine members, none of whom live below the third terrace.*

The third: *The Drowning of Karet Bay happened because a trade consortium redirected water for profit. The courts ruled it a crime. The legal principle was established. Three generations later, the CEA redirected the maintenance budget that keeps this district standing. The only difference is that this time, the institution doing the taking IS the institution that does the ruling.*

The writing is precise, furious, and well-informed. Whoever writes these understands the material allocation system better than most CEA administrators you've met. The arguments are structured like academic papers compressed into broadsides—thesis, evidence, implication—but the language burns where academic language merely describes.

The trail leads down the fishmarket lane, past shuttered stalls that smell of brine and old ice, to a narrow courtyard behind the last warehouse. The ink on the final pamphlet is still tacky.
choice2_label: Wait and observe from the shadows.

text:
You wait. Old habit. The Academy teaches observation before engagement, and some lessons stick even when the textbook is closed.

You press yourself into a doorway across from the courtyard entrance. The shadows here are deep—the nearest brazier is twenty meters back, and the alchemical lantern above the fishmarket door has been dark for weeks, judging by the dust on the glass. You are, for practical purposes, invisible. You settle in and watch.

Ten minutes. The courtyard is still. A cat crosses the cobblestones with the proprietary confidence of something that owns the night. A water pipe gurgles somewhere behind the warehouse wall. The maintenance hum of the district is quieter here, muffled by the buildings, and in the silence you can hear the harbour—the slow slap of water against the seawall pilings, the creak of moored boats adjusting to the tide.

Then movement.

A figure emerges from a narrow gap between the warehouse and the adjacent building—a gap you hadn't registered as passable. Average height, hood up, moving with the specific confidence of someone who knows every exit from this courtyard and has used most of them. They carry a satchel over one shoulder. They cross to the far wall, remove a pamphlet from the satchel, apply paste with a flat brush, press the paper to the stone, and smooth it with practiced hands. The whole operation takes less than thirty seconds.

They turn to leave. They stop. They look directly at you.

'You're the Scholar. The one from this morning.' The voice is level. Neither surprised nor alarmed. The voice of someone who accounted for the possibility of being watched and has already decided what to do about it.

Ash. That's what the workers call them, because the pamphlets look like they were printed in a forge. You can't tell their age—the hood, the dim light, the deliberate anonymity. Their posture is relaxed but not careless. The posture of someone who is always partly ready to leave.

'I've been watching you all day, Scholar.' The voice is measured, controlled. Not aggressive. 'You arrived this morning. You've taken readings at the substation, the seawall, the drainage outflows. You've talked to the dock coordinator, the Freehand elder, the workers. You've been very thorough. Very methodical.' A pause. 'Very much exactly what the system designed you to do.'

They lean against the courtyard wall. The stone behind them is covered in old paste marks—layers of pamphlets, posted and torn down and posted again. An archaeology of dissent.

'The system designed you to observe. To calculate. To quantify the damage in terms the institutions can process. And then it designed you to write a report, submit it through the proper channels, and leave.' They tilt their head. 'The report will be received. It will be acknowledged. It will be filed. And nothing will change. You know this. You've seen the filing numbers. You know how many reports Scholar Mireth has submitted about districts in structural decline.'

The courtyard is very quiet. You can hear the harbour. You can hear the maintenance hum. You can hear the click of the structural reinforcement circle on the warehouse wall cycling off and on.

'I'm curious,' Ash says. 'What you plan to do about it.'
choice2_label: "I file accurate reports. That's my function."
choice3_label: "You're Red Balance."
choice4_label: "Who are you, exactly?"

text:
'The Weighing of Red Harrow,' Ash says, as if that explains everything. For a certain kind of person in this republic, it does.

'Everyone claims it. The CEA says Red Harrow proves that sacrifice must be managed by institutions—that without coordinated exchange, the cost falls unevenly and people die. The Freehands say it proves that sacrifice must be chosen, not assigned—that the people at Red Harrow held the line because they decided to, not because a committee calculated it was optimal.' Ash's voice sharpens. 'Red Balance says it proves that the people who created the problem should bear the cost of fixing it. That the valley was drowning because a dam was built to serve the upper settlements, and the people who built the dam should have been the ones standing in the flood.'

They look at you. The hood shadows their face but not their eyes. The eyes are very steady.

'Which version did they teach you at the Academy?'

This is not a safe conversation. Red Balance is, depending on who you ask, a political philosophy, a dissident network, or a bogeyman the CEA invokes to justify surveillance funding. Discussing it in a dark courtyard with an anonymous pamphleteer who has been tracking your movements all day is precisely the kind of thing the Academy's field safety protocols were designed to prevent.

It is also the first genuinely interesting conversation you've had since you arrived in this district. Everyone else—Toris, Mireth, even the workers—talks about the problem. Ash is talking about what to do with the problem. The distinction matters more than it should.
choice1_label: "All three. We're trained to see the pattern, not pick a side."

text:
'Accurate reports.' Ash repeats the words back to you the way you'd repeat a diagnostic reading that confirmed a structural failure. Flat. Clinical. Conclusive.

'Scholar Mireth has filed fourteen accurate reports about districts in structural decline over the last six years. I know this because the filing numbers are public record, even if the contents aren't. Fourteen districts. Fourteen reports documenting material shortfalls, infrastructure degradation, and the specific administrative decisions that caused them.' They hold up a hand, counting.
