'Do you know how many of those fourteen reports resulted in material reallocation to the affected district?'

You don't answer. You suspect you know.

'Zero.' Ash lets the word sit in the courtyard like a stone dropped into still water. 'Do you know how many resulted in promotions for the filing Scholar? Three. Mireth herself received a commendation after the Thornwall report. Excellent methodology. Comprehensive data. A model of field assessment practice.' Their voice doesn't change pitch, but something underneath it hardens. 'Thornwall's seawall collapsed eight months later. Eleven people were displaced. The commendation is still on Mireth's record.'

The silence that follows is not empty. It's full of the specific weight of a truth you've been carrying since this morning without looking at it directly.

'The system doesn't reward accurate reports, Scholar. It rewards reports that confirm what the people in power already wanted to do. Your accuracy isn't a threat to the system. It's a feature. It makes the filing process look rigorous. It makes the archive look comprehensive. It makes the inaction look considered rather than negligent.'

Ash straightens. 'Your report will be accurate. It will also be useless. Unless you make it impossible to ignore.'

'Red Balance.' Ash says the name the way you'd say the name of a disease someone else diagnosed. 'Red Balance is a bogeyman, Scholar. A name the CEA uses for anyone who suggests that the people who created a problem should bear the proportional cost of fixing it. Which is—if you think about it—just equivalent exchange applied honestly. The founding principle of the republic. The thing carved into the Council Hall doors.'

They pull their hood back slightly. You still can't see much—the courtyard is too dark, and they've positioned themselves with the faint light behind them. Deliberate. Everything about Ash is deliberate.

'I write pamphlets. I document the things the institutions won't: the material allocation numbers, the maintenance shortfalls, the gap between what the CEA reports and what the district experiences. I make sure the people who live here know what's being done to them, and by whom, and according to what budget line.' They spread their hands. 'If that makes me Red Balance in the eyes of the CEA, I think that says considerably more about the CEA than it does about me.'

You note what Ash didn't say. They didn't deny the philosophy. They reframed the label. There's a difference between 'I'm not Red Balance' and 'Red Balance is a meaningless term,' and Ash chose the second.

The pamphlets on the wall behind them are layered—weeks of them, maybe months. Each one a specific argument, a specific set of numbers, a specific accusation backed by data. This is not spontaneous outrage. This is a sustained campaign by someone with access to information, the skill to contextualize it, and the patience to build an argument one broadside at a time.
choice1_label: "But you do believe in forcing the cost onto those responsible."

text:
A real conversation. The kind the Academy warns you about—not because the ideas are dangerous, but because dangerous ideas presented well are harder to dismiss than dangerous ideas presented badly, and Ash presents very well.

'Equivalent exchange,' Ash says, 'properly understood, means that those who take more than their share must return it. The republic was founded on this. The Weighing was fought over this. And for one generation—maybe two—the system worked. Cost was distributed. Sacrifice was shared. The institutions existed to ensure that no one bore more than their proportion.'

They begin to pace. The courtyard is small enough that three steps take them wall to wall.

'Then the institutions grew. They accumulated power. They began to decide not just how cost was distributed but who was eligible to have cost distributed to them. And now we have Karet Bay. A district where the cost of the transit rail—which serves the upper terraces—is paid in collapsed infrastructure by people who will never ride it.'

They stop. Face you.

'The Drowning of Karet Bay happened because a trade consortium redirected water for profit. The courts ruled. The principle was established: environmental harm is harm to people. It's the law.' Their voice drops. 'And then Administrator Toris redirected the maintenance budget for the transit rail, and nobody ruled anything, because this time the institution doing the taking IS the institution that does the ruling. The court and the perpetrator are the same body.'

Ash is eloquent. Ash is dangerous. Ash might be right. The uncomfortable truth is that nothing they've said contradicts your own calculations. They've simply drawn the conclusion you've been avoiding.
choice2_label: "I need to think about this."

text:
Ash reaches into their satchel and produces a folded paper. They unfold it against the courtyard wall, smoothing the creases with the same practiced hands that smooth their pamphlets. It's a diagram—hand-drawn, densely annotated, technically precise.

The CEA material conduit system for Karet Bay and the adjacent districts. You recognize the schematic because you studied a simplified version at the Academy. This version is not simplified. This version shows every transfer node, every junction, every routing decision point. It shows the flow rates, the scheduling intervals, the maintenance windows. It shows, in red ink, the three critical transfer points where the conduit narrows to single-channel capacity.

'The supply chain has three critical transfer points in this district,' Ash says, tracing the red marks. 'Here, here, and here. Single-channel. No redundancy. If even one is disrupted—not destroyed, just disrupted—the materials stop flowing upriver for days. Maybe weeks. The transit rail project loses its supply chain. The upper terraces notice. The Council notices.'

They fold the diagram. Their movements are careful, precise. The movements of someone who understands that what they're holding is evidence of criminal intent if it's found on the wrong person.

'Long enough for someone—' they look at you, and for the first time there's something in their expression that isn't controlled, something that might be hope or might be desperation '—to file the kind of report that can't be ignored. The kind that arrives while the system is already in crisis. The kind that turns accurate data into political pressure.'

They hold the folded diagram between two fingers. 'I'm not asking you to do anything tonight, Scholar. I'm asking you to know that the option exists.'
choice1_label: Take a copy of the diagram.
choice2_label: Decline.

text:
The dockside tavern at night is a different creature from the one you sat in during the evening. The same room, the same tables, but the population has shifted. The after-shift crowd is here now—louder, looser, drinking the cheap ale that tastes like someone described hops to a person who had never encountered them and then that person brewed a beer.

You find a corner. The tavern is warm with bodies and brazier heat, and the noise wraps around you like insulation. Nobody bothers you. A Scholar in a dockside tavern at night is unusual enough to notice and unremarkable enough to ignore—you're clearly not CEA enforcement, and you're clearly not buying enough ale to matter economically.

A woman near the bar is telling a story to a group of younger workers. Her voice carries the rhythm of a tale told many times—not rehearsed, exactly, but worn smooth by repetition, the way water wears stone. She's telling them about the Weighing of Red Harrow.

Her version is different from the Academy's version. You learned it as a case study in coordinated sacrifice: the mathematical proof that distributed cost saves more lives than concentrated heroism. The optimal solution. The version that justified the creation of the CEA and the entire institutional framework of the republic.

Her version doesn't mention optimization. In her version, the people who held the line at Red Harrow didn't do it because they calculated it was the most efficient distribution of sacrifice. They did it because the water was rising and their neighbors were in the valley and they couldn't stand on the ridge and watch. It wasn't math. It was the thing that comes before math—the thing that math was invented to describe and manage and, eventually, replace.
choice1_label: Listen to the rest of the story.

text:
The woman finishes her story. The ending is different too.

In the Academy version, the Weighing succeeds. The cost is distributed. The valley is saved. The principle of equivalent exchange is proven, and the republic builds its institutions on the foundation of that proof. It's a triumph of rational governance. It's the reason you have a job.

In her version, the Weighing succeeds, but the people on the ridge don't come down for three days. They can't. The alchemical exchange drained something from them that doesn't have a name in the official reports—not energy, not vitality, something else. Something the calculations didn't account for. 'My mother said her grandmother didn't sleep right for two years after,' the woman says. 'Said she'd wake up reaching for something that wasn't there. The cost they talk about in the history books—the fuel, the circles, the measured exchange—that's the cost they could count. The other cost, they just stopped mentioning.'

The younger workers are quiet. The tavern noise fills the silence around their table like water around stones.

One of them says: 'My grandmother was at Red Harrow.'

Another: 'Everyone's grandmother was at Red Harrow.'

The first: 'No. Not everyone's. Some people's grandparents were in the valley, being saved. That's who runs the Council now. The saved ones. The ones who stood on dry ground while other people held the water back.' A pause. 'Funny how that works.'

The tavern is quiet for a long time after that. The ale tastes the same. Everything else tastes different.

You walk back through the night district. The hour is late enough that the market stalls are closing—vendors packing their wares into crates, folding canvas, banking the coals in their brazier drums. The night economy retreating until tomorrow's night shift creates tomorrow's demand.

The lanterns are dimmer now. Some have run out of fuel entirely—dark spots in the chain of light along the canal path where the district simply stops being visible. A maintenance circle on a water pipe flickers amber, fails, holds dark for three seconds, restarts with a sound like a caught breath. Further on, a structural reinforcement band on a tenement corner glows its steady blue, then dims, then brightens, then dims again—a pulse that looks almost organic, almost alive, almost like the building is breathing.

The district's infrastructure hums its broken song, and in the dark, without the daytime noise to mask it, you can hear every failing note. The water pump cycling wrong. The drainage valve breathing. The structural circles flickering on and off like a heart with an irregular rhythm. Each one a small failure. Each one acceptable on its own. Each one part of a pattern that, taken together, spells something your calculations have already named.

You know more than you did this morning. You know the numbers, the politics, the human cost that doesn't fit in a ledger column. You know what Ash is planning. You know what the workers endure. You know what the woman at Red Harrow understood that the Academy's version leaves out.

You're not sure any of it helps. You're not sure it doesn't. The seawall hums in the dark, and you walk toward whatever comes next.
choice2_label: Check on the seawall now.

text:
You burn a fuel block. Not a partial activation, not a measured discharge—a full Tier 2 block, fed into your diagnostic plate until the copper housing glows amber and the readout matrices reach maximum penetration depth. Extravagant. The kind of expenditure that would make Mireth's left eye twitch if she were watching.

She is not. The stone is.

The scan punches through thirty feet of reinforced masonry and into the foundation bedrock below the waterline. You crouch at the wall's base where the stone meets the harbor mud, boots sinking into the kind of slick grey sediment that suggests a long and committed relationship between this district and the concept of drainage failure.

The readout builds. Layer by layer, the seawall's internal structure resolves on your plate like a patient presenting symptoms they have been hiding for months.

It is worse than the surface assessment suggested.

The surface cracks you documented earlier are cosmetic compared to what is happening underneath. The structural matrices in the foundation stone—the deep alchemical bonds that hold the entire wall together—are degrading from the inside out. Not uniformly. Not from age. From something active, something chemical, something that is eating through the wall's foundations the way a slow acid eats through a beaker: invisibly, completely, and with absolute indifference to whatever the beaker was supposed to be holding.

You have two options for where to look next. Neither promises good news. The foundation circles below, where the original maintenance work was done. Or the drainage intake, where whatever is killing this wall is getting in.
choice2_label: Check the drainage intake.

text:
The foundation circles are beautiful work. Even failing, even corroded, you can see the precision of their original inscription—the clean geometric proportions, the efficient fuel routing, the structural harmonics tuned to reinforce the stone's natural crystal lattice. This is Tier 2 work by someone who understood that Tier 2 is not a ceiling but a discipline. Kaelen's father's generation. People who built things to last because the alternative was the bay coming in.

The circles are dying.

Not from age. Not from fuel starvation, though that would have killed them eventually. From chemical attack. The toxic compounds seeping through the drainage system have been dissolving the inscribed matrices—literally eating the alchemical patterns out of the stone. You can see the boundary with painful clarity: healthy stone on one side, still resonant with decades-old circle work, and corroded stone on the other, where the inscription channels have been reduced to shallow, meaningless grooves.

You run your calipers along the boundary line. It has advanced eleven centimeters in the last six months. You calculate the rate against the remaining healthy stone and the result sits in your ledger like a diagnosis you did not want to write.

Cascade failure threshold: three to five weeks at current degradation. Not months. Not a problem for the next assessment cycle. A problem for the people sleeping above this wall right now.

The circles were designed to hold for decades. They held. What they were not designed to hold against was the district's own drainage system being turned into a delivery mechanism for their destruction.
choice1_label: Map the failure points in detail.
choice2_label: Return to the surface.

text:
The drainage intake is a square aperture at the wall's foundation level—two feet across, fitted with a corroded iron grate, and currently delivering a slow but steady flow of fluid that your diagnostic plate identifies as containing seventeen distinct chemical compounds, none of which belong in a structural foundation's water supply.

You take samples. Your plate catalogues them with the dispassionate thoroughness of an instrument that does not have opinions about what it measures. Copper sulfate derivatives. Catalyst breakdown products. Residual bonding agents. The chemical signature is unmistakable: this is drainage network output. The same contaminated water flowing through the district's underground conduits—the same system carrying Elara's purifier byproducts if her operation is running, the same system backed up with seven months of industrial runoff that the maintenance budget used to handle and no longer does.

The seawall is drinking it.

The intake was designed for clean groundwater—a passive hydration system that kept the foundation stone's alchemical matrices at optimal moisture levels. An elegant piece of engineering, from an era when the drainage network delivered clean water because someone was paying to keep it clean. Nobody redesigned the intake when the water changed. Nobody thought to. The maintenance schedules that would have flagged the contamination were the same schedules that were defunded when the materials were redirected to the transit rail.

One decision caused another caused another, and now the wall that protects six thousand people is slowly dissolving itself from the bottom up, one drainage cycle at a time. You document everything. The plate does not editorialize. You do.
choice2_label: Document everything and continue.

text:
Two hours. You spend two hours in the dark, wet foundation zone of the Karet Bay seawall, pressing your diagnostic plate against stone after stone, mapping every point where the structural matrices have degraded past recovery threshold.

Your hands go numb from the cold water. Your knees ache from crouching on uneven substrate. Your fuel reserve drops to levels that would concern you if you were thinking about yourself, which you are not, because the data is building a picture and the picture is the kind of thing that does not let you stop looking.

One hundred and forty-seven failure points. You map each one. Location, depth, degradation percentage, projected timeline to cascade. Your diagnostic plate builds a structural profile of the entire foundation—a three-dimensional model of decay that has never existed before in any CEA file, any maintenance report, any assessment document.

Because no one assessed it. Because the assessment budget was cut. Because the assessment budget was redirected to the transit rail. Because the transit rail was deemed higher priority by people who do not live behind this wall.

The data is not ambiguous. The seawall's maintenance was not merely neglected. It was actively undermined by drainage contamination that was itself a direct consequence of the infrastructure cuts that defunded the drainage maintenance that would have prevented the contamination. Each failure feeds the next. The cost did not accumulate—it compounded.

You close your ledger. Your hands are shaking, but the map is complete. The first honest structural assessment of the Karet Bay seawall exists now, in your handwriting, on a diagnostic plate that cost more fuel than this district's monthly allocation. Nobody asked for it. The data does not care.

You draw the containment circle on the stone around the drainage intake. The same principle Elara used for her water purifier—isolation, filtration, containment—but at a scale that makes her basement operation look like a sketch compared to a mural.

Your chalk moves with the steady precision of three years' training. The circle has to be large enough to encompass the entire intake, strong enough to resist the constant water pressure, and complex enough to filter the seventeen chemical compounds your plate identified. You are designing a circle you have never drawn before, in conditions that would make your Academy instructors file a formal objection, using fuel reserves you cannot afford to spend.

You spend them.

The activation pulls from your personal energy reserves like a tide pulling at a shoreline—steady, inevitable, erosive. The circle ignites in pale amber light, the containment matrices interlocking around the drainage intake. Water still flows through, but the chemicals hit the filtration layer and stop. The toxic compounds precipitate out of solution, crystallizing on the circle's inner surface like frost on a window.

The circle holds. The intake is sealed. Clean water passes through; poison does not.

It will not reverse the damage already written into the foundation stone. Those failure points are permanent scars. But the degradation rate will slow from weeks to months—maybe longer, if the circle holds and someone maintains it.

Your hands are shaking. Your vision softens at the edges, the world acquiring the particular blur of someone who has spent more energy than they had. You lean against the cold stone and breathe.

The wall holds you up. You suppose that is fair. You just did the same for it.

You climb the access ladder on arms that feel like they belong to someone who has been doing this much longer and complaining about it much less. The surface air hits you like a reminder that the world above the waterline still exists and still has opinions about what you should do next.

The harbor stretches out before you—grey water, grey sky, the distant geometry of the transit rail catching what passes for light in this district. Below your feet, behind the stone you were just touching, the seawall's foundations are quietly failing. You know the exact rate. You know the exact cause. You know, within a margin of error that would satisfy any assessment board, exactly when the cascade failure will begin.

That knowledge sits in your chest like a stone of its own.

The seawall's condition is worse than anyone in this district knows. Worse than the CEA's projections account for. Worse than Toris's comfortable fifteen-percent failure model suggests. You have the data. You have the structural survey. You have, in your ledger and on your diagnostic plate, the most complete picture of Karet Bay's infrastructure crisis that exists anywhere.

What you do not have is a clean answer for what comes next.

The question of the wall felt abstract this morning, when it was numbers in a briefing and a line on Mireth's assignment sheet. It feels less abstract now. You can still feel the cold stone under your palms. You can still hear the deep groan of a structure that is holding because it was built by people who built things to hold, and it is running out of reasons to keep doing so.
choice2_label: Go to the CEA district office.

text:
The field camp is a folding desk, a stack of diagnostic plates in varying states of depletion, and a fuel inventory that consists of two Tier 1 blocks and a piece of chalk that has been sharpened to a point suggesting either extreme precision or extreme scarcity. Probably both.

A Scholar sits behind the desk—thirty-five, maybe, with the lean economy of someone who has been doing fieldwork long enough that the field has started doing work on them. Thin fingers, precise movements, the focused expression of a person running calculations they finished in their head ten minutes ago and are now merely confirming on paper for the benefit of the institutional record.

They look up as you approach. The assessment takes about two seconds: your kit, your seal, your age, your posture. You have the impression of being measured, found adequate, and filed.

'Mireth's new one. She mentioned you might come around.' The voice is flat. Not unfriendly. Just calibrated for efficiency, the way a diagnostic plate is calibrated—giving you exactly the information you need and nothing you do not. 'Scholar Nev. I'd shake hands, but mine have chalk dust on them and yours probably do too.'

Their desk is covered in material flow charts—lines of supply and demand drawn in blue and red ink, converging and diverging across a district map that has been annotated to the point of illegibility by anyone who is not the person who annotated it. The work is meticulous. The conclusions, from what you can see, are devastating.

Nev follows your gaze to the charts and shrugs. 'Welcome to the pattern. It gets worse the more you look at it.'
choice2_label: Ask about their assignment.
choice3_label: Ask about the equipment outside the CEA office.

text:
'Scholar Nev. Seven years in field evaluation. Currently auditing material flow for the harbor authority—which means I am documenting things I am not allowed to change, for people who are not going to read them.'

Nev says this without bitterness. It is a measurement, not a complaint. The same tone your diagnostic plate uses when it reports structural failure: here is what is happening, expressed in units that do not care about your feelings.

They look at your ledger—the open pages, the fresh annotations, the particular density of someone who has been writing all day and has not stopped finding things to write about. 'How far into your assessment are you?'

You tell them. The crane. The material grades. The seawall readings. The warehouse manifests, if you found them. The drainage network. Elara's purifier. The whole picture, or as much of it as you have assembled in a single day that feels like it started approximately one geological epoch ago.

Nev listens without interrupting. When you finish, they nod—not surprised, not impressed, just confirming.

'Yes. That's the pattern.' They tap a red line on their district map. 'I have seen it in two other districts. Venmere and Thornside. Same budget mechanism, same material redirection, same downstream infrastructure degradation. It usually takes about three months longer than this to get this bad.'

They look at you. The expression is not pity. It is recognition—one surveyor acknowledging another, standing at the edge of the same data and looking down at the same conclusion.

'Karet Bay is ahead of schedule. That is not a compliment.'
choice2_label: Return to the CEA building.

text:
Nev turns their district map toward you and taps a series of red lines that converge on a single point in the upper city.

'Material flow audit. Harbor authority commissioned it six weeks ago—someone noticed the maintenance budgets were not balancing, which is bureaucratic for things are falling apart and we would like to know whose signature is on the falling-apart form. My job is to follow the materials from source to destination and document where the numbers stop matching reality.'

They trace a line from Karet Bay upward through three intermediate distribution nodes to the Highpoint Transit Rail.

'The transit rail project is consuming three hundred and forty percent of its original material budget. Not a typo. Not a rounding error. Three hundred and forty percent. That budget is coming from somewhere, and the somewhere has names and addresses and people living in it.'

They show you the full map. Lines drawn from six districts—six—all converging on the rail project like tributaries feeding a river that only flows uphill. Karet Bay. Venmere. Thornside. Oldgate. The Millworks. Duskwater. Each one a district where maintenance budgets were quietly redirected, where infrastructure assessments were delayed or cancelled, where the slow arithmetic of deprivation is working its way toward a structural conclusion.

'You have been looking at one district,' Nev says. 'I have been looking at six. The picture is the same at every scale. The only thing that changes is the size of the number at the bottom.'

They slide a summary page across the desk. 'Karet Bay is the worst. You are not wrong about that. But it is not alone.'
choice2_label: Ask about the other districts.

text:
'The equipment?' Nev glances across the street at the field kit stacked against the CEA office wall—diagnostic plates, calibration tools, a fuel case that nobody has opened or collected. 'Yes. That was here when I arrived three days ago. Different Scholar. Recalled to the capital before finishing their assessment.'

They say 'recalled' the way you might say 'rained'—as a weather event, impersonal and predictable.

'It happens. The institution sends someone to evaluate a district. The evaluation starts producing data that contradicts the approved narrative. The Scholar gets reassigned to a project that requires their specific expertise somewhere else. The assessment goes into the pending file, which is the institutional equivalent of a shallow grave with good drainage.'

Nev picks up a diagnostic plate, examines it, sets it down. The gesture is habitual—a Scholar who cannot stop assessing things, even when the thing being assessed is the absence of another Scholar.

'The equipment stays because no one was sent to collect it. That is how you know a district has been written off. When a district matters, someone comes for the equipment. When it does not, the equipment becomes furniture.' They look at you with the particular steadiness of someone delivering a professional observation. 'You are here because Mireth sent you with specific authorization. That means someone with enough institutional weight decided Karet Bay deserves a second look. Or it means Mireth decided that on her own, which is more interesting and considerably more dangerous.'

They return to their calculations. The equipment across the street continues to wait for no one.

'Three months from now—' Nev holds up a hand, counting on thin fingers. 'Something structural fails. A wall. A pipe. A crane.' They glance at you. 'A seawall, perhaps. Someone gets hurt or killed. The CEA investigates. The investigation report says inadequate maintenance led to structural failure.'

They lower one finger.

'Nobody writes inadequate maintenance was the direct and documented consequence of a budget reallocation that I personally signed off on. Nobody writes the maintenance was defunded to pay for a transit rail that serves a district where no one has ever needed to boil their water before drinking it. Nobody writes I knew the exchange rate and I accepted it because the people paying the cost do not attend the same meetings I do.'

Another finger.

'The passive voice is doing extraordinary work in these reports. Materials were redirected. Maintenance schedules were adjusted. Infrastructure assessments were deferred. Were. By whom? The passive voice is the bureaucratic equivalent of fog—everything is happening, nothing is being done, and certainly nobody is doing it.'

Nev looks at you. Not with anger. With the precise, exhausted clarity of someone who has watched this happen before and documented it correctly and changed nothing.

'Your report will be accurate. Mine will be accurate. And the transit rail will be finished on schedule. And six months after that, someone will stand in the ribbon-cutting photograph and talk about progress. And Karet Bay will still be here, running on paste and chalk and whatever Elara can keep running in her basement.' They pause. 'Or it will not be here. Depends on the wall, I suppose.'
choice2_label: You have accepted that?

text:
'That is not acceptable.'

You say it before you have finished thinking it, which is not how you were trained to communicate. The Academy teaches measured responses. Calibrated language. The precise delivery of conclusions supported by evidence. What you just said is an opinion—raw, unweighed, the kind of statement that a first-year would make before learning that opinions are liabilities in institutional assessment.

Nev does not flinch. They look at you the way a surveyor looks at a crack in a wall—noting it, measuring it, determining whether it is structural.

'No,' they say. 'It is not. That is the correct assessment. The question is not whether it is acceptable. The question is what you are willing to exchange for making it unacceptable to someone who matters.'

They tap their material flow chart. 'I have filed fourteen reports in seven years. Three were implemented. Two of those were implemented incorrectly, which created new problems I then had to document. The third was implemented correctly and then defunded eighteen months later when the budget cycle changed.' They look at you. 'Acceptable is not a moral category. It is an institutional one. Institutions accept things that individuals cannot, because institutions do not sleep in the buildings they are defunding.'

The silence between you has the specific weight of two people who agree on the problem and disagree on what agreement requires.

'If you have got something stronger than outrage,' Nev says, 'I am listening. Outrage is a fuel block—it burns hot, but it does not last. Evidence lasts. Documentation lasts. What is in your ledger?'
choice2_label: Regroup—you need Senna's manifests before you can make this conversation stick.

text:
'You have accepted that?'

Nev's expression does not change. But something behind it shifts—a recalculation, the way a structural reading changes when you apply a different load assumption.

'Accepted is an interesting word,' they say. 'I accept that water flows downhill. I accept that fuel blocks have a finite energy yield. I accept that institutional inertia is a measurable force with predictable effects on material allocation.' They pause. 'I do not accept that six districts should be stripped to fund a rail line. I simply measure the distance between what I do not accept and what I can change, and I work within that distance.'

They hold up their material flow charts—six weeks of meticulous documentation, blue and red ink marking supply lines like veins and arteries in a system that is slowly bleeding out.

'This is not acceptance. This is preparation. Every data point I record is a brick in a wall that someone, eventually, can use to build something. Maybe that someone is me. Maybe it is you. Maybe it is a Scholar twenty years from now who pulls my report out of a dusty archive and says: someone saw this, someone wrote it down.'

Nev sets the charts back on the desk with the care of someone handling something that matters more than it weighs.

'Seven years teaches you the difference between giving up and taking the long measurement. I measure. I document. I file reports that no one reads, because the day someone reads them, the data needs to be there.' They look at you directly. 'What I have not done—what I have been waiting for—is someone with fresh data and enough institutional backing to turn documentation into action. So. What have you got?'
choice2_label: Return to the CEA building.

text:
Nev pulls the map closer and taps each district in turn.

'Venmere—portside, same type of maintenance work as here. Their crane network has been running on Tier 0 fuel for four months. Two failures last week, both logged as operator error.' A finger moves north. 'Thornside—residential, mostly. Their water treatment circles failed in autumn. The repair materials were requisitioned, approved, and then diverted at the distribution node. The approval still exists. The materials do not.'

They continue. Oldgate—industrial, where the bonding paste mills are producing at half capacity because the input materials were redirected. The Millworks—the irony is not lost on Nev; the district that manufactures infrastructure materials cannot get infrastructure materials for its own maintenance. Duskwater—the newest settlement on the list, where the damage is still early enough that the residents have not yet realized the maintenance schedule they were promised is not coming.

'The pattern is identical at every scale. Materials are requisitioned for maintenance. The requisition is approved. The materials are redirected at the distribution stage to the transit rail project. The district receives either degraded substitutes or nothing. The maintenance schedules adjust around the shortage. The infrastructure degrades. The degradation compounds.'

They tap Karet Bay on the map. A red circle, darker than the others, annotated with numbers you can read from here.

'Yours is the worst because yours has the seawall. The other districts will fail slowly—pipes, walls, cranes, one at a time, each one filed as an isolated incident. Karet Bay fails all at once, because the seawall is a single point of failure for six thousand people.' They look at you. 'You know that already. You have data I do not. The question is whether we combine what we have.'
choice2_label: Return to the field camp.

text:
You open your ledger and lay out the warehouse manifests—the material grade records, the substitution documentation, the delivery schedules showing Tier 2 materials signed for and Tier 0 materials actually delivered.

Nev leans forward. Their eyes move across the documents with the specific intensity of someone seeing data they have been missing for six weeks. They pull out their own material flow charts—the supply chain traced from the distribution end—and begin laying them alongside yours.

'You documented the receiving end,' they say. 'I documented the sending end. Together—'

They align the timelines. The numbers match. Not approximately. Not within acceptable variance. Exactly. Every material shipment that left the central depot marked for Karet Bay matches a delivery record showing degraded substitutions. Every reallocation Nev traced to the transit rail corresponds to a shortage you found in the warehouse. The two data sets interlock like two halves of a diagnostic reading.

'This is good work,' Nev says, and means it. You can tell because they say it the same way they say everything else—as a measurement, not a compliment. 'Together, these two data sets are proof. Not a pattern. Not a suggestion. Not concerning indicators that warrant further review. Proof. Documented, timestamped, independently verified proof that the material reallocation was systematic, deliberate, and directly responsible for the infrastructure failure in this district.'

They look at you carefully. The expression is not excitement. It is the face of someone standing at the edge of a decision they have been avoiding for seven years.

'The question is what you do with proof in a system that was designed to produce the problem you have just proved.'
choice2_label: I will handle this my way.

text:
Nev is quiet for a long time. The diagnostic plates on their desk catch the late light. Outside, the CEA building sits with its polished seal and its maintained walls and its filing system designed to receive exactly the kind of information you are proposing to generate.

'A joint report carries more weight,' they say, finally. 'Two independent field evaluators, different assignments, different methodologies, reaching the same conclusion from opposite ends of the supply chain. The Academy cannot file that in pending review. The Council cannot dismiss it as a single-observer anomaly. It would be the most comprehensive infrastructure failure documentation produced in—' They stop. Calculate. 'In twelve years. Since the Venmere Port Collapse report, and that one took six months and two fatalities before anyone listened.'

They pause again. The pause has a different texture this time—not calculation but cost assessment.

'It would also put both of us on formal record as directly contradicting the CEA's budget narrative. You understand what that means for a career. Mireth has institutional cover. We do not. A joint report names us both. It says: these two Scholars looked at the system and found it broken, and they are telling you it is broken, with their names attached.'

Nev looks at the ceiling. Then at you.

'I will co-sign.' The decision lands like a measurement being recorded—final and precise. 'But only if your evidence is complete. Every data point verified. Every timeline cross-referenced. I do not put my name on anything that has gaps, because gaps are where institutions hide. You give me complete data, I give you my signature. That is the exchange.'

They extend a hand. Chalk dust and all.

Nev nods. The gesture is precise—neither disappointed nor relieved. It is the acknowledgment of a measurement taken and a conclusion reached, by someone who respects the process regardless of the outcome.

'Then do it properly.' They return their attention to the material flow charts as though the conversation has been filed and they are already working on the next calculation. Then they stop. Look up again. The pause has the quality of something they have been saving—a piece of professional advice that has cost them something to learn and costs them something to share.

'I have seen three Scholars break against this system. Three good ones—thorough, principled, the kind the Academy points to during graduation speeches and then sends into districts that will test every principle they were taught.'

They hold up three fingers.

'Two of them broke because they were not thorough enough. They had the right conclusions but insufficient evidence, and the institution used the gaps to disqualify the whole. If you are going to challenge a system, your documentation has to be airtight. Perfect. The kind of evidence that a review board cannot dismiss and an Overseer cannot reframe.'

One finger remaining.

'One broke because she was too thorough and not careful enough about who she showed it to. She gave her complete assessment to the wrong intermediary, and the data was quietly reclassified before it reached anyone who could act on it. Thoroughness without strategy is just ammunition for the other side.'

They lower their hand. Pick up their chalk. The conversation is over.

'Good luck, Scholar. File everything. Trust the right people. And keep a copy somewhere they cannot reach it.'

The decision makes itself the moment you stop pretending there is time for a better one. The seawall's timeline is measured in hours now, not days. The CEA operates in business days. The arithmetic is simple and devastating: official channels will not produce a response before the bay produces a catastrophe.

The district needs time. You can buy it, but not alone.

You cross the dark streets at a pace between running and the measured stride of someone who is trying very hard not to run because running causes panic and panic is a cost you cannot afford to add to the ledger tonight. The Freehands safehouse is fourteen minutes away. You have walked this route before, in daylight, with different urgency. The buildings look different at 0200—darker, more honest, the repairs and patches visible as shadows instead of details.

Brin answers her door with the expression of someone who has been expecting this knock. Not tonight, specifically. But eventually. She is wearing a coat over sleep clothes and has already put her boots on, which tells you everything about how long she has been awake and how much she has been listening to the district's walls.

'How bad?'

'Weeks, not months. Maybe days. The foundation survey—'

'I do not need the methodology. How bad?'

'The lower section will fail first. The tenements along the eastern waterfront. Six thousand people in the surge zone.'

She does not waste time asking questions she knows you have already answered for yourself. She looks past you into the dark street and her face does the same calculation yours did twenty minutes ago. Then she steps back from the door.

'Come in. We need to move fast.'
choice2_label: Alert Kaelen's dock crew.
choice3_label: Call the CEA emergency line—put the failure on record before you improvise.

text:
Brin activates the network. You watch it happen and understand, for the first time, what the Freehands actually are.

Not a repair collective. Not an underground charity. An infrastructure. A living, functioning infrastructure built from trust and proximity and the simple accumulated fact of people who have been relying on each other because nobody else was reliable. The network Brin activates in the next sixty minutes is more responsive, more efficient, and more precisely targeted than anything the CEA could deploy in six hours.

Runners move through the district—quiet, purposeful, waking specific people who can wake other specific people. No announcements. No panic. No official channels, because official channels would require authorization that would require review that would require the very system that created this crisis to acknowledge that the crisis exists, and the wall does not have time for institutional self-awareness.

Instead: a knock on a door. A few words. A nod. A family packing a bag. A neighbor checking on an elderly couple. A mother carrying a sleeping child toward the high ground, guided by someone who knows which streets flood first because they have lived here long enough to learn what the maintenance schedules should have prevented them from needing to know.

By 0300, the lower waterfront tenements are emptying. Not fast enough for your calculations. Fast enough for the reality.

Brin coordinates from her kitchen table with a map and a piece of chalk and the calm, focused intensity of someone who has been preparing for a night like this without knowing she was preparing. The Freehands network was built for repair work. Tonight it becomes an evacuation chain, and the transition is seamless, because the skills are the same: assess the damage, move the resources, protect the people.
choice2_label: Go to the seawall.

text:
The docks never fully sleep. Kaelen is there—night shift, hauling cargo that does not stop needing to move just because it is dark, performing the kind of labor that exists in the gap between what the schedule demands and what the body can provide.

He sees you coming. Reads your face. Does not ask for your calculations or your evidence or your institutional authority—reads your face the way he reads a load-bearing structure, the way his father read the seawall's circles, with the practiced assessment of someone who understands stress in materials and in people.

'How many hours?'

'Maybe twelve. Maybe less. The lower section will go first—the eastern waterfront tenements.'

He turns to his crew without hesitation. Eight dock workers, mid-shift, exhausted from hours of labor that was already underpaid and under-resourced. He does not explain. He does not justify. He does not ask permission from an authority that has never asked permission from him.

'Everyone stops what they are doing. We are moving families to the upper warehouse.'

And they move. The dock workers become an evacuation team without formal authorization, without an institutional mandate, without a single piece of paperwork establishing their credentials for the task. They become it because the task exists and they are here and the people who are supposed to do this are not. The transition is immediate—from cargo to people, from commerce to survival, from the work they are paid for to the work that needs doing.

Kaelen organizes it with the same efficiency he brings to everything: clear, physical, direct. Teams of two for each tenement block. Elderly and children first. Load-bearing routes only—no shortcuts through structures he does not trust. He knows which buildings to trust. He knows which ones are held together by habit.
choice2_label: Go to the seawall.

text:
You dial the CEA emergency line. It rings four times. A night clerk answers with the practiced flatness of someone paid to receive information between the hours of midnight and six, in a system that does not expect actionable information to arrive during those hours.

You provide your Scholar identification. Your field assessment number. The seawall structural data. The projected failure timeline. The surge zone population estimate. You provide it clearly, precisely, in the measured language of institutional communication, because the system requires measured language and you are, despite everything, still trained to speak its dialect.

The clerk takes your report. Reads it back to you with meticulous accuracy.

'A junior field evaluator is predicting imminent seawall failure based on an unauthorized independent assessment conducted outside normal operational hours.'

The silence that follows is the sound of a system processing information it was not designed to receive. Not because the information is wrong. Not because the system cannot understand it. Because the system's architecture routes emergency data through the same approval channels as routine data, and those channels operate on a schedule that was designed for a world where emergencies have the courtesy to occur during business hours.

'I will file this with the morning shift,' the clerk says. They are not being negligent. They are following procedure. The procedure was not built for this.

You hang up. The line goes dead with a soft click that sounds exactly like a door closing. Official channels have been notified. Official channels will respond at official speed. The bay operates on bay time, and bay time does not wait for an authorization stamp.

You put down the receiver. You have complied with institutional protocol. Now you comply with the wall.

For three hours, you are not a Scholar. You are a body that carries things and a voice that gives directions and a pair of arms that helps an eighty-year-old woman down stairs that were not designed for eighty-year-old women, in a building that was not designed to be evacuated, in a district that was not designed to be abandoned at three in the morning because the wall that was designed to hold is not holding.

The work is physical in a way your training never prepared you for. Your energy reserves—already depleted from a day of diagnostic work, from the seawall survey, from every circle you drew and every fuel block you burned—scrape against empty. You keep moving. The families keep moving. The Freehands network keeps moving. Everyone keeps moving because stopping is not an option the wall has offered.

By 0500, the seawall-adjacent buildings are emptied. Families camp in the upper warehouses, the Freehands safehouse, Kaelen's dock staging area—every structure above the surge line that has walls and a roof and enough floor space for people who left their homes carrying blankets and children and the kind of silence that happens when you leave a place you are not sure you will come back to.

Children sleep on folded blankets. Dogs patrol nervously, reading the tension in the air with more accuracy than any diagnostic plate. An old woman has brought her chair—carried it herself, three blocks, uphill—and is sitting in it with the serene determination of someone who survived the Drowning's aftermath, who survived the reconstruction, who survived the defunding, and who will survive this too, in her chair, with her dignity, daring the bay to try.

You have done what you can for the people. Now the wall.

You do not face the wall alone.

The Freehands network holds the evacuation—Brin's people stationed at every route, guiding families, securing shelters, doing the work of a functioning emergency system with none of the funding and all of the competence. Kaelen's dock crew provides muscle and the irreplaceable knowledge of people who have worked this waterfront their entire lives—who know which sections will fail first not from calculation but from decades of watching the stone, hearing it, feeling the vibrations through their boots.

You provide the calculations. Where the wall will fail. How to manage the cascade. Where to reinforce. Where to retreat.

The three of you—Scholar, dockworker, organizer—are the infrastructure the district was supposed to have. You are the emergency system. You are the maintenance budget. You are what remains when the institutions withdraw and the people do not.

The wall fails at 0547. The lower eastern section—exactly where your structural survey predicted. Stone separates from stone with a sound like the world clearing its throat. The bay enters with the patient inevitability of water that has been waiting to do exactly this. But the tenements are empty. Every one of them. The flooding is contained by barriers the dock workers built from shipping crates and industrial bonding paste in three hours of frantic, precise, backbreaking work. The barriers hold because Kaelen built them the way his father built circle work—correctly, under pressure, with the understanding that doing it right is not optional when lives are downstream.

The transit rail loses power for forty-eight hours while emergency materials are redirected back to the district. Nobody dies. Nobody.

The cost is distributed. A hundred small sacrifices instead of one enormous one. Workers give time. Brin gives materials. Kaelen gives leadership. Elara gives her purifier's fuel reserves to stabilize the barriers' bonding compounds. You give your calculations and every remaining joule of energy in your body, until your hands shake too badly to hold the chalk and someone else holds it for you and draws the circles you describe.

It is the Weighing of Red Harrow, eighty-three years later, in a district that history was preparing to forget. The principle that cost must be shared. That no single hand should pay what many hands can carry. That the republic was built on the idea that the exchange includes everyone, even the people at the bottom of the hill, even the people behind the wall, even the people whose names never appear on the authorization forms.

Many hands carry. Many hands held. The wall fell, and the district stood.

In the aftermath, the machinery of accountability begins to turn—slowly, reluctantly, the way all institutional machinery turns when the thing it must acknowledge is the thing it produced.

The joint report—yours and Nev's—is filed simultaneously to the Measured Scholars' Academy and the Revolutionary Council. It includes the warehouse manifests. The structural survey. The seawall assessment. The material flow analysis from six districts. And the documented evacuation of the Karet Bay surge zone, conducted without a single CEA-authorized action, saving an estimated six thousand lives through the combined efforts of a repair collective, a dock crew, a basement alchemist, and a junior field evaluator who was sent to investigate a crane.

Toris is reassigned. The word used is lateral transfer. The destination is a records office in a district where nothing structural fails because nothing structural was ever built. He will spend the next three years filing material allocation reports for a district with no materials to allocate. The passive voice will have less work to do there.

The transit rail project is audited. Three other districts receive emergency material allocations. Senna—Toris's junior administrator, who kept the real files in her lower desk drawer—is promoted to acting district coordinator. She accepts the position with the expression of someone who has been doing the actual work for months and is unsurprised to finally receive the title.

Brin's Freehands network is formally recognized. Not legalized, exactly—the institutional vocabulary has not evolved that far—but acknowledged. The distinction matters less than you would think. Brin does not need a certificate. She needs fuel blocks and access to maintenance supplies. She gets both.

Kaelen's crew receives the seawall maintenance contract they should have held seven months ago. The contract is backdated, which means someone in the Council's legal office understood what should have held means and decided to put it in writing. The dock workers begin repairs the following week. They know what they are doing. They have always known.

You return to the Academy. Mireth reads your report in her office, behind her desk, with the same expression she wears for everything: controlled, precise, giving nothing away. She reads all two hundred and forty-seven pages. She does not skip sections.

At the end, she closes the folder. Looks at you.

'This is not the kind of report that gets filed.'

You wait. Your hands are still bandaged from the circle work. Your energy reserves are, according to the Academy physician, inadvisable.

'It is the kind of report that gets taught.'

She was right about something she said yesterday morning, standing in the common hall with her ink-stained fingers and her stack of incident reports. Good work is not the same as right work. They operate on different scales, measure different costs, serve different purposes. But sometimes—if you are thorough enough, and if you are brave enough, and if you do not try to carry it alone—they are the same thing.

**[ENDING: THE DISTRIBUTED COST]**

*The cost was real. The cost was shared. In a world where someone always pays—sometimes the bravest thing is to make sure everyone carries a piece, and nobody carries it alone.*

The theater basement smells of tallow and damp stone. The troupe cleared out an hour ago—Petra is upstairs stacking chairs, her footsteps deliberate overhead. Down here, Dima has claimed a workbench, spreading his notebook open under three candle stubs arranged with the precision of someone who has learned to optimize insufficient light.

You sit across from him. The notebook is not what you expected.

It is a system. Names organized by household. Dates cross-referenced against material delivery schedules. Fuel readings—crude but consistent—taken at the same four locations every week for six months. Testimony fragments in small, careful handwriting. Margin notes connecting complaints filed to responses never received.

'I've been collecting this for six months,' Dima says. He doesn't look up from the page he's smoothing flat. 'But I'm fifteen. Nobody files a fifteen-year-old's report.'

He looks at you. The candlelight catches the ink stains on his fingers—extensive, permanent-looking, the hands of someone who has been writing things down long enough for the evidence to become physical.

'You're a Scholar. They'll file yours.'

He's right. The credential matters more than the content. That is, itself, a data point worth recording.

You pull your field ledger closer. 'Show me how you've organized this.'

choice2_label: Focus on the infrastructure data first.

text:
You and Dima work at the low table, the chronicle's architecture taking shape between your field ledger and his notebook. Three pillars. You draw them on a blank page and Dima copies the diagram into his own records with the fidelity of a court transcriber.

Physical evidence: the material readings, the structural data, the fuel allocation records. Personal testimony: the workers, the elders, the people who watched the failure happen in real time. Institutional record: the CEA documents, the filed complaints, the paper trail of decisions made and not made.

'Every good assessment needs corroboration from multiple angles,' you tell Dima. 'One source is an accusation. Two is a pattern. Three is a case.'

He writes that down. You watch him write it down. Something about seeing your own training maxims recorded in a fifteen-year-old's notebook makes them feel simultaneously more and less true than they did in the lecture hall where you first heard them.

Three pillars. You need all of them.

choice3_label: Find CEA documents.
choice4_label: Assemble the full chronicle.

text:
The pre-dawn dock is cold and smells of brine and rendered fuel. Workers arrive in clusters of two and three, hands wrapped in cloth, breath visible. Dima knows them by name. They know Dima by the notebook.

'He's all right,' a woman named Maren tells you, before you've asked a question. She's in her forties, forearms roped with the particular muscle of someone who has spent decades moving heavy things in confined spaces. She sits on an overturned crate and tells you about the day the maintenance circles stopped receiving fuel.

'We thought it was a supply delay. Everyone thinks it's a supply delay at first. You wait a week. Then two. Then three weeks pass and you realize nobody's coming, and the circles are degrading, and if you don't start doing it yourselves the whole dock section goes.' She pauses. 'So we started doing it ourselves. With our own supplies. On our own time.'

Her account is precise—dates, locations, which circles failed first, which ones they jury-rigged, which ones they couldn't save. Dima writes everything. His pen moves steadily. He's done this before. You can see it in the way Maren talks to him without looking at the notebook.

She trusts it's accurate. She's right.

text:
Gerd is next. He's a pipe fixer—thick-necked and deliberate, with the permanent squint of someone who spends too much time looking at things too close. He sits where Maren sat and speaks with the cadence of a man recounting something he has recounted before, to people who did not listen before.

'First the water went bad. Not all at once—you'd get a brown day, then a clear day, then two brown days. Then the walls started sweating. Condensation where there shouldn't be any, because the thermal regulation circles were failing. Then the cracks.'

He holds up three fingers.

'It wasn't one thing. It was everything, slowly, all at once. Like the whole district was exhaling and nobody bothered to check if it was still breathing in.'

He looks past you at the dock, where the morning shift is arriving. Workers with cloth-wrapped hands and careful steps.

'Nobody important was watching,' Gerd says. 'So nobody important noticed.'

Dima's pen doesn't hesitate. You notice he underlines the last sentence. Twice.

You write in your ledger: *cascade failure pattern consistent with systematic maintenance withdrawal.* The clinical language feels insufficient. You write it anyway. Something has to go in the column.
choice2_label: Return to the hub.

text:
Kaelen. You didn't expect his testimony to be the hardest.

He doesn't sit. He stands at the edge of the dock, arms crossed, looking at the water while he talks. The words come slowly, each one examined before release—the speech pattern of someone who has learned that words, once given, cannot be retrieved.

'My father did circle work on the seawall for twenty-three years. Original infrastructure. First-generation post-Drowning repair. He built bonding sequences designed to last forty years with standard maintenance fueling.' Kaelen's voice is steady. 'They lasted thirty-one. They would have lasted forty. They would have lasted longer than him.'

He turns. His hands are not steady.

'Someone decided his work wasn't worth maintaining. Someone in an office with clean walls and full fuel blocks looked at a budget line and decided that the thing my father built—the thing that keeps this district above water—was an acceptable place to save money.'

Dima writes it all. Every word. The pen scratches in the silence after Kaelen stops talking.

You don't say anything. There is nothing in your training that covers the correct professional response to a man describing the slow, administrative murder of his father's legacy.

Some testimony doesn't need follow-up questions.

Hanna lives on the third floor of a building whose staircase has been reinforced with salvaged timber at least twice. She's eighty-three. She answers the door already talking, as though the conversation started before you arrived and you're simply late.

'Sit down. Not that chair, the other one. That one's for the cat.'

There is no cat visible.

'Third time,' she says, before Dima has finished explaining why you're here. 'This is the third time I've watched this district die slowly.'

She counts on fingers swollen with age.

'The first was the water. The Drowning. I was three. My mother carried me uphill for two days. When we came back, everything below the second terrace was gone.'

Second finger.

'The rebuilding. They promised. Thirty years of promises. They rebuilt the port—the commercial part, the part that makes money. The residential district they *stabilized.*' She says the word like it's something she found on the bottom of her shoe. 'Stabilized means they stopped it from getting worse and called it fixed.'

Third finger.

'And now this. The fuel reallocation. The cracks. The water going bad again.' She lowers her hand. 'Eighty years. Three collapses. Same district. Same people paying.'

Dima writes. You notice his hand is shaking slightly. Hanna notices too.

'Write it steady, boy,' she says. 'Shaky handwriting doesn't hold up in court.'
choice2_label: Return to planning.

text:
Old Tomas receives you with the formality of a man who has been expecting someone official for approximately seven months and has opinions about the delay.

'Three complaints,' he says. He's already reaching into a drawer before you've sat down. 'Three complaints. Three form numbers. Filed in person at the district intake office.'

He produces the receipts. They're real—stamped, dated, numbered. You hold them and read the careful handwriting: descriptions of water pressure drop, structural condensation, visible cracking in load-bearing bonding paste. Each complaint precise enough to have been written by a field evaluator.

'I kept the receipts,' Tomas says. 'People told me I was being difficult. I told them I was being documented.'

Filed. Acknowledged. The intake stamps confirm receipt. The follow-up field—ACTION TAKEN—is blank on all three.

Three formal complaints about infrastructure failure in a residential district. Received, recorded, and then absolutely nothing. The paper trail of institutional indifference, preserved in triplicate by a man who understood that systems only work when someone holds them to their own rules.

'You can have copies,' Tomas says. 'I want the originals back. They're evidence.'

He's not wrong. They're the most damning evidence you've collected today, and you spent the morning documenting a failing seawall district.

Your Scholar credentials open the district CEA filing office the way a key opens a lock that hasn't been used in months—with effort and a concerning grinding sound. The clerk on duty looks at your authorization seal with the expression of someone who recognizes bureaucratic inevitability and has decided not to resist it.

'Records room is through there. Mind the boxes.'

The boxes are considerable. The filing room is a graveyard of administrative optimism—cabinets labeled by quarter, arranged in an order that was presumably chronological before someone stopped caring approximately seven months ago. Dust lies on the upper shelves with the permanence of geological strata.

You find the material allocation changes in the third cabinet. They are not where they should be—someone relocated them from the active files to the archive section. They're buried in a budget amendment appendix, subsection 4(c), titled *Operational Efficiency Adjustments.* The kind of title designed to discourage reading.

The documents show the fuel reallocation in clinical detail. Quantities, dates, authorization codes. The numbers match what you've been seeing in the field—the gap between what Karet Bay was allocated and what it received, expressed in the neutral language of administrative procedure.

Dima reads over your shoulder. 'They wrote it down,' he says quietly. 'They wrote down exactly what they did.'

'They always do,' you say. 'That's what records are for.'
choice1_label: Copy the key documents by hand. Thorough, but exhausting.
choice2_label: Photograph the filing system itself—the dust and disorder are evidence of neglect.

text:
In the back of the third cabinet, filed under *Resident Correspondence—Resolved*, you find them.

Three complaints. Different dates, different handwriting, same subject: material redirection affecting residential infrastructure in the Lower Dock District. Each one formal, detailed, specific. Each one stamped at the bottom with an official CEA review mark and the same three words: REVIEWED - NO ACTION REQUIRED.

Each stamp bears a signature. The signature is Toris's.

You check the dates. The first complaint was filed eight months ago. The second, six months. The third, four. The system didn't fail to notice. It noticed three times—three separate occasions where a district resident documented a problem, filed it through proper channels, and received in return the institutional equivalent of silence with a stamp on it.

Three occasions where Toris—specifically, with his name and his authority and his ink—looked at the problem and decided it wasn't one.

Dima stares at the stamps. His notebook is open but his pen has stopped.

'That's a signature,' he says quietly. 'That's not a system failing. That's a person deciding.'

You make copies of all three complaints. The originals stay in the cabinet, in the wrong section, where someone filed them so they wouldn't be found easily.

They've been found.

The theater basement. Full night. Petra brings bread, cheese, and a jar of something she claims is tea. The theater troupe—four performers and a stage manager who doubles as a carpenter—provide their satirical records: scripts annotated with audience reactions, demographic notes, community feedback collected after each performance. 'We've been doing social research,' Petra says. 'We just didn't call it that.'

You lay out the three pillars. Worker testimony: Maren's precise timeline, Gerd's cascade description, Kaelen's account of his father's seawall work. Elder accounts: Hanna's eighty-year history, Tomas's filed-and-ignored complaints with their damning blank follow-up fields. CEA records: the budget amendments, the material reallocation tables, and the three stamped complaints that prove the system was informed and chose inaction.

Cross-referencing takes hours. Dima's organizational system turns out to be rigorous—his six months of data collection maps onto your field observations with unsettling accuracy. Where your instruments detected structural degradation, his notebooks recorded which families were affected. Where the CEA records show fuel redirection, his interviews explain what that redirection felt like at street level.

Forty-seven pages. Physical evidence. Personal testimony. Institutional record. Dated, signed, cross-referenced. Every claim supported. Every number contextualized. Every institutional failure connected to a human cost.

It is the single most thorough document you have ever produced. It is also the first you have ever produced that you are certain will matter—because it was built by the people it describes.

Dima looks at you across the workbench. 'Is it enough?'

'It's a start,' you say. 'A very thorough start.'
choice2_label: Add your own formal Scholar's assessment as an appendix.

text:
You take the final blank pages and begin the appendix.

Technical analysis. Structural failure timelines. Material degradation curves calculated from your field readings. Cost projections: what the repairs will require, what the continued neglect will cost, what the seawall failure alone will do to the district's infrastructure viability over the next five years.

Everything you were trained to produce. Every formula, every framework, every assessment methodology drilled into you during four years at the Academy.

But you write it differently this time. Not as an abstract system analysis floating above human data, but as a framework around it. The structural failure timelines reference Maren's testimony. The material degradation curves annotate Gerd's cascade description. The cost projections cite Hanna's eighty-year history as context for why this district cannot absorb another rebuilding cycle that never finishes.

The numbers serve the stories. Not the other way around.

Dima reads over your shoulder as you write the final paragraph.

'Is this what your reports usually look like?' he asks.

You consider the stack of field assessments you've filed over two years. Technically precise. Humanly empty. Documents designed to be processed, not read.

'No,' you say. 'This one's better.'

Dima nods. He doesn't write that down. Some things don't need to be in the record to be true.

Four copies. Dima's handwriting on the originals, your Scholar's notation in the margins, the theater troupe's supplementary records bound at the back. Four identical documents, forty-seven pages each. One hundred and eighty-eight pages of accumulated truth stacked on the workbench in the candlelight.

Dima wants one copy to stay in the district. 'It belongs here,' he says, and he's right—the record should live where the cost was paid. Petra wants one for the theater network. It will travel through the performance circuit to other cities, other districts, other audiences who will hear this story in whatever form the troupe translates it into. That's two copies accounted for.

Two remain. This is the decision that determines how far the truth travels and through which channels it arrives.

The Academy will give the chronicle institutional credibility—your name, your credentials, the formal weight of a Measured Scholar's assessment. The Revolutionary Council will give it political reach, if anyone reads it, if anyone acts, if the system that created the problem can be trusted to respond to documentation of the problem.

Then again. There are other paths. Other networks. Other ways for a document to find the people who will use it rather than file it.

Two copies. The truth is the same in each one. The destination changes what it becomes.
choice1_label: Send one to the Academy, one to the Council. The institutional path.
choice2_label: Send both to independent press contacts. The public path.
choice3_label: Send one to the Academy, one through Ash's network.
choice4_label: Reread the marginal note in your old primer—the four layers and the alternate dossiers.

text:
In the basement lamplight you dig out your first-year primer, Structural Assessment Doctrine—mostly diagrams of load-bearing arches and scribbles about ethical leakage in public works.

Someone's marginal hand (not yours; the ink is older) has drawn four numbered layers of commentary:

(1) Mandatory inspection sequence. Beats along a route the commission will not let you skip, because the argument of the assessment fails if any one vanishes from the record.

(2) Radial hub routing. The open districts between those beats: many doors, many detours, but the spoke always resolves back toward the next mandatory beat or the hub that fed it.

(3) Ledger memory; accumulated attestation, the margin insists. The doctrine is explicit: the ledger remembers. What you witnessed, what you signed, what you refused to sign—later options read the accumulated state. There is no pretend reset.

(4) Parallel case files—alternate dossiers, the same annotator adds—complete alternate cases with their own mandatory beats, running in the same city while you are elsewhere. The main sequence's beats still pass; you are simply not there to countersign them.

You shelve the book beside the chronicle stack. Dima glances over—asks if you're all right. You say yes. Whatever that annotator was drinking, it was stronger than scholar tea.

Still: the metaphor is uncomfortably precise for a seawall diagram—and for the four copies waiting on the workbench.
choice1_label: Return to the workbench and the four copies.

text:
The chronicle is distributed. Four copies, four paths, four chances for the truth to outlast the institution that created the problem.

The seawall crisis resolved without you.

Kaelen's crew—working on instinct and experience and the bone-deep understanding of people who know their own waterfront—evacuated the seawall-adjacent buildings when the first cracks widened past tolerance. No deaths. The wall partially failed during the high-tide surge, flooding three streets to waist height. Forty-one people injured. Six hospitalized. One hundred and twelve displaced from buildings that were never structurally sound enough to survive what everyone knew was coming.

You weren't there. You were in a theater basement, cross-referencing fuel allocation records with personal testimony by candlelight while the district you were sent to assess paid the cost you had calculated. You chose the record over the rescue. The mathematics of that choice are not complex: the seawall failed whether you were present or not. The chronicle exists because you were not.

The cost of that calculation will live in you alongside the forty-seven pages that now exist because of it.

Three months later.

Petra's theater network has performed a piece based on the chronicle in four cities. The audiences don't clap at the end. They sit in silence. Petra says that's better than applause.

The Measured Scholars' Academy has opened a formal review of material allocation practices in Orvish's lower districts. Your appendix—the one where the numbers serve the stories instead of replacing them—was cited in the review authorization. Senna, the regional coordinator, has been called to testify. Her testimony is scheduled for three weeks from now. She has not yet responded to the summons.

Toris has been suspended pending investigation. The three stamped complaints—REVIEWED - NO ACTION REQUIRED—are now evidence in a formal misconduct inquiry. He is, by all accounts, surprised that anyone found them. The filing system was supposed to take care of that.

And Dima—fifteen years old, with ink-stained fingers and the careful handwriting of someone who has always known that the truth needs to be written down before it can be heard—is working on a second volume. He has enlisted three other teenagers from the dock crews. They call themselves the Karet Bay Record Office. They have no funding, no official authority, and no intention of stopping.

**[ENDING: THE CHRONICLER]**

*The cost was real. The cost was yours. In a world where someone always pays—sometimes paying means keeping the record so the cost is never forgotten.*

The afternoon at the Drowning Memorial wears a bureaucrat's sunlight—bright enough to read by, indifferent to whether the reading comforts anyone. The plaque catches it on the wall before you, bronze letters spelling names of workers lost to infrastructure failure. Someone has left fresh flowers at the base. The petals are already curling.

The basement's rupture still sits under your tongue—copper and stubborn quiet—while the plaque offers grief in approved proportions.

Elara stands a respectful distance from the inscription, as if giving the dead their margin. When your shadow crosses the stone, she meets your eyes once—acknowledgement without performance. She could be waiting. She could have timed the district the way she times pressure; either way, she is not pretending this is coincidence.

"I chose this place on purpose," she says. "Public. Witnessed. Not my basement, not the CEA's halls—just the district's receipt, where neither of us gets to pretend the numbers were hypothetical."

She studies your face with the same attention she gave the purifier—diagnostic, not sentimental.

"I've been working on something. Not the purifier—something else. The residential water network. The pipes the CEA keeps patching with pressure increases instead of actual repair." She pauses. "The kind of work the district actually needs done."

Her hands are in her pockets. Her expression is carefully neutral in the way that people are careful when they're about to offer something that could be refused.

"No credentials. No reports. No institutional approval. Just the work." She nods toward the residential quarter. "I could use someone who understands the theory. Someone whose alchemy isn't self-taught."

The offer sits between you like an equation with variables you haven't solved for. To one side, the weight of everything stamped and sealed. Ahead of you, a woman who fixes things without permission.
choice2_label: Ask what kind of work she means.
choice3_label: Decline and return to the CEA building.

text:
"The water distribution network in the residential quarter," Elara says. She speaks the way she works—directly, without ornament, each word placed where it needs to go. "It was designed thirty years ago for a population half the current size. The original alchemical pressure circles were calibrated for twelve hundred households. The district has twenty-three hundred now, and the CEA's response has been to boost the input pressure rather than redesign the distribution pattern."

She pulls a folded paper from her jacket. A sketch—hand-drawn, annotated in her small precise handwriting. You recognize junction markers, flow calculations, pressure gradients.
