The work of someone who understands hydraulic alchemy not as theory but as something that happens to real pipes carrying real water to real people.

"Increased pressure works until the old pipes fail. And the old pipes are failing. Three bursts this month in the Narrows alone. One of them contaminated the water supply for two blocks—forty families boiling their drinking water because the CEA's solution to insufficient infrastructure is to push harder on the infrastructure that's insufficient."

She folds the paper back into her pocket with the careful motion of someone protecting something valuable.

"What I'm doing is unauthorized. I'm redesigning the distribution pattern using local materials and circle work I can maintain myself. Tier 0 and Tier 1 components. Nothing that requires CEA supply chains, because CEA supply chains don't supply this district anymore." The dry observation lands without emphasis. She doesn't need to emphasize what you already know.

"It's also the only thing that will work before someone dies of contaminated water. That's not rhetoric. That's hydraulic engineering."
choice2_label: Decline.

text:
Elara leads you through a side door, down concrete steps worn smooth by decades of feet, into the basement of the building above her purifier. The space is small—perhaps four meters by six—and organized with the exacting precision of someone who cannot afford to waste time looking for things. Tools hang on a pegboard in outlined silhouettes, each shape labeled in the same small handwriting you saw on the water network sketch. Materials are sorted by Hazard Index tier in clearly marked containers: Tier 0 in open bins, Tier 1 in sealed jars, the single Tier 2 component she possesses—a half-empty container of bonding catalyst—locked in a metal box bolted to the wall.

The workbench dominates the room. Its surface is scarred oak, and chalk dust has been ground into the wood grain so thoroughly that it will never come out. Hundreds of circles have been drawn and erased and redrawn here. The ghosts of them remain in the wood like geological strata—layers of practice, of failure, of refinement.

"This is where I learned that alchemy isn't a credential," she says. "It's a practice."

She spreads her water network plans across the workbench. Hand-drawn on drafting paper, annotated at every junction, every pressure point, every material specification. The plans are not beautiful in the Academy sense—no elegant symmetry, no optimized geometries. They are beautiful in the way that a well-used tool is beautiful: shaped by function, refined by repetition, marked by the hands that made them work.

You lean in. The plans are better than they have any right to be.
choice2_label: Ask about her training.
choice3_label: Help immediately.

text:
You study Elara's plans the way the Academy taught you—systematic assessment, material analysis, structural integrity projections. And then you study them again the way they actually deserve to be studied, which is as an act of practical genius achieved entirely outside the system that claims a monopoly on genius.

The distribution redesign uses Tier 0 and Tier 1 materials in combinations that don't appear in any Academy textbook. Not because they're wrong—they're demonstrably right—but because the textbooks assume access to Tier 2 components. Every Academy solution you were taught begins with the premise that proper materials are available. Elara's solutions begin with the premise that they aren't, and work backward from there to something that functions anyway.

"Textbooks assume you have Tier 2," she says, watching you trace the junction specifications. "We don't. Haven't for seven months. So I work with what exists."

The junction circles use a nested activation pattern you've never seen. It takes you three minutes of staring to understand how they work, and when you do, the elegance of it hits you like a rebuke. She's achieving eighty percent of Tier 2 performance using Tier 0 components arranged in a geometry that exploits resonance harmonics between adjacent circles. It's the alchemical equivalent of building a clock from scrap iron—technically inferior, practically brilliant, and impossible to find in any textbook because the people who write textbooks have never needed to try.

Your clean Academy hands suddenly feel like a liability.
choice2_label: Discuss the theory with her.
choice3_label: Ask about the scope of the network problem.

text:
"I trained with a Freehand alchemist in Orvish for three years." Elara says it the way other people say they went to school—factually, without apology, without the defensive edge that might suggest she thinks it requires defending. "No Academy. No certification. No credential. Just a woman named Thessa who had been doing circle work since before the Republic standardized it, and who taught me by making me do it until I got it right."

She pauses, and something crosses her face that might be grief or might be gratitude—the two emotions being, in your experience, more closely related than most people admit.

"I learned by doing. By failing. By fixing what I failed. Thessa's teaching method was: 'Draw the circle. If it doesn't work, find out why. If it works, find out how.' Three years of that." She holds up her hands. You look at them—really look, with a Scholar's trained attention.

The scars are small and numerous, concentrated on the fingertips and palms. Faint alchemical residue sits in the creases of her skin like watermarks in paper—the kind that doesn't wash off because it's been absorbed over years of direct contact with reactive materials. Calluses have formed where chalk is held, where circles are drawn, where corrections are made by hand on surfaces too irregular for instruments.

"Your hands are clean, Scholar." She says it the way she says everything—as observation, not accusation. "That's how I know you haven't done real work yet."

She's right. It isn't an insult. It's an assessment as precise as any you've made today, delivered by someone who measures competence by evidence rather than credential.

For twenty minutes, you and Elara have a conversation that the Academy would not approve of and that you will remember for the rest of your career—however long that turns out to be.

Elara's approach to alchemy is fundamentally different from yours. You were trained top-down: begin with the optimal solution, then adapt it to available conditions. She works bottom-up: begin with available materials and conditions, then build toward the best achievable outcome. Your method produces elegant solutions that require specific inputs. Hers produces inelegant solutions that work with whatever is at hand.

Neither approach is wrong. You say this aloud, and the admission costs more than you expected, because the Academy trained you to believe that optimal was synonymous with correct.

"In a district where Tier 2 materials haven't arrived in seven months," Elara says, not unkindly, "elegant solutions are a form of fiction."

You discuss resonance harmonics. She shows you how Tier 0 chalk, applied in specific moisture conditions, creates temporary bonds that mimic Tier 1 stability. You show her the mathematical framework behind her intuitive junction patterns—the formal theory she arrived at through practice alone. She stares at the equations.

"That's what I've been doing?"

You nod. She laughs—a short, sharp sound. "Thessa would have loved this. She always said the math was in the hands."

The exchange leaves you with something unfamiliar: the recognition that your education, while rigorous and expensive and institutionally certified, has prepared you for a world that doesn't exist here. In the world that exists here, Elara's education is the one that works.

The first repair site is underneath a tenement building on Keel Street—a water junction box accessible through a rusted hatch in the basement floor. Three families depend on this junction for their water supply. You know this because one of them is standing in the basement doorway, watching, holding a kettle of boiled water because the unboiled kind has been making her children sick.

The junction is worse than the plans suggested. The pipe is corroded through in two places, the existing maintenance circle has degraded to the point of visual failure—chalk lines blurred, activation points dissolved by moisture—and the temporary patch someone applied is leaking a thin brown stream that smells of rust and something organic you don't want to identify.

Elara works. You watch. Her technique is fast and economical—she strips the failed circle with a scraper, cleans the pipe surface with an alcohol solution, redraws the maintenance circle in a modified geometry using Tier 0 chalk, and activates it with a finger-touch that channels just enough personal energy to start the reaction. No instruments. No fuel blocks. No wasted motion.

The circle catches. You feel the resonance hum through the pipe—lower than a Tier 2 circle, but steady. The corrosion stops spreading. The leak seals. Clear water flows.

The woman with the kettle watches the clean water run. She doesn't say anything. She doesn't need to. You've read enough structural assessments to recognize when something has been fixed. You've never watched it happen to a person's drinking water before. The two experiences are not, it turns out, the same.
choice2_label: Assist Elara at the next site.

text:
The next junction is two buildings over—same model, same vintage, same state of neglected decay. Elara gestures at it the way a teacher presents a problem set. "Your turn."

You draw the circle. Your lines are technically superior to Elara's—cleaner geometry, more precise activation points, better energy flow channels. The Academy trained you well, in the same way that a factory produces excellent components for machines that may or may not exist. Your circle is beautiful. Your circle is also draining you faster than it should.

The problem is habit. The Academy teaches self-fueled activation as the default technique—channel your own energy to start the circle, then let the ambient field sustain it. In a proper Tier 2 environment, the ambient field picks up the load within seconds. Here, with Tier 0 materials and depleted ambient reserves, the field doesn't pick up anything. You're powering the entire circle yourself, and the junction is larger than you estimated.

Elara watches with the patience of someone who has seen this exact mistake before.

"You're overengineering it," she says, when your hands start to shake. "The pipe doesn't need to last fifty years. It needs to last until someone with proper materials can do it right. You're building a cathedral when the job calls for a roof."

She's right and you know she's right and the knowing doesn't make it easier, because everything in your training insists that adequate is another word for failure.

The circle holds. The cost is in your hands and behind your eyes, where the energy deficit has settled like a debt you'll be paying for hours.
choice2_label: Push through with your method.

text:
You work alongside Elara through the afternoon. Four more junctions, each in a different building, each with its own particular species of deterioration. A rhythm develops—she leads, you support, and somewhere between the second and third junction, you stop thinking about the Academy's way of doing things and start thinking about what works.

By the second junction, you're handing her materials before she asks. By the third, you're preparing the pipe surfaces while she draws the circles. By the fourth, you're improvising your own variations—using your theoretical knowledge to optimize her practical geometry, finding refinements that neither formal training nor street experience alone would have produced.

The families watch. Some bring things—a stool for the bad basement with no light, a lantern for the worse basement with no floor, tea in cracked cups, the implicit thank-you of people who have learned not to expect help and don't quite trust it when it arrives. A man in the third building tells you his daughter boiled all their water for four months and still got sick. He says it calmly. He has had time to be angry. The anger has become a kind of patience that looks, from the outside, like resignation but isn't.

Your energy drops in measured increments, like a fuel block burning down—steady, predictable, the cost of work done honestly. Elara monitors you the way she monitors her circles: with practical attention, checking for the signs of failure before failure becomes the kind you can't fix.

By the end of the fourth junction, your hybrid technique flows as naturally as anything the Academy taught you. More naturally. Because this time the theory serves the practice, instead of the other way around.

You simplify. The word tastes like defeat, and defeat tastes like chalk dust and copper, which are the flavors of doing something real in a place that is also real.

You strip your circle design down. Remove the redundant stability loops. Eliminate the aesthetic geometry—the beautiful spirals that make Academy circles look like illuminated manuscripts and accomplish nothing functional. Reduce the activation channels from four to two. Use Elara's moisture-bonding technique instead of your self-fueled ignition.

The repair is adequate. The word sits in your mouth like a stone. Adequate. Not elegant. Not permanent. Not the kind of work that earns commendations or gets published in the Proceedings of the Measured Academy. Just functional. Just sufficient. Just enough.

Elara nods. "That's the hardest lesson. The best solution isn't the optimal one. It's the one that works with what you have."

You move to the next junction. And the next. By the third repair, something has shifted—not just in your technique but in the part of your mind that evaluates technique. You stop comparing your work to the Academy standard and start comparing it to what was there before: corroded pipes, failed circles, contaminated water. Against that metric, adequate is extraordinary. Against that metric, the repair you just completed is the most important piece of alchemy you've ever done.

Three junctions later, you've developed a hybrid approach that neither of you could have created alone. Your theory, her practice, shaped by the specific constraints of a district that the system forgot. It's not in any textbook. It works.

You do it your way. The Academy way. Full activation geometry, proper energy channels, self-fueled ignition sustained to completion. The circle you draw on the corroded junction pipe is, objectively, beautiful—the kind of precise, multilayered work that gets held up in practicals as an example of what trained alchemy looks like when it's done right.

It's also consuming you.

The self-fueled technique works by drawing on your personal energy reserves to power the circle until the ambient field takes over. In a properly maintained district with Tier 2 materials and a functional alchemical infrastructure, the handoff takes seconds. Here, the ambient field is so depleted that the handoff never comes. You're powering the entire circle—every activation point, every stabilization loop, every precise and beautiful and entirely excessive element of your Academy-standard design—from your own reserves.

By the midpoint, your hands are trembling. By three-quarters, your vision swims and the chalk lines blur and you're drawing from memory and muscle reflex because your conscious mind is occupied with not collapsing. The energy deficit is a physical thing—a hollowing, a drawing-down, the sensation of being poured out like water from a vessel that can't be refilled this quickly.

Elara catches your arm when you finish. "Steady. You're burning yourself."

You are. The repair will last years. The junction is sealed, stabilized, protected by a circle that would pass any Academy inspection. The pipe gleams. Your hands don't stop shaking for twenty minutes.

The cost was real. But the water runs clean, and somewhere above you a family turns on a tap without boiling the water first. You're not sure the math works out. You're not sure it doesn't.

Word spreads the way word spreads in communities that the system has forgotten: quickly, accurately, and through channels that no official communication network could replicate. By the time you and Elara finish the last junction, a small crowd has gathered at the building entrance. They don't look like a crowd—they look like people who happened to be in the same place, because people in districts like this have learned that gathering draws attention and attention draws the kind of people who disperse gatherings.

An old woman brings tea. It's strong and sweet and served in a cup that has been mended twice, and it's the best thing you've tasted all day. She doesn't tell you her name. She tells you which building she lives in and how long the water has been bad.

A child—eight, maybe nine, with the watchful eyes of someone who has learned to read situations early—tugs at your sleeve. "Are you a real alchemist?"

Elara answers before you can. "The realest."

The child considers this. Nods. Runs back to tell someone.

The community's response to unauthorized infrastructure repair is not outrage or suspicion or the nervous deference of people encountering officialdom. It's gratitude—quiet, practical, expressed in tea and nods and the specific kind of eye contact that says: I see what you did, and it mattered.

And then it's requests. Three more buildings need help—the water in the Narrows, the drainage system behind the fishmarket, the pressure problems on the upper floors of the Atherton block. Seven more after that. Fourteen after those. The district has been waiting—not passively, not with resignation, but with the focused patience of people who knew that eventually someone would do what needed doing. They just didn't know when.
choice2_label: Stop and consider the consequences.

text:
You stop. Not physically—your hands keep holding the teacup the old woman gave you—but somewhere behind your sternum, in the place where professional judgment lives, something seizes like a gear that's found a stone.

What you've been doing is unauthorized alchemical work on residential infrastructure. Your Scholar credentials don't cover this. Your field evaluation authority explicitly excludes direct modification of civilian structures—it's in Section 12 of the Assessment Protocols, a passage you memorized and never expected to violate. If Toris finds out, your assessment is compromised. If the Academy finds out, your credentials are revoked. If both find out, your career doesn't end—it ceases to have existed, retroactively redefined as a cautionary anecdote in the next edition of the Protocols.

Elara sees your expression. She's been waiting for it, you realize. Not with dread—with the practical recognition of a woman who has watched credentialed people reach this exact point and choose the credential.

"You're thinking about your credential."

"I'm thinking about what happens if this goes wrong."

"Things are already going wrong, Scholar." She gestures—at the building, at the street, at the district visible through the gap between tenements: cracked walls, improvised repairs, infrastructure held together by the equivalent of hope and Tier 0 chalk. "We're just doing something about it."

The teacup is warm in your hands. The water in it is clean because of what you did today. The career in your pocket is a document that says you're qualified to assess situations exactly like this one and then write reports about them that will be read by people who will authorize further assessments.

The gap between what the credential permits and what the situation requires has become a chasm.
choice2_label: Return to the official investigation.

text:
The fishmarket wall.

The building is four stories of old stone and older alchemy, built during the first decade of the Republic when infrastructure was a promise and materials were available to keep it. Seven businesses occupy the ground floor—fishmongers, a baker, a woman who repairs nets and sells rope. Thirty families live above. The load-bearing wall on the eastern face has been failing for months, the structural reinforcement circles degrading in the same slow spiral of material starvation that's killing everything else in the district. A crack runs from foundation to second floor, widening at a rate that your Scholar training lets you calculate with unwelcome precision: two weeks, maybe three, before cascading failure.

This is not a water junction. This is not a pipe repair. This is structural modification of an occupied residential and commercial building—the line that separates maintenance from construction, improvisation from engineering, unauthorized repair from unauthorized construction. On the other side of this line, there is no version of your career that survives.

You do it anyway.

The decision doesn't feel like a decision. It feels like the last step in a calculation that started when you saw the crane anomaly readings, continued through the warehouses and the manifests and the water junctions, and arrives here: at a wall that will fall on people if you don't fix it, with the knowledge of how to fix it, and the choice between your credential and their ceiling.

Elara is beside you. Brin's people are watching the approaches. The district that has been waiting for someone to do the necessary thing is watching you decide to do it.

The chalk feels different in your hands. Heavier. Realer. You draw the first line.
choice2_label: Work fast before anyone official notices.

text:
Six hours. You take six hours because the wall deserves six hours and because the people sleeping above it deserve someone who isn't rushing.

Elara provides materials from her network—Tier 0 chalk in quantities, Tier 1 bonding agent she's been hoarding, the half-container of Tier 2 catalyst that represents everything she has of institutional-grade supply. You use them the way a surgeon uses sutures: precisely, economically, with the awareness that there is no more where this came from.

The work is a slow negotiation between what the wall needs and what you have to give it. You restructure the support matrix one section at a time—dissolving the failed circles, cleaning the stone, redrawing the geometry in your hybrid technique. Each new circle must integrate with the ones above and below it. Each activation must be carefully fueled—too little and it won't hold, too much and you burn yourself out again.

Brin's network provides cover. A lookout at each end of the street. A woman in the fishmarket who watches the road and coughs loudly when she sees uniforms. The infrastructure of community self-preservation, deployed to protect the act of infrastructure self-repair. The irony would be worth savoring if you had the energy to spare.

By hour four, your hands move automatically. By hour five, you've stopped thinking about the Academy and started thinking in the language of the wall itself—its weight, its grain, its particular way of settling into its own history. By hour six, the circle network is complete. The wall hums with steady, low-grade resonance. Not Tier 2 performance. Not optimal. But real. Solid. Sufficient.

You step back. Your body feels like it's been wrung out by someone who was thorough about it. But the building stands. Tomorrow, the building will still stand.

Two hours. Speed, because every minute you spend on this wall is a minute the CEA might notice, and the CEA noticing is a variable you cannot control and would prefer to avoid introducing until the wall is no longer in danger of falling on people.

You and Elara work in tandem—a rhythm developed in the water junctions, accelerated now by urgency and the particular focus that comes from knowing the stakes. She draws the lower sections while you handle the upper. Your circles aren't as precise as the careful approach would allow, but they're solid—the hybrid technique, stripped of all nonessential geometry, applied at the speed your hands can manage.

The energy cost is brutal. You're fueling circles faster than your reserves can comfortably sustain, running a deficit that accumulates with each activation like compound interest on a debt you're taking out against your own body. Elara is doing the same—you can see it in the tightness around her eyes, the slight tremor in her chalk hand that wasn't there an hour ago.

Halfway through, a CEA patrol passes the end of the street. Two officers on their usual route. Elara doesn't look up. You don't look up. The fishmonger at the corner stall calls a greeting to the officers, loud enough to draw their attention, casual enough to seem ordinary. They wave. They keep walking. They don't look down the alley where two unauthorized alchemists are restructuring a building's support matrix with materials that aren't in any requisition system.

The repair takes two hours. It's not as thorough as six hours would have produced—some sections are stabilized rather than fully repaired, held by circles that will need reinforcement within months. But the wall holds. The crack has stopped growing. The thirty families above the fishmarket will sleep tonight under a ceiling that will still be there in the morning.

Morning comes the way mornings come in Karet Bay: slowly, grey, tasting of salt and the particular weariness of a district that wakes up tired. You watch it from Elara's workshop, sitting on the floor with your back against the workbench, too exhausted to climb the stairs.

The wall holds. You know this because Elara checked at dawn, pressing her palm flat against the stone the way a doctor checks a pulse, and nodded once. The fishmarket opens. People buy fish from stalls that would have been buried under four stories of rubble by now. A baker pulls bread from an oven that sits against a wall that your circles are holding together. The net-mender opens her shutters above a street that is still a street and not a debris field.

Nobody knows what you did except the people who helped you do it. The families above the fishmarket will eventually notice that the crack stopped growing. The fishmongers will eventually stop flinching when heavy carts pass. The baker will eventually forget that she spent the last two months wondering if today was the day the ceiling came down.

But the Scholar credentials in your pocket feel different now. Not heavier—just less relevant. A document certifying your authority to assess and report, carried by a person who has just done something that no assessment or report could have accomplished. The gap between what the credential represents and what you've become is no longer a gap. It's a border you crossed, and borders only work if you stay on the correct side.

The CEA will find out. The work was too visible, too effective, too much the kind of thing that makes institutional authority nervous. When they do, your career as a Measured Scholar ends. Not with failure. With competence. The system has no category for that.
choice2_label: Push on—more work to do.

text:
The CEA revokes your field evaluation credentials within the week. The official notification arrives by courier—a sealed document, institutional letterhead, the particular weight of paper that the bureaucracy reserves for communications it considers important. You open it in Elara's workshop, sitting at the workbench where you've been sleeping, because you've been sleeping here since the fishmarket wall and you haven't yet found a reason to stop.

Mireth's letter is included, separate from the formal revocation. You recognize her handwriting—precise, slightly leftward-leaning, the script of someone who was taught penmanship as a form of professional discipline. The letter is brief:

"Your work in Karet Bay was technically outstanding and professionally indefensible. The structural modifications you performed exceeded your assessment authority by a margin I lack the vocabulary to quantify diplomatically. The Academy cannot support unauthorized structural modification of civilian buildings, regardless of the outcome. Your assessment privileges are suspended indefinitely."

There's a postscript, in smaller handwriting: "The readings you transmitted were the most detailed field data we've received in three years. The irony is not lost on me."

Elara reads the letter over your shoulder. She smells of chalk dust and the herbal solution she uses to clean her tools.

"Suspended indefinitely," she says. "That's institutional for 'you scared them.'" She hands you a cup of something dark and aromatic that is definitely not tea and is probably not entirely legal to distill in a residential basement. "So. What now?"

What now is: you stay. The word doesn't feel like defeat. It feels like the answer to an equation you've been solving since you arrived—the variable that balances the expression, the value that makes the cost and the outcome equivalent at last. There is work to do. You know how to do it. The district needs someone who shows up.

You show up.

Your body is telling you things you've been trained to measure in other people's infrastructure and have never been forced to measure in yourself. Energy reserves critical. The deficit isn't a number anymore—it's a physical sensation, a hollowing behind your sternum that makes each breath feel like drawing from an empty well. Your hands are shaking. Not the fine tremor of fatigue—the deeper, structural tremor of a system running past its tolerances.

Elara sees it. She's been watching you the way she watches her circles: with practical attention, monitoring for the signs that precede collapse.

"Stop." Her voice is flat and firm. "You're past the safety margin."

But there's another building. You can see it from here—the Atherton block, four streets over, where the upper-floor drainage has been failing for weeks and the structural damage from water infiltration is following the same pattern you've seen all day. Another wall. Another family. Another piece of infrastructure that will fail if no one acts, and you are someone, and you know how to act.

This is how distortion starts. You know this because you studied it at the Academy—not as a personal risk but as a theoretical phenomenon, safely described in textbooks with diagrams and probability tables. The unbalanced exchange. The alchemist who draws from reserves that don't exist, forcing the conversion to find fuel somewhere, and the somewhere is always the alchemist's own physical structure. Organic matter converted without consent. The technical term is somatic transmutation. The common term is the one that matters: distortion.

One more repair. One more building. One more person you can't walk away from. The equation is simple and the equation is a lie, because there is always one more building and the cost of one more is always more than one.
choice2_label: One more.

text:
You draw the circle. Your hands move with the muscle memory of a day's practice, finding positions and geometries that your conscious mind is too depleted to direct. The chalk line wavers—you can see it wavering—but the pattern is close enough. Close enough is what you've learned today. Close enough is what kills you.

The activation requires energy you don't have. Your reserves are a number below zero, a deficit that exists in the theoretical space where the body's alchemical potential has been fully expended and the exchange begins looking for alternative fuel sources. You know what happens next. You learned it in a lecture hall, sitting in a comfortable chair, taking notes in clean handwriting with clean hands.

The circle activates. The resonance is wrong—a pitch too low, a frequency that vibrates in your bones rather than in the materials. The stone wall ripples, not like liquid but like something remembering that it was once liquid, that solidity is a temporary condition, that everything is convertible if you push hard enough.

You look down at your hands. Crystal is forming in the joints of your fingers—slow, precise, beautiful in the way that all alchemical processes are beautiful when they're working exactly as designed. Your knuckles catch the light. The crystal is clear, with a faint amber hue. It doesn't hurt yet. It will.

Distortion. Somatic transmutation. The exchange found its fuel, and the fuel was you.

The wall holds. Your hands don't. Your wrists stiffen. The crystal spreads.

Elara catches you as your knees give way. She's saying something—shouting something—but the sound is distant now, filtered through the ringing in your skull and the copper taste flooding your mouth. "I told you to stop. I told you." She's crying. You want to tell her the wall is fixed, that the building will stand, that thirty families will wake up tomorrow under a solid ceiling. But your mouth doesn't work the way it used to, because your jaw is doing something it shouldn't, and your vision is narrowing to a single point of light.

The point of light contains—for one perfect, terrible moment—the exact calculation of what you paid. Every variable, every coefficient, every term in the equation balanced at last. The exchange is always balanced. That's the first thing they teach you at the Academy, and it's the last thing you learn in Karet Bay.

The cost was real. The cost was yours. The wall holds.

[GAME OVER — THE COST OF CRAFT]

Six months later. The season has turned twice since you arrived in Karet Bay with a field satchel and a credential and the institutional confidence of someone who had never been asked to fix anything they'd assessed. The satchel is worn now. The credential is revoked. The confidence has been replaced by something less comfortable and more useful: competence earned by doing, tested by failing, refined by the daily practice of showing up in a place that needs you and doing the work that needs doing.

You live in Karet Bay. The sentence would have horrified you six months ago—a Measured Scholar, living in a failing district, doing unauthorized infrastructure work with a Freehand-trained alchemist in a basement workshop. It doesn't horrify you now. It's just accurate.

Elara teaches you the things the Academy never could. How to read a building by touching its walls, feeling the resonance of its support structures through your palm the way a physician reads a pulse. How to listen when someone tells you what they need, instead of telling them what you've determined they should have. How to work with what exists rather than mourning what doesn't. How to let adequate be enough.

You teach her the things the Academy taught you. Stress analysis—the formal mathematics behind her intuitive structural assessments. Material science—the chemistry of the bonding agents she uses by instinct. Energy optimization—the theoretical framework that explains why her circle geometries work, which she finds alternately fascinating and hilarious. "I've been doing eigenvalue decomposition," she says one evening, staring at your equations. "For three years. Without knowing the word." She laughs until she cries.

Together, you've repaired thirty-two buildings, two water mains, and the southern section of the seawall. The seawall work took three weeks and nearly killed both of you and was the most important thing you've ever done. The district calls you "the Scholar who stayed." You don't correct them, because the correction would require explaining that you're not really a Scholar anymore, and the explanation would require caring about a distinction that has ceased to mean what it used to.

Your formal assessment of the crane anomaly was never filed. The data didn't disappear—Dima included your structural readings in his chronicle, with meticulous attribution, and Nev's independent report to the Republic's oversight committee referenced your field measurements. The system got the data. It just didn't get it through the channels the system designed for receiving data, which means the system will spend more energy arguing about the methodology than acting on the conclusions. This surprises no one.

The work continues. Every morning you wake up in a district that is marginally better than it was yesterday, because yesterday you and Elara fixed something. Not everything. Not enough. But something, which is the difference between a place that is failing and a place that is being maintained by people who refuse to let it fail.

The cost was real. The cost was yours—your career, your credentials, your clean hands and your institutional standing and the comfortable certainty that someone else would do the hard part while you wrote the assessment. In a world where someone always pays, you chose to pay with the only currency that mattered: showing up and doing the work.

Your hands are not clean anymore. They are scarred and calloused and stained with alchemical residue that has settled into the creases of your skin like a second set of lines, a second map, the permanent record of every circle drawn and every junction sealed and every wall held together by the stubborn insistence that buildings should not fall on people.

You hold them up to the morning light. They look like Elara's now. They look like they belong to someone who has done real work.

[ENDING: THE CRAFT]

Kaelen finds you in the back room of the Freehands safehouse, which is remarkable for two reasons. First, because the Freehands safehouse has a back room, which suggests a level of organizational infrastructure that your report will need to carefully not mention. Second, because Kaelen has cleaned up.

He is wearing a different shirt. This is the dock worker equivalent of arriving in formal evening wear. The burn scars on his forearms are visible below rolled sleeves, and his hands—the same hands that drew a Level 2 reinforcement circle on a forty-year-old crane with improvised paste—are folded carefully on the table in front of him, as though he has rehearsed this.

"The crew has been talking," he says. "They trust you."

He sits across from you. The lamplight catches the lines of his face, and you realize he looks tired in a way that has nothing to do with sleep.

"We have a plan for the seawall. Not a Scholar's plan—a workers' plan. Distributed repairs using the Freehands network, community labor, shared cost. The Red Harrow principle, applied to infrastructure." He watches your face while he says it, the way you watch a diagnostic plate for the moment it tells you something you don't want to know. "We need someone who can do the calculations. Someone the crew trusts. Someone who has seen the numbers and chose to stay anyway."

He means you. The Scholar who stayed. The field evaluator whose career trajectory now resembles the structural integrity of a Tier 1 bonding paste under repeated stress loads—technically viable, practically uncertain, and heading in a direction the original design did not anticipate.

"What do you say, Scholar?"
choice2_label: Ask about the risks.
choice3_label: Decline.

text:
"Risks?" Kaelen holds up a hand and begins counting on fingers that have clearly had a long professional relationship with heavy objects.

"Unauthorized structural work on critical infrastructure. CEA interference if anyone notices—and someone always notices. Running out of materials before we finish, which means we'd leave the seawall half-repaired, which is arguably worse than leaving it alone because a partially reinforced structure fails differently than an unreinforced one." He pauses. "Running out of people willing to work for free. Someone getting hurt because we're not professionals—except we are professionals, we've been doing this work for twenty years, we just don't have the paperwork."

He runs out of fingers on one hand and switches to the other.

"Oh, and there's a CEA inspection scheduled for next week. If they find unauthorized circle work on load-bearing infrastructure, everyone involved gets fined or arrested. Not fined and then arrested—one or the other, depending on whether the inspector has met quota for the month." He lowers his hand. "That's the real risk. Not the work. The work we can do. It's the part where we get caught doing it by the people who should have done it themselves."

The silence that follows is the silence of someone who has laid all his cards on a table that isn't very clean and is waiting to see if you'll sit down anyway.
choice2_label: Decline.

text:
The meeting takes place around a table in Brin's safehouse that was clearly designed for six people and is currently accommodating twelve through the aggressive application of optimism and folding chairs.

You recognize faces from your time in the district: Gerd, the pipe fixer whose improvised circle work held the tenement quarter's water supply together through sheer stubbornness. The woman who told the Red Harrow story at the docks, sitting with her arms crossed and the posture of someone who has earned her opinions through direct experience. Two young workers from the crane crew who look at Kaelen the way structural supports look at load-bearing walls—like he's the only thing keeping them upright.

Brin is there, arms crossed, standing against the far wall in the posture of someone who has hosted enough of these meetings to know exactly when things will go sideways and how long she can wait before intervening. She nods at you once. It is exactly one nod more than you expected.

Kaelen stands and presents the plan. He has drawn it on a piece of salvaged paper in the careful, slightly oversized handwriting of someone who learned to read late and has been making up for it ever since.

The plan is this: coordinate every available worker in the district for a continuous forty-eight-hour repair operation. Target the three critical failure points—the seawall, the water mains, the fishmarket retaining wall. Use the Freehands network for labor, materials, and communication. Run three shifts to keep fresh hands on the work at all times.

"Distributed cost," he says. "Everyone carries a piece. Nobody carries it alone."

The room is quiet. Not skeptical quiet—thinking quiet. The quiet of people calculating what they can afford to give.
choice2_label: Suggest improvements.
choice3_label: Observe silently.
choice4_label: This is beyond your assignment — walk away.

text:
You spread your diagnostic data across the table. The workers lean in—not because they can read alchemical notation, but because they can read the expression of someone who is trying to help and has useful information.

You explain the seawall's failure points using language stripped of academic abstraction: here is where it is weakest, here is where a repair will do the most good, here is the sequence that minimizes material waste and maximizes structural gain. You lay out the water system's vulnerabilities—the three joints where Tier 1 paste has been doing the work of Tier 2 reinforcement for months, slowly degrading under pressure it was never designed to hold. You calculate the material requirements, the fuel costs, the energy expenditure per shift.

For the first time all day, your calculations feel useful. Not as an abstract assessment that will sit in a filing cabinet while buildings fail, but as a tool that people can pick up and use. A bridge between knowing what's wrong and doing something about it.

Gerd studies the material estimates and whistles low through his teeth. "So we need this much material, this many circles, this many people, and someone who can draw reinforcement patterns that don't look like they were done by a dog with a piece of chalk?"

Everyone looks at you.

"My circles are adequate," you say, which is the Scholar's way of saying yes.

You study Kaelen's plan in silence for three minutes while the room watches you the way dock workers watch a crane under load—waiting to see if it holds.

Then you start making modifications. Priority ordering: seawall first, because its failure mode is catastrophic and immediate; water mains second, because the tenement quarter has been on reduced flow for six weeks and reduced flow becomes no flow faster than people expect; fishmarket wall third, because it is the most stable of the three and can wait another forty-eight hours without significant risk escalation.

You suggest material conservation techniques from your training—methods for extending Tier 1 bonding paste by mixing it with specific mineral compounds that increase adhesion without requiring additional fuel. You draft a schedule that accounts for worker fatigue, noting that circle work performed by exhausted hands is circle work that fails under stress, and that a rotating three-shift system with mandatory rest periods will produce better results than continuous labor.

Kaelen listens to every word. When you finish, he nods once—the nod of a man who has been carrying a plan and just felt someone else take part of the weight.

"That's what we needed," he says. "Someone who can see the whole system." He looks at the room. "We go tomorrow night. Scholar's plan, workers' hands."

You do not correct the attribution. It is a workers' plan. You just helped it stand up straighter.

You sit back and watch the meeting unfold. This is what you were trained to do—observe, assess, calculate. Old habits. Comfortable ones.

The workers debate. They argue about priorities, about resources, about who can spare the hours and who has family obligations that can't bend. A young woman from the crane crew says the fishmarket wall should come first because her grandmother lives behind it. Gerd says the water mains are more urgent because eighty families are on reduced flow. Brin says both of them are wrong and the seawall takes priority because when seawalls fail, everything behind them fails too.

Brin mediates with the patience of someone who has been resolving disputes since before most of this room was born. Kaelen leads by listening—an unusual quality in a foreman, the ability to hold space for disagreement without rushing toward resolution. When the argument loops, he restates both positions clearly and asks what they'd need to know to decide. It is, without anyone acknowledging it, a structured decision framework. The kind they teach in the second year at the Measured Scholars academy. Kaelen has never been inside the academy. He reinvented the method from the raw material of necessity.

It's democracy in its most physical form—people deciding together how to distribute the cost of fixing what someone else broke. Nobody appoints a leader. Nobody files a motion. Nobody invokes parliamentary procedure or regulatory precedent. They just figure it out.

You make notes in your ledger. Not for the report. For yourself.

Materials. The eternal problem. You can have all the skilled hands and good intentions in the world, but without bonding paste and fuel blocks, intention is just a word for what you wanted to do before reality intervened.

The Freehands network has enough Tier 1 material stockpiled for the water main repairs—Brin's people have been quietly accumulating supplies for months, a crate here, a salvaged pallet there, the slow patient work of people who have learned that official supply lines don't reach this far down. The fishmarket wall can be covered by Brin's salvage operation, which has been pulling reusable bonding material from decommissioned structures across the district.

But the seawall. The seawall needs Tier 2 materials—reinforcement paste rated for sustained structural loads, the kind that doesn't degrade under repeated stress cycles. The kind that hasn't existed in this district since the CEA redirected the maintenance allocation seven months ago.

Kaelen leans forward. "The CEA staging area at the district boundary. They've still got crates of our rerouted maintenance materials sitting there, waiting for transport upriver. Fourteen crates, last I counted. Tier 2 paste, fuel blocks, bonding agents—everything we need for the seawall."

He looks at you steadily.

"It's our material. They took it from our allocation. We're taking it back."

The room is quiet. This is the part of the plan that leaves fingerprints.
choice2_label: Suggest buying black-market materials instead.
choice3_label: Find another way.

text:
The night operation at the CEA staging area begins at 0200 and moves with the precise, wordless efficiency of people who spend their lives loading and unloading crates—just in the other direction this time.

Kaelen's crew knows the staging area layout because they built most of it. They know which gates stick, which sight lines are blind spots, which section of the perimeter fence has been quietly unfixed since a storm took it down three months ago and the repair requisition got lost somewhere between filing and caring. You provide the technical assessment: reading crate markings, identifying which containers hold the Tier 2 paste and which are bulk filler material that would waste their limited transport capacity.

Two hours. Fourteen crates. Enough Tier 2 bonding material for the seawall repairs and then some.

The crates are distributed through the Freehands network before dawn—broken into smaller loads, moved through the district's informal channels, stored in basements and back rooms across Karet Bay. By the time the CEA's morning shift notices the inventory discrepancy, the material has ceased to exist as a line item and become part of the district.

"That," says someone on the crew as the last crate disappears into the network, "was the most productive theft I've ever been part of."

You don't correct the word "theft." The paperwork says the materials were allocated to this district. The paperwork is, for once, not wrong.

The black market operates out of a series of connected basements in the warehouse district, distinguished from legitimate business primarily by the absence of anyone who would admit to being in charge and the presence of several people who look like they would prefer you hadn't come.

The materials available are Tier 1—workable but not ideal for sustained seawall reinforcement. They'll hold under normal conditions. Under sustained storm stress or heavy tidal load, they will begin to degrade. It is a compromise. All available options, at this point, are compromises.

The cost is steep. Brin negotiates with the calm, unflinching patience of someone who has been buying and selling in these basements since before the current proprietor was born. The seller—a thin man with nervous hands and a surprisingly sophisticated understanding of bonding paste chemistry—looks at your Scholar insignia and doubles the price.

Brin looks at the seller.

The expression on her face is difficult to describe in language suitable for official documentation. It contains elements of disappointment, professional evaluation, and the quiet certainty of someone who has three decades of salvage network contacts and an encyclopedic memory for who owes what to whom.

She says something that is not fit for a chronicle, a scholarly record, or the delicate constitution of anyone who has not spent significant time in the company of dock workers.

The price returns to normal.

You pay from the crew's pooled funds. The materials are loaded and moved before the seller can reconsider his life choices.

You suggest a third option. Using the diagnostic plate data from your assessment, you can identify which existing structures in the district have material reserves that can be safely redistributed—walls that were over-reinforced in previous repair cycles, decommissioned infrastructure whose bonding material is still viable, structures scheduled for demolition whose Tier 2 components can be extracted and repurposed.

It is, you explain, a calculated redistribution. Not theft. Not black market procurement. A systematic reallocation of existing resources based on structural priority analysis. The seawall gets what it needs. The donor structures lose material they can afford to lose. The numbers work. You've checked them twice.

Kaelen is skeptical. "Your way is slower. We'd need two extra days to extract and prepare the material."

"But it's legal. Or close enough. If we get caught with CEA crates, the whole operation stops before it starts. If we get caught redistributing existing district materials based on a Scholar's structural assessment, that's—" You search for the right word. "That's a filing irregularity."

"A filing irregularity," Kaelen repeats, the way someone repeats a phrase in a foreign language they don't entirely trust.

"At worst."

He looks at the crew. The crew looks at him. Someone shrugs.

"Your way, Scholar. Slower. Careful. Very Scholar of you." There is, surprisingly, no contempt in this. If anything, it sounds like respect wearing unfamiliar clothes.

The first repair: the water mains in the tenement quarter.

Twenty workers organized into teams by Brin, directed by your calculations, fueled by a combination of pooled Tier 1 blocks and something that might be determination or might be stubbornness but is functionally indistinguishable from either. You draw the reinforcement circles yourself—clean lines, proper geometry, the circles your instructors would have approved of applied to infrastructure your instructors would have pretended didn't exist.

The work is physical, communal, and exhausting. Your hands ache. Your personal energy reserves are dropping and you can feel it in the way the chalk wants to waver, the way precision becomes a thing you have to fight for instead of a thing that comes naturally. Kaelen works beside you, and when your hand shakes on a critical line, he steadies your arm without comment—one worker helping another.

When the last circle activates and the water system pressurizes for the first time in six weeks, there is a sound from inside the building. A pipe groaning back to life. Then water running. Clean water, flowing through repaired mains into homes that have been carrying it up three flights of stairs in buckets.

A woman on the second floor opens her window and applauds.

One person clapping. Slowly. Then another window opens. Then another. The sound of people who have been waiting for this, who had stopped believing it would come, watching it arrive anyway.

You stand in the street below with chalk on your hands and plaster dust in your hair, and for the first time in your career, the math feels like it was worth doing.
choice2_label: Take a rest.

text:
Tea. Bread. Five minutes of sitting still on an overturned crate behind the tenement building while the crew rotates shifts around you.

Kaelen sits down next to you with the controlled descent of someone whose knees have opinions about the last six hours. He accepts tea from a woman you don't recognize—another Freehands member, materializing from the network the way they do, carrying supplies that don't appear in any inventory.

"You're not what I expected from a Scholar," he says, staring at the street.

"What did you expect?"

"Someone who watched."

You look down at your hands. They are covered in chalk dust, bonding paste residue, and honest dirt—the grime of physical work performed in poor conditions with inadequate tools. There is a blister forming on your right palm where the stress gauge rubbed during the mains repair. Your fingernails are cracked. The callus that is beginning to form on your index finger is in the same place you've seen it on every dock worker you've met today.

They don't look like a Scholar's hands anymore.

You're not sure they should.

The problem arrives the way problems always arrive in Karet Bay—wearing institutional authority and terrible timing.

The CEA inspection has been moved up. Tomorrow. Not next week, as the published schedule indicated—tomorrow, first thing, a full structural compliance audit of the lower dock district with particular attention to unauthorized circle work on load-bearing infrastructure. Someone tipped them off. Someone always tips them off.

Brin delivers the news with the flat expression of a woman who has been evading institutional attention for thirty years and recognizes the sound of a net closing.

"Full inspection team. Three auditors, two enforcement officers. They'll check every load-bearing surface in the district." She pauses. "Including the ones we just fixed."

The math is immediate and unforgiving. The water mains you repaired are covered in fresh circle work—your circle work, drawn with precision that will immediately identify it as trained Scholars' work performed without authorization. The bonding paste is new. The fuel residue is fresh. An auditor with functioning eyes will see it in thirty seconds. An auditor without functioning eyes will trip over it.

Kaelen looks at you. His face has the expression of a man standing at a junction where all available paths lead somewhere difficult.

"If we stop now, the water mains hold. That's something. But the seawall doesn't get fixed, and next storm season, everything behind it is at risk." He glances at the crew. "If we keep going, we have to deal with the inspection. One way or another."
choice2_label: Stop the operation and go official.

text:
You could stop. Walk away from this table, this safehouse, these people, and go back to being a Scholar. File the report. Submit the assessment. Let the system grind through its processes—the forms, the committees, the quarterly reviews—and eventually, in its own time, in its own way, produce an outcome that arrives three months after the buildings it was meant to save have already fallen down.

The water mains are fixed. That's something. That's more than anyone expected from a junior field evaluator sent down to check a crane.

The seawall still needs work. But that's someone else's problem now. Except it isn't. You know the numbers. You drew the diagnostic yourself. You can see the failure cascade in your mind as clearly as you can see the people sitting around this table—the sequence of structural collapses that begins with the seawall and ends with the tenement quarter's foundations failing under tidal stress loads they were never designed to absorb.

Someone else's problem is a phrase that contains a hidden cost, and you have spent all day learning to see hidden costs.

Kaelen looks at you without judgment. Without pressure. Without the expression of someone trying to convince you of anything. Just the steady gaze of a man who has made his choice and is waiting to see if you'll make yours.

"Nobody's making you stay," he says. "Nobody would blame you for walking. You've already done more than any Scholar who ever came down here."

He means it. That's the worst part.
choice2_label: Leave.

text:
You pull out your Scholar's authorization seal and your institutional access ledger. Your hands are very steady—the steadiness of someone who has made a decision and is watching themselves make it from a slight distance, the way you'd watch a structural element reach its load limit.

You file a procedural delay request for the CEA inspection, citing "ongoing assessment requiring undisturbed site conditions per Scholars' Protocol 7, subsection 3: field evaluator discretionary hold." It is a real protocol. It does grant field evaluators the authority to delay institutional interference with active assessment sites. It was designed for situations where an inspector's presence might disturb delicate diagnostic readings.

It was not designed for this.

The request buys seventy-two hours. Three days. Enough time to finish the seawall if the crew works continuous shifts. It is also a fraudulent use of institutional authority, filed under your name, with your seal, attached to your credentials. When Toris finds out—not if, when—your career in the Measured Scholars is over. Not damaged. Not set back. Over.

Kaelen watches you file the request. He says nothing until the seal is pressed and the document is sealed.

"That's one of those things you can't un-do."

"I know."

"Welcome to the crew, Scholar."

The title means something different now.

The seawall repair operation begins at dusk and does not stop.

Forty workers. Three shifts. Kaelen commanding the crews with the same focused intensity he brought to Crane Seven—the attention of a man who understands that the cost of failure isn't abstract, it's the people standing next to him. Brin coordinating the material supply through the Freehands network, crates appearing from basements and back rooms across the district like a supply chain that exists only in the minds of people who trust each other. You directing the circle work, drawing reinforcement patterns on ancient stone by lamplight, your chalk lines cleaner and faster than anything you produced in the academy—because in the academy you were drawing for grades, and here you are drawing so that buildings don't fall on people.

The whole district is working together in the dark. Neighbors carrying supplies to workers they've never met. An old woman on the fishmarket street boiling tea in industrial quantities and passing cups to anyone whose hands are free. A child running messages between work sites with the speed and navigational confidence of someone who has spent their entire life in these streets and knows every shortcut, every low wall, every gap in every fence.

It is the most beautiful thing you have seen in Karet Bay. Not beautiful in the way the upper city is beautiful—designed, maintained, paid for. Beautiful in the way a load-bearing structure is beautiful when you understand what it's holding up.
choice2_label: Try to cover everything.

text:
The workers trust you completely. When you call for a shift change, they change. When you redirect resources from the fishmarket wall to the seawall's critical southern section, they follow without hesitation—not because you're a Scholar, not because of your credentials or your seal or the authority that comes with institutional backing. Because you are standing in the dark with chalk dust on your hands doing the same work they are doing, and they have decided you are one of them.

The critical section of the seawall—the fifty-meter stretch where your diagnostic readings showed Tier 0 bonding paste holding back tidal forces it was never rated for—receives proper Tier 2 reinforcement for the first time in seven months. You draw the circles yourself, the most important work you have ever done, while Kaelen holds the lamp and Gerd mixes the paste and a young woman from the crane crew passes you tools with the quiet efficiency of someone who has found her place in a system that works.

By dawn, the wall holds. Not perfectly—the northern section still needs another two days of work, and the junction points between old and new material will need monitoring through the next tidal cycle. Not permanently—nothing is permanent, that's the first thing they teach you about structural engineering, everything is just time and maintenance and the willingness to keep showing up.

But enough. The bay pushes against the repaired section and the section pushes back. The forces balance. The math resolves.

Forty workers stand on the dock and watch the sunrise hit a wall that isn't falling down.

Nobody says anything. There isn't anything to say that the wall isn't already saying.

Not enough trust. Not enough coordination. The operation is spreading too thin, pulled in three directions by three critical failures that each demand full attention and can't all have it.

Workers are exhausted—running on their third shift without adequate rest, their circle work getting sloppy, their hands shaking on the tools the way yours shook on the water main repair before Kaelen steadied your arm. But there are too many arms to steady now and not enough hours in which to steady them. Arguments break out about priorities: the seawall crew wants more material, the water main team says they're not finished, someone at the fishmarket wall is shouting that the entire southern section is delaminating and nobody is listening.

You try to hold it together with calculations. Reallocation formulas, priority matrices, resource optimization models—the analytical tools that got you through the academy and got you this assignment and have been, until this moment, sufficient. But calculations need people to execute them, and people need to trust the person doing the calculations, and trust is the one resource you cannot generate by working harder.

Kaelen is shouting—not at anyone, at the situation, at the gap between what they planned and what is happening. Brin is pulling workers off the seawall to handle a water main emergency because water is immediate and seawalls are eventual, and the logic is sound but the cost is the seawall section you spent all night reinforcing, now undermanned and under-supplied.

The operation is failing. Not catastrophically—not yet—but in the slow, grinding way that infrastructure fails. One compromise at a time. One resource too few. One hour too late.
choice1_label: Cut your losses and secure what you have.
choice2_label: Push through.

text:
The CEA arrives before dawn.

Three enforcement vehicles. Armed officers with authorization-revocation seals and the particular expression of people who have been sent to make an example. Someone called them—not the scheduled inspection, not your delayed audit, but someone else entirely, someone who saw forty workers doing unauthorized structural work in the dark and decided that what was happening was not community repair but criminal activity.

The operation collapses. Workers scatter into the Freehands network—the same network that organized them now providing escape routes through basements, back alleys, and doors that weren't there yesterday. But not everyone makes it. Kaelen is arrested at the seawall, his hands still covered in bonding paste, caught in the act of reinforcement like it's something to be ashamed of. Brin disappears so completely that you are not certain she was ever standing next to you, which is both impressive and deeply unsettling.

You are detained at the staging area with your Scholar credentials voided on the spot and your procedural delay request—your fraudulent, career-ending, seventy-two-hour delay request—presented as evidence of institutional conspiracy to undermine CEA enforcement authority.

The seawall section you reinforced holds. You can see it from the enforcement vehicle's window, standing against the morning tide like a promise someone kept. The sections you didn't reach—the northern stretch, the junction points, the areas where workers were pulled away to handle the water main crisis—won't. The next storm will tell you exactly how much of the cost you failed to carry.

In the interrogation room, under institutional light that makes everything look like evidence, you think about Mireth's briefing. Don't get creative down there. She was right. You got creative. The cost was everyone else's freedom.

[GAME OVER — THE LINE BREAKS]

Dawn breaks over Karet Bay and the seawall holds—the one you drew for, the one yesterday's numbers said would go first.

There is more to do before anyone calls the district's maintenance honest—ledger lines to reconcile, stretches still waiting their turn—but the failures you measured as hours away are held in check for now. The fifty meters of southern wall that your diagnostics flagged as catastrophic risk, the water main junctions that had been held together by optimism and Tier 0 paste, the fishmarket retaining wall that Gerd's crew reinforced with the focused determination of people who refuse to let a building fall on a fish—solid. Reinforced. Functional.

Forty workers did in three days what the CEA failed to do in seven months. The math on that is uncomfortable for everyone who approved the maintenance budget reallocation, and you intend to make sure the math is published.

Your Scholar credentials are struck from the active registry before the next seal-setting posts—fast enough that the wax might still be warm when the notice reaches you. The formal notification arrives at Brin's safehouse, which is now your mailing address, which says something about how quickly your life has rearranged itself around new load-bearing structures. Toris files a formal complaint so detailed it has appendices. The Revolutionary Council opens an investigation—into Toris, not you, because the district's elected delegate, who was not awake for the repair operation but woke up to find six thousand constituents very enthusiastic about it, decided that popular support was a form of authorization the CEA couldn't override. The argument is improvised law, thin on precedent and heavy on receipts, and it holds. It will be cited in future case law by people who have no idea it was hammered out before the fifth bell by a woman who had been trading salvage in basement markets since before the current council was elected.

Kaelen offers you a position on the dock crew.

"It pays worse than being a Scholar," he says. "Hours are longer. The work wrecks your body. There's no pension, no institutional housing, and nobody will ever ask you to write a twenty-page report about the structural integrity of someone else's suffering."

You take it.

Brin's network absorbs you the way the district absorbs everything—slowly, practically, without ceremony. You learn to do circle work without diagnostic plates, drawing by feel and experience instead of measurement, the way Kaelen's father must have drawn when he reinforced the seawall the first time. Your hands develop calluses in the places where tools rest and chalk wears skin. They look like the hands of someone who has done real work, and when you look at them, you understand for the first time what the cost actually means—not the calculation of it, not the abstract mathematics of structural load distribution, but the simple, physical knowledge that what you built will hold.

The cost was real. The cost was shared. In a world where someone always pays—sometimes the line holds because everyone holds it together.

[ENDING: THE LINE]

Dawn comes up tired over Karet Bay. The seawall does not look like a triumph. It looks like work stopped mid-sentence.

What you locked in before the operation frayed—the lengths you drew for, the spans where crews actually got stone and paste into place before trust split and bodies peeled away—still take the morning tide. The rest stays in the numbers you already read: northern runs, junctions you never reached, stretches where three different urgencies pulled the same hands in three directions. The next storm will not forgive the gaps. It will only measure them.

Your Scholar credentials are struck from the active registry before the next seal-setting posts. The formal line reaches you at Brin's safehouse, which is your mailing address now, which tells you how fast load-bearing things can rearrange. Toris files a complaint thorough enough to need its own table of contents. The Revolutionary Council opens proceedings—who gets named depends on which faction's voice carries this week, and the arguments sound less like law than like people improvising authority after a night no ledger predicted. None of that hands you your old title back. Enough of it keeps you from vanishing entirely.

Kaelen still offers you a place on the dock crew.

'It pays worse than being a Scholar,' he says. 'Hours are longer. The work eats your shoulders. No pension, no institutional roof, and nobody will thank you for a twenty-page assessment of why someone else's corner of the world is cracking.'

You take it.

Brin's network folds you in the way the district folds in anyone useful—no speech, just shared shifts, borrowed chalk, circle work done by feel when plates are not an option. Your hands roughen where tools rest; the wear means something different than equations on vellum. The cost was real, and unevenly paid. What held did not hold because the story stayed clean. It held because enough people chose the line before they chose the alibi.

[ENDING: THE LINE]

The night market hums with its usual commerce of things that aren't strictly supposed to be sold. You're navigating between a stall hawking "medicinal" fuel distillates and one offering clearly stolen diagnostic plates when someone falls into step beside you.

No hood this time. You can see their face—mid-twenties, sharp features, the kind of bone structure that looks designed for arguments and has probably won most of them. Burn scars run along both forearms, the distinctive patterning of alchemical feedback. Self-fueled work. The kind that costs you something personal.

"You've seen the numbers," Ash says. Not a greeting. Not a question. The pamphleteer apparently considers social preamble a form of institutional delay. "The institution won't fix this because the institution IS this. Every day you wait for proper channels, more material flows upriver and the seawall gets closer to failing."

They stop walking. The market noise folds around you like a privacy screen.

"I have a plan. Three CEA material transfer points—the staging area, the pumping station, the distribution office. We disrupt them. Force the materials to stay in the district." Ash's voice is calm, precise, the tone of someone presenting a field report rather than a conspiracy. "Not permanently. Just long enough for the right people to notice."

You stand in the middle of a night market being recruited for infrastructure sabotage by someone who buys pamphlet ink in bulk. The republic's institutional framework did not prepare you for this particular scenario.
choice2_label: Ask who the "right people" are.
choice3_label: Decline.

text:
"The transit rail project has three sponsors on the Revolutionary Council." Ash ticks them off on scarred fingers. "Alderman Dresser. Committee Chair Valis. Deputy Secretary Moune. Between them, they've invested enough political capital in that railway to build a second one."

They lean against a market post. The casual posture of someone who has rehearsed being casual.

"If the material flow stops, they lose money. If they lose money, they start asking questions about why a junior field evaluator's crane assessment led to a logistics disruption that stalled their pet project. The disruption becomes an investigation. The investigation finds what you found." Ash lets that sit. "The redirected allocations. The starved districts. The seawall maintenance that exists on paper and nowhere else."

They smile. It's not a pleasant smile. It's the smile of someone who has run the numbers on justice and found the answer comes with a cost.

"The system responds to cost. So we give the system a cost it can't ignore."
choice2_label: Decline.

text:
The plan is precise. Three transfer points, three disruptions, executed across a narrow window of opportunity.

Ash produces a folded sheaf of diagrams from inside their coat—hand-drawn, meticulous, annotated in a notation system you recognize immediately. Academy standard. Whoever drew these understands infrastructure alchemy at a professional level, the kind that takes years of formal training and a particular obsession with flow dynamics.

"Point One: the warehouse staging area." A glance that suggests they know exactly what you've been investigating. "Point Two: pumping station seven—regulates material flow through the underground conduit network. Point Three: the CEA distribution office where Toris's people assign the allocations."

Each diagram details the target's alchemical architecture: circle configurations, flow directions, structural dependencies. The level of preparation is either reassuring or alarming, depending on how you feel about well-organized criminals.

"Each one requires a different approach. Each one is reversible—we're disrupting, not destroying." Ash folds the last diagram with care. "The materials won't be damaged. They'll just be redirected. Back to where they were supposed to go."

The word "redirected" does a lot of work in that sentence. It is doing the work of about six more honest words, several of which would include "crime."
choice2_label: Decline.

text:
Ash was a Scholar. The admission comes out flat, like a structural assessment.

"Two years at the Academy. Field theory, infrastructure assessment, applied exchange mathematics." No false modesty. No pride. The recitation of a credential that no longer applies. "I saw three excellent reports filed about three different districts. All accurate. All properly formatted. All submitted through the correct channels."

They hold up three fingers and fold them down one at a time.

"All ignored. The third district had a building collapse eight months after the report was filed. Seven people died. My report predicted it—not the collapse specifically, but the structural degradation that made it inevitable. The math was right there. In the margins. Next to the official stamp that said someone had read it."

The burn scars. You've been trying not to stare at them.

"Self-fueled alchemy." Ash follows your gaze. "Emergency structural support during the collapse. I held a wall up for forty minutes while everyone got out. Forty minutes of channeling your own body's reserves into circle work that was never designed for flesh." They flex their fingers. The scars pull tight. "It's not a technique they teach at the Academy. It's a technique you discover when seven people are about to die and you're the only one in the room who understands load distribution."

A pause. The night market fills the silence with the commerce of people who have learned to solve problems outside of official channels.

"The Academy gave me a commendation. The district got a new budget review. The next year, the budget was cut again." Ash looks at you with an expression that is not anger. It is the thing that comes after anger, when the anger has been measured and found insufficient. "I didn't quit because the system was broken. I quit because the system was working exactly as designed."
choice2_label: Decline.

text:
Phase one: intelligence gathering. You and Ash scope the three transfer points over two nights with the methodical patience of people who have been trained to assess infrastructure. One currently credentialed. One formerly. The irony is structural.

Point One: the warehouse staging area. Rows of supply crates, CEA logistics staff, a security rotation that runs with the precision of someone in middle management being genuinely competent at their job. You may have been here before. If so, the familiarity has a different weight now.

Point Two: pumping station seven. Underground, accessible through maintenance tunnels beneath the warehouse district. The station regulates material flow through a network of conduits—alchemical arteries that should be feeding the district but have been rerouted to serve the transit rail project instead.

Point Three: the CEA distribution office. Where the numbers live. Where allocations are assigned, transfers authorized, and the paperwork that makes redirection look like policy is generated in triplicate and filed with institutional confidence.

Each target requires a different approach. Each carries its own particular flavor of professional risk. You find yourself thinking of this in assessment terms—threat vectors, structural vulnerabilities, load-bearing assumptions. The Scholar's toolkit, applied to the Scholar's opposite.
choice2_label: Start with the pumping station.
choice3_label: Start with the distribution office.

text:
